conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is bronchiectasis, and what is its consequence?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Permanent, irreversible dilatation of bronchi → impaired secretion clearance → recurrent infection and inflammation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How does bronchiectasis differ from COPD and asthma in its defining abnormality?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Unlike COPD (obstruction) or asthma (reversible narrowing), bronchiectasis is defined by dilated, mucus-pooling airways.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What concept ('the spine') explains everything in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: The vicious cycle — it explains why sputum is copious, why it progresses, and why management targets clearance and infection.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What are the steps of the vicious cycle in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Bronchial injury (infection, inflammation) → airway + elastin damage (neutrophil elastase destroys wall) → permanent dilatation (irreversible bronchial widening) → impaired mucociliary clearance (mucus pools in dilated airways) → recurrent infection (bacteria colonise static mucus) → back to start.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What causes the airway and elastin damage step of the vicious cycle?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Neutrophil elastase destroys the airway wall.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Besides wall damage, what else does neutrophil elastase drive, and what does it explain?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Mucus hypersecretion — explaining the copious, purulent sputum. Management targets both arms: break the cycle by clearing mucus and treating infection.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the most common cause of bronchiectasis, and what should always be asked about?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Post-infectious — childhood pneumonia, whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis), TB. Always ask about recurrent childhood LRTIs.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the key genetic cause of bronchiectasis, and its features?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Cystic fibrosis — bilateral, upper lobe predominance, Pseudomonas colonisation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Besides post-infectious and CF, what are other common causes of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: COPD (frequent coexistence); idiopathic (~50% in adults).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is Kartagener's syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Bronchiectasis + situs inversus + sinusitis — caused by primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia). The ciliary defect is the mechanism, not one of the three components.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is ABPA, and how does it cause bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Which immunodeficiency-related causes of bronchiectasis should be considered, and what is checked?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Immunodeficiency — HIV, hypogammaglobulinaemia (check Ig levels).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How can obstruction cause bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Foreign body, enlarged TB lymph nodes (e.g. in children).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the cardinal symptom of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Chronic cough + copious purulent sputum.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What are the symptoms of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Chronic cough + copious purulent sputum (cardinal feature); recurrent chest infections; haemoptysis (can be massive and life-threatening, from an eroded bronchial artery); progressive breathlessness, wheeze, fatigue.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Why can haemoptysis be massive and life-threatening in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: From an eroded bronchial artery.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What are the examination findings in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Coarse crackles — typically at the bases (or wherever disease is located); clubbing (chronic suppurative lung disease); wheeze (from airway oedema); signs of cor pulmonale in advanced disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for bronchiectasis, and its key signs?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: HRCT chest. Signet ring sign: airway lumen wider than its accompanying artery. Bronchial wall thickening, lack of airway tapering, mucus plugging, cysts.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the signet ring sign on HRCT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: The airway lumen is wider than its accompanying artery.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What might CXR show in bronchiectasis, and what is its limitation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: May be normal or show 'tramtrack' lines (thickened parallel bronchial walls). Insensitive — HRCT is always needed to confirm.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the role of sputum MC&S in bronchiectasis, and the common organisms?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Essential in exacerbation. Common organisms: H. influenzae (commonest), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (persistent green sputum), S. aureus.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Which is the commonest organism in bronchiectasis, and which causes persistent green sputum?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: H. influenzae is commonest; Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes persistent green sputum.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What cause workup investigations are done in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Immunoglobulins (hypogammaglobulinaemia); sweat test (CF); Aspergillus serology/IgE (ABPA); nasal ciliary biopsy (Kartagener's).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the mainstay of management for bronchiectasis (mucus arm), and what does it include?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Airway clearance — chest physiotherapy (active cycle of breathing technique [ACBT], postural drainage); oscillatory PEP devices (Flutter/Acapella — vibration loosens mucus); mucolytics (hypertonic saline nebulisation); done regular and daily, not just during exacerbations.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How is infection treated/prevented in bronchiectasis (infection arm)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Prompt antibiotics for exacerbations (increased cough, sputum volume, purulence); S. aureus → flucloxacillin; persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → oral ciprofloxacin first-line (IV dual anti-pseudomonal therapy if severe or ciprofloxacin fails); prophylactic azithromycin (≥3 exacerbations/year) — check ECG (QT) + LFTs, and exclude non-tuberculous mycobacteria (macrolide monotherapy risks NTM resistance), first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How is a Pseudomonas exacerbation (persistent green sputum) treated in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Oral ciprofloxacin first-line; IV dual anti-pseudomonal therapy if severe or ciprofloxacin fails.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: When is prophylactic azithromycin used in bronchiectasis, and what must be checked first?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: For ≥3 exacerbations/year — check ECG (QT) + LFTs, and exclude non-tuberculous mycobacteria, first (macrolide monotherapy in undiagnosed NTM breeds resistance).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What supportive/other management measures apply in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Smoking cessation; flu + pneumococcal vaccines; bronchodilators if dyspnoeic; treat underlying cause (CF, ABPA, immunodeficiency); surgery — localised resectable disease or end-stage transplant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What are the complications of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Massive haemoptysis (life-threatening); pneumonia, empyema; pneumothorax; respiratory failure; cor pulmonale; metastatic abscess (e.g. cerebral); non-TB mycobacteria colonisation; Aspergillus colonisation / ABPA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the gold standard for bronchiectasis and its signs?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: HRCT = gold standard; signs = signet ring (dilated airway > artery) + tramtracks (CXR).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the cardinal feature of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Copious purulent sputum + chronic cough + clubbing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the commonest cause and the key genetic cause of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Commonest cause = post-infectious (ask about childhood LRTIs); CF the key genetic cause.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the commonest organism, and how is persistent green sputum managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Commonest organism = H. influenzae; persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → oral ciprofloxacin first-line (IV dual anti-pseudomonal therapy if severe or if ciprofloxacin fails).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: define Kartagener's and ABPA.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Kartagener's = bronchiectasis + situs inversus + sinusitis (caused by primary ciliary dyskinesia); ABPA = asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the mainstay of management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Airway clearance physio + treat infection (break the vicious cycle).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: when is azithromycin prophylaxis used and what is checked first?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Azithromycin prophylaxis if ≥3 exacerbations/yr — check QT + LFTs and exclude non-tuberculous mycobacteria first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Exam pearl: what is the key danger of haemoptysis in bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Haemoptysis can be massive and life-threatening.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the key management pillars of bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: (1) Postural drainage/physiotherapy; (2) treat acute exacerbations (antibiotics); (3) long-term prophylactic azithromycin in frequent exacerbators; (4) treat underlying cause; (5) consider inhaled antibiotics (tobramycin/colistin in Pseudomonas).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the definition of a bronchiectasis exacerbation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Worsening of 3 or more symptoms for >48 hours: dyspnoea, cough, sputum volume/purulence, haemoptysis, fatigue/malaise — requires antibiotic treatment (targeted to the chronic colonising organism).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: EXAM PEARL: What HRCT finding confirms bronchiectasis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Bronchial lumen diameter greater than adjacent pulmonary artery ('signet ring sign') + lack of bronchial tapering + visualisation of bronchi within 1 cm of pleura — seen on HRCT chest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: In a bronchiectasis exacerbation, what must be done before the first dose of antibiotic — and do you wait for the result?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Send sputum for MC&S BEFORE starting — but do NOT wait for it. Start empirically straight away, choosing the drug from previous culture results, then modify once sensitivities return.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How long is a course of antibiotics for an acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis, and how does that differ from community-acquired pneumonia?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: 14 days (BTS expert consensus) — not the 5-day course used for CAP. Always 14 days if the patient is P. aeruginosa-infected; 7–10 days only in mild disease with a rapid response.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is the empirical first-line oral antibiotic for a bronchiectasis exacerbation, and the alternative in penicillin allergy?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Amoxicillin — it covers H. influenzae, the commonest organism. Doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Then organism-directed: S. aureus → flucloxacillin; Pseudomonas aeruginosa → ciprofloxacin.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How is a FIRST isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Attempt eradication: systemic antibiotics (typically oral ciprofloxacin) for 2 weeks, followed by inhaled antibiotics for 3 months. Consultant-initiated — a first isolate is a reason to act, not to observe.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: How is CHRONIC Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in bronchiectasis managed, and at what threshold?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: It cannot be eradicated, so it is suppressed: long-term nebulised antibiotics if there are ≥3 exacerbations/year, chosen and started by the specialist respiratory team rather than in primary care. The same ≥3 exacerbations/year threshold triggers azithromycin prophylaxis in those without chronic Pseudomonas.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: Who teaches airway clearance in bronchiectasis, and when is pulmonary rehabilitation offered?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: A respiratory physiotherapist assesses, teaches and reviews the technique (ACBT, postural drainage, oscillatory PEP device) — it is a trained daily skill. Pulmonary rehabilitation is offered if MRC dyspnoea grade ≥2 (functionally disabling breathlessness).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.front: What is monitored at bronchiectasis follow-up, and what should prompt referral to secondary care?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis.back: Monitor symptoms and exacerbation frequency, sputum culture, and spirometry (usually obstructive — it tracks decline; HRCT makes the diagnosis). Refer for frequent exacerbations, a new Pseudomonas isolation, or when long-term antibiotics are being considered — all consultant-initiated.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Define interstitial lung disease (ILD).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Diseases causing inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium → impaired gas exchange.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the unifying functional signature on spirometry across all ILDs?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Restrictive spirometry — FEV1/FVC normal or ↑ (FVC falls proportionally more than FEV1), ↓FVC, ↓TLCO.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In ILD, why is the FEV1/FVC ratio normal or raised despite the disease?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Because FVC falls proportionally more than FEV1 (restrictive pattern), so the ratio is preserved or increased.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the two organising anchors used to structure ILD?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Zone of fibrosis (upper vs lower) and a per-condition template (features → Ix → Mx).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: List the clinical features common to most ILDs.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, fine inspiratory crackles, restrictive PFTs (↓FVC, FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓TLCO), and HRCT as the key diagnostic investigation. Clubbing is characteristic of fibrotic ILD (IPF, asbestosis, CTD-ILD) but is typically absent in sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key diagnostic investigation for ILD?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: HRCT.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Why is the zone of fibrosis described as the single most-tested object in ILD?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Anchoring the zone of fibrosis on CXR / HRCT early narrows the differential immediately.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What mnemonic captures the UPPER zone causes of fibrosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: CHARTS — Coal worker's pneumoconiosis, Hypersensitivity pneumonitis / Histiocytosis, Ankylosing spondylitis, Radiation fibrosis, Tuberculosis, Silicosis / Sarcoidosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic for upper-zone fibrosis, what does 'C' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic, what does 'H' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis / Histiocytosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic, what does 'A' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic, what does 'R' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Radiation fibrosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic, what does 'T' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Tuberculosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In the CHARTS mnemonic, what does 'S' stand for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Silicosis / Sarcoidosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which ILD is the classic LOWER-zone cause headed by idiopathic disease?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which connective tissue disorders cause lower-zone fibrosis, and which is the exception?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: RA, systemic sclerosis and SLE cause lower-zone fibrosis; ankylosing spondylitis (a spondyloarthropathy, often grouped with them) is the upper-zone exception.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which drugs cause lower-zone pulmonary fibrosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the 'ABM' drug mnemonic for lower-zone fibrosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Amiodarone, Bleomycin, Methotrexate.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which occupational exposure causes lower-zone fibrosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Asbestosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the HP exception to the zonal classification?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is upper/mid zone in the chronic phase — it sits in CHARTS but fibrosis can be mid-zone.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Why is ankylosing spondylitis the odd-one-out among conditions grouped with connective tissue disorders in ILD?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: It causes upper-zone fibrosis, unlike the true CTDs (RA, SSc, SLE) which are lower-zone; AS is actually a spondyloarthropathy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Summarise the unifying PFT pattern of all ILD (exam pearl).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: All ILD = restrictive: FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓FVC, ↓TLCO — and HRCT is the key investigation for all.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which conditions make up the upper-zone (CHARTS) group?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis, HP/Histiocytosis, Ankylosing spondylitis, Radiation, TB, Silicosis/Sarcoidosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which conditions make up the lower-zone group, and what is the exception?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: IPF, connective tissue disorders, drugs (ABM), asbestosis — exception: AS (a spondyloarthropathy, not a true CTD) is upper-zone.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Describe the classic clinical and treatment picture of IPF.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Honeycombing + bibasal crackles + clubbing; antifibrotics (pirfenidone / nintedanib); poor prognosis ~3–4 years.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What antifibrotic drugs are used in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Pirfenidone and nintedanib.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the prognosis of IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Poor — roughly 3–4 years.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the characteristic BAL and treatment features of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Organic antigen → BAL lymphocytosis, NO eosinophilia; treat by avoiding the antigen + steroids.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the features and treatment of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Asthma/CF + Aspergillus → eosinophilia + ↑IgE + proximal bronchiectasis; treat with steroids → itraconazole.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key distinguishing contrast between HP and ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Eosinophilia + ↑IgE = ABPA, not HP — HP has BAL lymphocytosis with no eosinophilia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which drugs cause drug-induced fibrosis in the lower zone?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Amiodarone, Bleomycin, Methotrexate ('ABM') + nitrofurantoin.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Name the classic hypersensitivity pneumonitis vignettes and their antigens.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Bird (droppings), farmer (mouldy hay), malt worker (barley / Aspergillus clavatus), mushroom worker (actinomycetes).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP vignette is associated with mouldy hay?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Farmer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP vignette is associated with barley / Aspergillus clavatus?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Malt worker.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP vignette is associated with actinomycetes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Mushroom worker.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP vignette is associated with droppings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Bird.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Define idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Progressive lower-zone fibrosis with no identifiable cause.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the typical age and sex distribution of IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Age 50–70, males > females.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the prognosis of IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Poor — median survival ~3–4 years from diagnosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Describe the symptoms of IPF.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Progressive exertional dyspnoea (insidious onset), dry non-productive cough, fatigue, weight loss.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the characteristic signs of IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles ('velcro crackles'), clubbing (present in ~⅔), and cyanosis in advanced disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the term used for the fine end-inspiratory crackles of IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: 'Velcro crackles'.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Is clubbing always present in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: No — it is common, seen in roughly half to two-thirds of patients, but its absence does not exclude IPF.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which zone is affected in IPF on CXR/HRCT, and why does this matter?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Lower zone / bibasal — this is the key differentiator from upper-zone ILDs.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the diagnostic investigation for IPF and its classic findings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: HRCT — honeycombing (subpleural cysts), reticular/linear opacities, traction bronchiectasis, with bibasal predominance. Biopsy is usually not needed if HRCT is classic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: When is a biopsy usually unnecessary in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: When the HRCT appearance is classic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the PFT pattern in IPF, and which value is the most sensitive marker of severity?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Restrictive: ↓FVC, FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓TLCO — TLCO is the most sensitive marker of severity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does the ABG show in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Hypoxaemia with normal or low CO₂ (type 1 respiratory failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What blood findings may occur in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: ANA and RF may be weakly positive (used to exclude connective tissue disease); CRP/ESR may be raised, but are frequently normal and are non-specific.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does the CXR show in IPF, and how does it compare to HRCT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Bibasal reticular shadowing — less sensitive than HRCT.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What disease-modifying antifibrotics are used in IPF, and what do they achieve?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Pirfenidone (anti-inflammatory + antifibrotic) or nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) — they slow progression but do not reverse fibrosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: How does nintedanib work in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: It is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What supportive management is used in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental O₂, treating comorbidities (GORD, pulmonary hypertension), and palliative care.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the role of lung transplant in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: The only curative option — for selected patients with progressive disease. Whether a single or bilateral transplant is performed is a transplant-centre decision.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key warning regarding steroids in IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: In chronic, stable IPF steroids are not beneficial and may be harmful — immunosuppression increased mortality — so do not use them. The exception is an acute exacerbation, where high-dose corticosteroids are standard practice on weak evidence, once infection, PE and heart failure have been excluded.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Immune-mediated lung inflammation from repeated inhalation of organic antigens.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which hypersensitivity reaction underlies the acute phase of HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type III (immune complex).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which hypersensitivity reaction underlies the chronic phase of HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type IV (cell-mediated).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In which zone does fibrosis occur in chronic HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Upper/mid zone.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the source and antigen for bird fancier's lung?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Source: pigeons, parrots, chickens. Antigen: bird droppings / feather proteins.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the source and antigen for farmer's lung?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Source: mouldy hay / grain. Antigen: Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula (thermophilic actinomycetes).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the source and antigen for malt worker's lung?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Source: contaminated barley. Antigen: Aspergillus clavatus.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What are the source and antigen for mushroom worker's lung?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Source: compost mushroom farms. Antigen: thermophilic actinomycetes.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP condition is caused by Aspergillus clavatus?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Malt worker's lung.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which HP condition is caused by Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Farmer's lung.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Describe the acute clinical features of HP and their timing.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: 4–8h post-exposure: dyspnoea, dry cough, fever and flu-like symptoms, wheeze, fine crackles. Resolves with antigen removal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key feature of acute HP regarding resolution?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: It resolves with antigen removal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Describe the chronic clinical features of HP.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: From persistent exposure: progressive dyspnoea, weight loss, productive cough, upper/mid-zone fibrosis — can become irreversible.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does HRCT show in HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Upper/mid-zone ground-glass opacities, nodules, and fibrosis in chronic disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key BAL finding in HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Marked lymphocytosis (low CD4:CD8 ratio).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does serology show in HP, and what does it confirm?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Specific IgG precipitins (e.g. anti-bird, anti-farmer's hay) — confirms exposure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key blood finding in HP that distinguishes it from ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: No eosinophilia (key distinguisher from ABPA); may have raised CRP/ESR.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the PFT pattern in HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Restrictive pattern (as all ILD); ↓TLCO.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Why is the absence of eosinophilia in HP examinable?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: No eosinophilia in HP is the key contrast with ABPA, which has eosinophilia + ↑IgE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the most important first step in managing HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Avoid the antigen (most important) — may allow recovery in acute disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the second-line management of HP after antigen avoidance?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Oral steroids for symptomatic relief and suppression.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: How is chronic irreversible fibrosis from HP managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Antigen avoidance and immunosuppression remain the basis of treatment. Where established fibrosis keeps progressing despite that, the ILD service may add an antifibrotic — it is managed like IPF in that respect only.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type I + type III hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which hypersensitivity reactions underlie ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type I and type III.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: In which patient groups does ABPA almost exclusively occur?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Asthmatics and CF patients.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What type of bronchiectasis does ABPA cause?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Proximal (central) bronchiectasis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: List the clinical features of ABPA.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Wheeze + worsening asthma control, cough with brown mucus plugs, dyspnoea, recurrent pulmonary infiltrates, and proximal (central) bronchiectasis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the significance of the background condition in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: A background of asthma or CF is almost always present — consider ABPA in any asthmatic with poor control despite treatment.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the key blood finding in ABPA, and how does it differ from HP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: ↑Eosinophils — a key positive finding (absent in HP).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What total serum IgE level is highly characteristic of ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: ↑↑ (often >1000 IU/mL).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does a positive Aspergillus-specific IgE (RAST) indicate in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type I sensitisation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does a positive Aspergillus IgG precipitins result indicate in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Type III sensitisation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does HRCT show in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Central / proximal bronchiectasis, mucus plugging, and fleeting infiltrates.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What does the skin prick test show in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Immediate reaction to Aspergillus antigen.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the first-line treatment for ABPA and its role?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Oral prednisolone (steroids) — reduces inflammation, controls acute exacerbations. Most patients need long courses.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the second-line treatment for ABPA and when is it used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Itraconazole (antifungal) — reduces Aspergillus load, steroid-sparing. Used when steroids alone are insufficient.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What background asthma management is recommended in ABPA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Optimise asthma treatment; monitor IgE levels to assess treatment response.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Summarise the HP vs ABPA comparison.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: HP → no eosinophilia, IgG precipitins only, avoid antigen + steroids. ABPA → eosinophilia + ↑IgE + Aspergillus RAST positive, steroids → itraconazole.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Which antifibrotic causes photosensitivity and which causes diarrhoea, and what monitoring do both need?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Pirfenidone → photosensitivity and rash (counsel on high-factor sunblock, covering up, sun avoidance); also nausea, anorexia, weight loss. Nintedanib → diarrhoea, very common and often dose-limiting. Both are hepatotoxic and need LFT monitoring before and during treatment.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: How often should IPF be reviewed, when should transplant be discussed, and when does palliative care start?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: NICE: review every 3–6 months, tightening to 3-monthly if progressing rapidly. Discuss lung transplantation 3–6 months after diagnosis — a defined timing, not 'when they deteriorate'. Palliative care has a role from diagnosis, not only at the end of life. At each review track symptoms, FVC and TLCO trend, exertional desaturation and oxygen need.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Name the key complications of IPF.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: Lung cancer (risk raised several-fold — a new nodule in a fibrotic lower zone is cancer until proven otherwise), pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale, venous thromboembolism, acute exacerbation, and progressive type 1 respiratory failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: Define an acute exacerbation of IPF and list what must be excluded.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: An acute, clinically significant, unexplained worsening of dyspnoea (typically within a month) with new bilateral ground-glass opacification superimposed on the background UIP pattern on HRCT. Must exclude: infection, pulmonary embolism, heart failure / fluid overload, and drug-induced pneumonitis (also consider aspiration — GORD is common in IPF).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.front: What is the prognosis of an acute exacerbation of IPF, and how does it square with 'steroids are not used in IPF'?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lu.back: In-hospital mortality approaches 50%, and is worse in those invasively ventilated; median survival afterwards is 3–4 months — so a ceiling-of-care discussion belongs in the management. Management is largely supportive, but high-dose corticosteroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics are used in practice despite weak trial evidence. This is the exception: the 'no steroids' rule refers to chronic IPF, where immunosuppression increased mortality.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What causes occupational lung diseases, and what is the resulting lung pathology?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Inhaled occupational dusts → inflammation and fibrosis (the pneumoconioses). Not every occupational lung disease is fibrotic, though: occupational asthma is an airway disease and is the most frequently reported work-related lung disease in the UK.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What lung function pattern do most pneumoconioses follow?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Restrictive / ILD pattern (cross-reference ILD). Occupational asthma is the exception — it is obstructive, and it is the commonest reported UK work-related lung disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the three-part template used to examine occupational lung diseases?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Occupation → CXR signature → cancer/TB risk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the medico-legal status of occupational lung diseases?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Most are compensable industrial diseases (IIDB) — isolated pleural plaques are the exception (not compensable).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which disease does coal dust cause, and what are its two forms?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pneumoconiosis — simple or PMF (progressive massive fibrosis).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which disease does silica cause, and what additional risk is associated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Silicosis — with ↑↑ TB risk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: List the spectrum of asbestos-related diseases.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pleural plaques (benign, commonest), asbestosis (lower-zone fibrosis), mesothelioma, and lung cancer (commonest asbestos malignancy — not mesothelioma).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which asbestos-related disease is benign and the commonest?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pleural plaques.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How much asbestos exposure is needed to cause mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Even minimal exposure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the commonest asbestos malignancy?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lung cancer — not mesothelioma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What dust/occupation, CXR signature, zone, and cancer/TB risk characterise coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Coal dust (mining, tunnelling); small nodules (simple), PMF masses (progressive massive fibrosis); upper zone; COPD risk, no ↑lung cancer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the CXR signature of coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Small nodules (simple); PMF masses (progressive massive fibrosis).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the cancer/TB risk profile of coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: COPD risk; no increased lung cancer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What dust/occupation, CXR signature, zone, and cancer/TB risk characterise silicosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Silica (engineered/artificial stone worktop fabrication — the current UK outbreak; also sandblasting, quarrying, pottery, foundries, slate, tunnelling); egg-shell hilar node calcification, upper nodules; upper zone; ↑↑ TB and ↑ lung cancer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the classic CXR signature of silicosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Egg-shell hilar node calcification; upper nodules.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the cancer/TB risk profile of silicosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: ↑↑ TB; ↑ lung cancer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What dust/occupation, CXR signature, zone, and cancer/TB risk characterise asbestosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Asbestos (construction, shipyards, insulation, pipe-lagging); bibasal fibrosis progressing to honeycombing — pleural plaques often coexist but are a separate benign marker of the same exposure; lower zone; lung cancer (multiplicative with smoking) and mesothelioma (independent of smoking).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the CXR signature of asbestosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Bibasal reticular shadowing progressing to honeycombing. Pleural plaques commonly coexist because they mark the same asbestos exposure, but they are a separate benign entity and are not part of asbestosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Why is asbestos described as 'the odd one out' among occupational lung diseases?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lower-zone fibrosis (all other pneumoconioses are upper), a benign-to-malignant spectrum, and very long latency.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which occupational lung diseases affect the upper zone and which affects the lower zone?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Coal and silica are upper zone; asbestos is lower zone — the only lower-zone pneumoconiosis. (Other lower-zone fibrosis: IPF, CTD-ILD and drugs — see the ILD topic.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Match each occupational lung disease to its CXR signature.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Coal = PMF masses; silica = egg-shell hilar calcification; asbestos = pleural plaques.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Why does silica increase TB risk?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Silica particles impair macrophage killing of mycobacteria → ↑↑ TB.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the commonest asbestos malignancy, and what is the classic exam trap?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lung cancer, NOT mesothelioma — the classic exam trap. Smoking + asbestos is multiplicative.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How do smoking and asbestos interact for lung cancer risk?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Multiplicative.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the significance and latency of pleural plaques?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pleural plaques are benign — no malignant potential, no follow-up needed. Latency 20–40 years — a marker of past exposure only.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What does it mean that asbestosis is dose-dependent, and how does this contrast with mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Asbestosis is dose-dependent — it needs substantial cumulative exposure (intensity × duration) — whereas mesothelioma has no safe threshold and brief or low-level exposure can be enough.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is melanoptysis and what causes it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Black sputum from coal PMF.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What proportion of simple pneumoconiosis progresses to PMF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Classically quoted as up to ~30%, but this applies mainly to higher radiographic-category disease; overall progression is lower and rises with profusion category and heavier/longer dust exposure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the medico-legal classification of occupational lung diseases, and what should be documented?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Most are compensable industrial diseases (IIDB) — isolated pleural plaques are the exception (not compensable). Document occupational history carefully.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the latency, chemotherapy, and prognosis of mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Latency ~45 years; pemetrexed + cisplatin chemotherapy (or nivolumab + ipilimumab immunotherapy, NICE first-line in unresectable disease); poor prognosis (~12 months median).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What chemotherapy regimen is used for mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pemetrexed + cisplatin (or nivolumab + ipilimumab immunotherapy — NICE first-line in unresectable disease).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the common name for coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: 'Black lung'.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Describe the pathological sequence of coal worker's pneumoconiosis.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Coal dust overwhelms macrophage clearance → macule formation → nodules → fibrosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which zone does coal worker's pneumoconiosis affect, and what is its lung cancer risk?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Upper-zone disease; no increased lung cancer risk (unlike silica and asbestos).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Describe simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: The commonest form, often asymptomatic. Small coal-dust macules + nodules on CXR. ↑COPD risk. Up to ~30% progress to PMF over years, mainly in higher radiographic-category disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What proportion of simple CWP progresses to PMF, and over what timescale?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Up to ~30% (mainly higher radiographic-category disease), developing over years; the risk rises with profusion category and heavier/longer dust exposure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is PMF (progressive massive fibrosis) in coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Nodules coalesce → large upper-lobe fibrotic masses (>1 cm).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the features of PMF in coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Black sputum (melanoptysis), progressive dyspnoea, mixed obstructive/restrictive PFTs, and cor pulmonale in advanced disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What size defines the fibrotic masses in PMF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Greater than 1 cm.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How is coal worker's pneumoconiosis managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Remove from exposure; smoking cessation (↓COPD progression); supportive care (inhaled bronchodilators, O₂); no specific treatment; compensable (IIDB).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Why is smoking cessation important in coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: It reduces COPD progression.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Describe the pathogenesis of silicosis and its most important risk.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Inhalation of crystalline silica → macrophage activation → fibrotic nodule formation. Upper-zone disease. The most important risk is reactivation TB — silica impairs macrophage killing of mycobacteria.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which occupations carry silicosis risk, and which is the highest?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Engineered/artificial stone worktop fabrication (the current UK outbreak); sandblasting (highest historic risk), stone quarrying, slate working, pottery, foundries, tunnelling, glass manufacturing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the characteristic CXR signature of silicosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Egg-shell calcification of hilar lymph nodes (characteristic, not pathognomonic — also seen in sarcoidosis); also upper-zone small round nodules that may progress to PMF-like confluent masses.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the key risks in silicosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: ↑↑ TB risk (most important — screen all silicosis patients with Mantoux/IGRA); ↑ lung cancer risk; progressive fibrosis even after exposure ceases.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Why must all silicosis patients be screened for TB, and how?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: TB is the most important risk — screen all silicosis patients with Mantoux/IGRA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Does silicosis progress after exposure stops?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Yes — progressive fibrosis continues even after exposure ceases.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How is silicosis managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Remove from exposure; screen and treat latent TB; supportive care; no disease-modifying treatment; compensable (IIDB).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is silicotuberculosis, and why does it matter?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Silicosis + TB — always screen silicosis patients for TB (Mantoux/IGRA + CXR); it causes rapid deterioration.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which asbestos fibre type is more dangerous, and what range of disease does asbestos cause?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Crocidolite > chrysotile; asbestos causes a spectrum of disease from benign to malignant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What makes asbestos unique among the pneumoconioses in terms of zone and latency?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lower-zone fibrosis (unlike all other pneumoconioses) and very long latency — often decades between exposure and disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which occupations are associated with asbestos exposure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Construction, shipbuilding, insulation, pipe-lagging, naval engineering.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are pleural plaques and their key facts?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: The commonest asbestos disease — discrete fibrous / calcified pleural thickenings. Latency 20–40 years. Often an asymptomatic incidental CXR finding.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the exam points for pleural plaques?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Benign — no malignant potential, no follow-up needed. A marker of past exposure only. Does NOT become mesothelioma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is diffuse pleural thickening and how does it differ from plaques?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: More extensive than plaques; may restrict lung expansion → restrictive PFTs; dyspnoea. Distinguish from plaques (diffuse vs discrete) — both are benign.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Describe asbestosis and its key facts.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lower-zone interstitial fibrosis. Dose-dependent (proportional to cumulative exposure). Latency 15–30 years. Features: progressive dyspnoea, bibasal end-inspiratory crackles, clubbing, restrictive PFTs + ↓TLCO.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the exam points for asbestosis regarding dose and imaging pattern?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Dose-dependent (length/intensity of exposure matters). Same PFT/HRCT pattern as IPF but lower zone. Honeycombing on HRCT.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How does the asbestosis pattern compare to IPF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Same PFT/HRCT pattern as IPF but lower zone, with honeycombing on HRCT.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is mesothelioma and how much exposure causes it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: A pleural malignancy. Even minimal/brief asbestos exposure can cause it. Latency up to 45 years.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the clinical features of mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Progressive dyspnoea, chest wall pain, weight loss, ± pleural effusion (~75–90%, very common).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the key exam points distinguishing mesothelioma (dose, smoking, treatment, prognosis)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: No safe threshold — even brief or low-level exposure can cause it. Not caused by smoking. Treated with pemetrexed + cisplatin; poor prognosis (~12 months).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Is mesothelioma caused by smoking?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: No — mesothelioma is not caused by smoking.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What are the key facts about asbestos-related lung cancer?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: The commonest asbestos-related malignancy (not mesothelioma). Multiplicative / synergistic risk with smoking. Classic exam trap — smoking cessation is critical to reduce this risk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Asbestosis vs mesothelioma — what is the key discriminator?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Asbestosis is dose-dependent and needs substantial cumulative exposure; mesothelioma has no safe threshold — even brief or low-level exposure can be enough. Different mechanisms — fibrosis vs malignant transformation of mesothelium.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Lung cancer vs mesothelioma in asbestos exposure — what is the key discriminator?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Lung cancer = commonest asbestos malignancy (not mesothelioma); smoking + asbestos = multiplicative risk for lung cancer. Mesothelioma risk is independent of smoking.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Pleural plaques vs asbestosis — what is the key discriminator?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Plaques = pleural only, benign, asymptomatic; asbestosis = parenchymal interstitial fibrosis, symptomatic, progressive. Both can coexist; plaques do NOT progress to asbestosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Do pleural plaques progress to asbestosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: No — plaques do not progress to asbestosis, though both can coexist.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What investigations are used in asbestos-related disease?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: CXR (pleural plaques, bibasal fibrosis); HRCT (honeycombing, plaques, thickening); PFTs (restrictive + ↓TLCO in asbestosis); thoracoscopic biopsy for mesothelioma; pleural fluid cytology.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What investigation confirms mesothelioma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Thoracoscopic biopsy (with pleural fluid cytology).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How is asbestosis managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Remove from exposure. No routine disease-modifying treatment (unlike IPF) — though nintedanib may be considered if a progressive fibrosing ILD phenotype develops. Supportive: O₂, pulmonary rehab. Monitor PFTs. Compensable (IIDB).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Are antifibrotics established for asbestosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Not routinely — unlike IPF; but nintedanib may be considered if a progressive fibrosing ILD phenotype develops.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: How is mesothelioma managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Pemetrexed + cisplatin (chemotherapy) or nivolumab + ipilimumab immunotherapy (NICE first-line, unresectable); surgery in highly selected cases; palliative MDT; O₂; analgesia. Poor prognosis (~12 months median survival).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is the most important intervention for anyone with asbestos exposure, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Smoking cessation — it reduces the multiplicative lung cancer risk substantially.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: What is Caplan syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Rheumatoid arthritis + pneumoconiosis (coal worker’s or silicosis) → multiple well-defined peripheral pulmonary nodules.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which occupation is driving the current UK outbreak of silicosis, and why is the exposure so intense?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Engineered / artificial stone worktop fabrication and installation — dry cutting, grinding and polishing. Engineered stone contains up to ~90% crystalline silica, versus roughly 5–30% in natural granite or sandstone, so it generates very high respirable crystalline silica exposure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Contrast classic silicosis with accelerated silicosis.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Classic silicosis: decades of exposure, older worker, natural stone (~5–30% silica). Accelerated silicosis: engineered/artificial stone (up to ~90% silica), symptomatic within roughly 3–10 years, workers in their 20s–40s, faster progression to progressive massive fibrosis. Consider silicosis in a 32-year-old stonemason.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Under RIDDOR, who makes the report, what triggers it, and which respiratory diseases are currently reportable?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: The EMPLOYER makes the RIDDOR report — triggered by the doctor's written diagnosis given to the worker/employer. Currently reportable respiratory diseases include occupational asthma (where work involves significant/regular exposure to a known respiratory sensitiser) and occupational cancer (which captures mesothelioma and asbestos-related lung cancer). The pneumoconioses (silicosis, asbestosis) were removed from RIDDOR in 2013 — so they are NOT currently reportable, but the position is under review. SWORD/THOR is the separate, voluntary, physician-facing reporting scheme.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Beyond writing 'remove from exposure', what are the three occupational-health actions after diagnosing an occupational lung disease?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: 1) Refer to occupational health — for redeployment or reasonable adjustments, not automatic job loss. 2) Notify the employer so exposure is controlled at source and other exposed workers are reviewed (the public-health step unique to occupational medicine — one index case implies a workforce). 3) Health surveillance — questionnaire plus spirometry under COSHH for workers exposed to respiratory sensitisers and Schedule 6 substances; this is why asymptomatic pneumoconiosis is detected at all.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Who claims IIDB, for what, and what are the disablement thresholds?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: IIDB is a claim the PATIENT makes to the DWP for a 'prescribed disease' — the hospital does not arrange it; the doctor advises and provides a clear diagnosis letter. Prescribed diseases include diffuse mesothelioma, pneumoconiosis (including asbestosis and silicosis), unilateral or bilateral diffuse pleural thickening, asbestos-related primary lung carcinoma and byssinosis. General threshold is ≥14% disablement, but pneumoconiosis and byssinosis are assessable from 1%, and diffuse mesothelioma is assessed at 100%.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which asbestos-related pleural change is a prescribed disease for IIDB, and which is not?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Diffuse pleural thickening (unilateral or bilateral) IS a prescribed disease. Isolated pleural plaques are NOT — they are a benign marker of past exposure causing no measurable disablement. This is why most, not all, occupational lung disease is compensable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: Which lump-sum compensation schemes exist for workers who cannot trace an employer or insurer, and what must happen when such a patient dies?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: The Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers' Compensation) Act 1979 and the Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme 2014 — a claimant takes one or the other, not both. A civil claim against a negligent employer or insurer remains a separate route and is usually the larger sum. A death attributable to an industrial disease MUST be reported to the coroner; the inquest usually provides the evidence of occupational causation that benefit and civil claims rely on, so omitting the referral can seriously prejudice the family's claim.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.front: In occupational asthma, what determines prognosis — and why does 'remove from exposure' mean something different here than in the pneumoconioses?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lu.back: Early removal from exposure offers the best chance of complete recovery. The longer exposure continues after symptom onset, the more likely symptoms and bronchial hyperresponsiveness become permanent; only about a third of workers recover fully, and hyperresponsiveness can persist for a decade after removal. Contrast: in the fibrotic pneumoconioses removal does NOT halt progression (silicosis progresses even after exposure ceases), whereas in sensitiser-induced asthma removal is potentially curative if early.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Define pleural effusion and its detection thresholds.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Excess fluid in the pleural space. Clinically detectable at >500 mL; visible on CXR at >300 mL.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What should a massive pleural effusion make you think of?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Malignancy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the organising fork in pleural effusion, and what decides it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Transudate vs exudate — this single distinction drives investigation and management, decided by Light's criteria.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What protein levels define transudate vs exudate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Transudate <30 g/L protein; exudate >30 g/L protein.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the mechanism of a transudative effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pressure imbalance — ↑hydrostatic or ↓oncotic pressure pushes fluid across intact pleura.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the mechanism of an exudative effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleural damage / inflammation — ↑capillary permeability leaks protein-rich fluid.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: List the causes of a transudative effusion.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Heart failure (commonest), hypoalbuminaemia (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), hypothyroidism, Meigs syndrome.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the commonest cause of a transudative effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Heart failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: List the causes of an exudative effusion.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pneumonia (parapneumonic), malignancy, TB, PE, RA / connective tissue disease, pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the typical appearance of a transudate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Clear, straw-coloured; often bilateral.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the typical appearance of an exudate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Variable; may be turbid, purulent, bloody; usually unilateral.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What are the memory hooks for transudate vs exudate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Transudate = the fluid is 'pushed' across (systemic disease, often bilateral); exudate = the pleura is 'leaky' (local disease, inflammatory).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When are Light's criteria used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: When protein is borderline (25–35 g/L).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How are Light's criteria applied to classify an effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Classify as exudate if ANY ONE criterion is met; must meet none of them to call it a transudate when borderline.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is Light's Criterion 1?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is Light's Criterion 2?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is Light's Criterion 3?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleural fluid LDH > ⅔ of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What are the symptoms of a pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Small → asymptomatic. Larger: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (exudates especially), dry cough.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What are the key examination signs of a pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Stony dull percussion (distinguishes from consolidation, which is dull), reduced/absent breath sounds, reduced vocal fremitus/resonance, reduced chest expansion ipsilaterally, and tracheal deviation away (massive effusion — mediastinal shift).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why does stony dull percussion help distinguish effusion from consolidation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Effusion is stony dull, whereas consolidation is dull (not stony dull).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When does a pleural effusion cause tracheal deviation, and in which direction?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: In a massive effusion — the trachea deviates away due to mediastinal shift.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How do you distinguish effusion from consolidation on examination?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Both give dullness on percussion, but effusion = stony dull + absent breath sounds + reduced fremitus; consolidation = dull + bronchial breathing + ↑vocal resonance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does CXR show in a pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Costophrenic angle blunting (>300 mL), meniscus sign, fluid in fissures, mediastinal shift (massive). Bilateral = transudate until proven otherwise.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does a bilateral effusion suggest until proven otherwise?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: A transudate.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the role of USS chest in pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Confirms fluid (vs consolidation); guides safe aspiration site; detects loculations.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the role of a diagnostic tap, and where is it performed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: First-line for an undiagnosed effusion — any effusion not clearly explained by a transudative cause. The site is chosen by ultrasound at the time (never blind off the CXR), entering above the rib below. Send: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, MC&S, ± amylase.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What samples are sent from a diagnostic pleural tap?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, MC&S, ± amylase.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When is CT thorax used in pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: If aspiration is non-diagnostic; pleural nodularity suggests malignancy; also for loculated collections.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When is pleural biopsy used, and how?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: For TB (Abrams needle) or malignancy (image-guided / thoracoscopic).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does purulent pleural fluid indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Empyema.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does turbid pleural fluid indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Infection / inflammation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does milky/creamy pleural fluid indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Chylothorax (thoracic duct leak).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does bloodstained pleural fluid indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Haemothorax / malignancy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does straw-coloured pleural fluid indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Typical of a transudate — but appearance alone cannot classify an effusion. TB and malignant exudates are commonly straw-coloured too. Use the protein level and Light's criteria.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What are the fluid biochemistry red flags suggesting an infected/complicated effusion needing drainage?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: pH <7.2 + ↓glucose + ↑LDH → infected/complicated (needs drainage).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does raised pleural fluid amylase suggest?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What does positive pleural fluid cytology indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Malignancy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is a transudative effusion managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Treat the underlying cause — diurese heart failure, correct hypoalbuminaemia, treat hypothyroidism. Aspiration if tense/symptomatic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is an exudative effusion managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Treat the underlying cause. Drainage if large/symptomatic (chest drain or aspiration). Send fluid for cytology/MC&S. Investigate for pneumonia, malignancy, TB.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is a malignant effusion managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: It recurs after simple aspiration. Drain, send fluid for cytology, then check re-expansion on the post-drainage CXR. If the lung re-expands: offer a CHOICE of talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC), guided by patient preference — both are first-line. If the lung is non-expandable ("trapped", >25% not apposed): the IPC is preferred, because pleurodesis cannot fuse surfaces that never touch. The IPC is NOT a rescue after failed pleurodesis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is pleurodesis and when is it used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Talc instillation — a sclerosant that fuses the pleural layers; used in malignant effusion after draining to dryness, as it recurs after aspiration.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is a small/asymptomatic effusion managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Conservative management + monitoring. Serial USS/CXR. Investigate aetiology.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What defines a simple parapneumonic effusion and how is it managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Clear, sterile; normal pH (>7.2), normal glucose, normal LDH. Antibiotics alone — resolves with treatment of pneumonia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What defines a complicated parapneumonic effusion and how is it managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Infected; pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000. Chest drain (intercostal) + antibiotics.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What defines an empyema and how is it managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Frank pus; pH <7.2, very low glucose. Chest drain ± intrapleural tPA (alteplase) + DNase; VATS if the drain fails.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the 'empyema triad' of biochemical markers that mandate drainage?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000 (or frank pus).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is the most common cause of haemothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Trauma (rib fractures → intercostal vessel injury). Also malignancy and iatrogenic (central line, post-thoracic surgery).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is a flail segment, and what is its consequence?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: ≥2 (typically ≥3) consecutive ribs fractured in ≥2 places → loss of chest wall rigidity → paradoxical movement (segment moves in on inspiration). Risk of respiratory failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is a haemothorax managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: A–E resuscitation; tranexamic acid early; large-bore chest drain — a large bore because blood clots and blocks a small tube. Early VATS (48–72 h) for a RETAINED haemothorax, i.e. clot the drain has failed to clear. Immediate thoracotomy if bleeding is massive or ongoing. (These surgical thresholds come from trauma practice rather than BTS.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why is a large-bore chest drain used in haemothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: To prevent clotting/empyema; size 28–40Fr.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When is VATS indicated in haemothorax, and when is thoracotomy?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Early VATS at 48–72 h for a RETAINED haemothorax — clot the drain has not cleared. Thoracotomy, not VATS, is the answer for a massive haemothorax or persistent ongoing bleeding.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What is Meigs syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Ovarian fibroma + ascites + right pleural effusion (transudate) — a classic eponym.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why does PE cause an exudate, and why is this a common exam trick?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: PE causes an exudate — not a transudate. This is a common exam trick.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What are the boundaries of the triangle of safety, and what is it for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Lateral border of pectoralis major (anterior), anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posterior), a horizontal line at the 5th ICS / nipple line (inferior), apex of the axilla (superior). Enter immediately ABOVE the superior border of the rib below — the neurovascular bundle runs at the inferior border of the rib above. Note the triangle is the landmark zone for CHEST DRAIN insertion; a pleural aspiration site is chosen by ultrasound at the time.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why must pleural aspiration be performed above the rib?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: To avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle, which runs in the groove at the lower border of each rib — so the needle is passed just above the rib below, within the triangle of safety, USS-guided.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: A patient with a large pleural effusion is being drained. What is the rule for how much fluid to remove, and what stops you?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: The rule is symptom-led, not volume-led. STOP DRAINING IMMEDIATELY if the patient develops cough, chest tightness or chest discomfort — these are the warning signs of re-expansion pulmonary oedema. BTS advises a maximum of 1.5 L in the first hour / at the first drainage, after which the remainder can be drained slowly. 1.5 L is a first-hour limit, NOT an absolute ceiling — draining to dryness is reasonable provided no respiratory symptoms develop. Higher risk: lung collapsed >7 days, younger patients, and where >3 L is drained.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: How is iatrogenic pneumothorax minimised during pleural aspiration, and when is a post-procedure chest X-ray actually needed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Ultrasound guidance substantially reduces the rate of iatrogenic pneumothorax — never tap 'blind' off the CXR alone. A post-procedure CXR is NOT routine after an uncomplicated aspiration. It IS indicated if air was aspirated, if multiple passes were needed, or if the patient becomes breathless or hypoxic.
