conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why are the antibiotics for pleural infection (empyema) different from those for community-acquired pneumonia, and how long is the course?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleural infection is frequently polymicrobial and anaerobic, so ANAEROBIC COVER IS REQUIRED — a standard CAP regimen is not enough. Options include a penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor combination, clindamycin, metronidazole or a carbapenem. The course is PROLONGED — commonly around 3 weeks or more, guided by clinical response (recommended durations genuinely vary between sources: BTS suggests around 3 weeks is probably appropriate, other guidance quotes 4–6 weeks). Contrast this with the 5–7 days memorised for CAP. Switch IV to oral once there is clinical improvement: pyrexia settled, inflammatory markers falling, radiological improvement.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: What size chest drain is first-line for pleural infection, and what is the escalation pathway if drainage stalls?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: A SMALL-BORE drain (≤14F) is first-line for pleural infection — as effective as a large tube and far less painful. (The large-bore 28–40 Fr drain belongs to haemothorax, not empyema.) Reassess early: if drainage has stalled with a residual collection, consider intrapleural tPA (alteplase) + DNase. Involve thoracic surgery early (VATS ± decortication) if antibiotics, drainage and fibrinolytics all fail. Aftermath: residual pleural thickening / fibrothorax gives a restrictive defect with reduced expansion on that side; a minority need decortication.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: Why can a 'trapped' (non-expandable) lung not be pleurodesed, and what is offered instead?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: Pleurodesis requires the visceral and parietal pleura to APPOSE — the sclerosant can only fuse surfaces that are actually touching. If the lung will not re-expand, the surfaces never meet and pleurodesis fails. So check re-expansion on the POST-DRAINAGE CXR: if the lung re-expands, offer a CHOICE of talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) guided by patient preference (BTS 2023); if the lung is non-expandable (>25% not apposed to the chest wall), an IPC is PREFERRED. Note the IPC is a first-line option, not a rescue after failed pleurodesis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.front: When should you NOT aspirate a pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusio.back: When the clinical setting strongly suggests a transudate — for example clear-cut decompensated heart failure with bilateral effusions — do not aspirate. Treat the underlying cause instead, and sample only if there are atypical features (unilateral effusion, fever, pleuritic pain, disproportionate size) or failure to respond to therapy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Air in the pleural space → partial or complete lung collapse.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the framing/approach for pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Classify (primary vs secondary) → assess symptoms + high-risk features (BTS 2023) → never miss tension (the emergency).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the key percussion contrast between pneumothorax and pleural effusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Hyperresonant (pneumothorax) vs stony dull (effusion).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Describe primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: No underlying lung disease. Tall, thin, young men; ruptured subpleural bleb/bulla. Smoking is a risk factor. Good prognosis — manage conservatively if minimally symptomatic, which under BTS 2023 applies even to a larger pneumothorax in a stable patient with no high-risk features.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the classic patient profile for primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Tall, thin, young men.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Describe secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Underlying lung disease — COPD (commonest), asthma, CF, bronchiectasis, TB, malignancy. Worse outcomes — lower threshold to drain; admit all.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the commonest underlying disease in secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: COPD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why are secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces managed more aggressively?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Worse outcomes — lower threshold to drain, and admit all.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What causes a traumatic / iatrogenic pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Rib fractures, biopsy, central line insertion, mechanical ventilation (barotrauma), chest drain complications.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is a tension pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: An emergency subtype — a one-way valve mechanism → progressive pressure build-up. Can occur from any cause.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What are the symptoms of a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain ± breathlessness. May be minimal in primary (small); marked dyspnoea in secondary (limited reserve).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What are the examination signs (air signature) of a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Hyperresonant percussion on the affected side, reduced/absent breath sounds, reduced chest expansion ipsilaterally, reduced vocal resonance/fremitus.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the percussion contrast between pneumothorax, effusion, and consolidation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Pneumothorax = hyperresonant (air); effusion = stony dull (fluid); consolidation = dull with bronchial breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the first-line investigation for pneumothorax, and what does it show?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Erect PA CXR — visible lung edge with absent peripheral lung markings.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is pneumothorax size measured, and what defines small vs large?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Horizontal distance from the lung edge to the chest wall at the hilum. <2cm = small; ≥2cm = large. (BTS 2023: size still describes the PTX but is no longer the sole management driver — symptoms + high-risk features lead.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: When is CT thorax used in pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: If bullous disease is suspected (distinguishes bulla from pneumothorax — avoids dangerous needling of a bulla); also for small/atypical cases or surgical planning.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why is tension pneumothorax a clinical diagnosis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for CXR. Treat immediately.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the role of oxygen in pneumothorax, and how is it given?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Supplemental oxygen accelerates pleural air reabsorption (roughly fourfold vs room air). Give it titrated to target saturations — 94–98%, or 88–92% in those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. known COPD) — not high-flow to everyone.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax <2cm AND no SOB managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Conservative — discharge, review 2–4 weeks, advise re: smoking/flying/diving. (BTS 2023: conservative is appropriate for a minimally symptomatic PSP regardless of size, if no high-risk features.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax ≥2cm OR with SOB managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Old algorithm: aspiration (16–18G cannula, ≤2.5L) → chest drain if it fails. BTS 2023: for a symptomatic PSP with no high-risk features, this is a shared decision between conservative care, an ambulatory one-way-valve device, aspiration, or a chest drain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax managed, and why is the threshold to intervene lower?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Underlying lung disease is itself a BTS 2023 high-risk characteristic, so these patients are admitted and most receive a chest drain (an ambulatory device where local expertise allows). A small, asymptomatic SSP may be observed under specialist supervision. The old <1cm / 1–2cm / >2cm ladder is BTS 2010 and no longer drives management.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Is needle aspiration the standard first step in a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: No. Aspiration belongs to the primary spontaneous pathway. In a secondary pneumothorax the underlying lung disease is a BTS 2023 high-risk characteristic, so most patients are admitted for a chest drain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is a symptomatic or high-risk secondary spontaneous pneumothorax managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Chest drain, with admission — outcomes are worse than in a primary pneumothorax.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is any pneumothorax that is bilateral, haemodynamically unstable, or has a persistent leak beyond 3–5 days managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Chest drain; refer thoracics; consider pleurodesis / bullectomy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How is a persistent air leak managed, and at what point is it referred?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: A leak persisting beyond 3–5 days (or recurrence) → refer to thoracic surgery for VATS bullectomy ± pleurodesis/pleurectomy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the mechanism of a tension pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: One-way valve: air enters pleura on inspiration but cannot escape → progressive ↑intrapleural pressure → mediastinal shift → kinked great vessels → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What are the clinical signs of a tension pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side, ↓air entry + hyperresonance on the affected side, distended neck veins, tachycardia → hypotension → arrest, severe respiratory distress.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: In which direction does the trachea deviate in a tension pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Away from the affected side.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the immediate management of a tension pneumothorax (step 1)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Needle decompression with a large-bore cannula (14G) at the 4th–5th ICS in the anterior axillary line (the safe triangle) → hiss of air confirms. In a ventilated or arrested patient, finger (open) thoracostomy is preferred. The older 2nd ICS midclavicular site is superseded — a standard cannula often fails to reach the pleura there in adults.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Where is needle decompression performed in tension pneumothorax, and when is it not the first choice?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Needle decompression with a large-bore cannula (14G) at the 4th–5th ICS in the anterior axillary line (the safe triangle) → hiss of air confirms. In a ventilated or arrested patient, finger (open) thoracostomy is preferred. The older 2nd ICS midclavicular site is superseded — a standard cannula often fails to reach the pleura there in adults.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the definitive management of a tension pneumothorax (step 2)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Chest drain — insert after needle decompression.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What confirms successful needle decompression in tension pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: A hiss of air.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What are the boundaries of the triangle of safety for chest drain insertion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Lateral border of pectoralis major (anterior), anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posterior), 5th ICS / nipple line (inferior), apex of axilla (superior). Always insert above the rib (neurovascular bundle runs below).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why is a chest drain inserted above the rib?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Because the neurovascular bundle runs below the rib.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: How does the underwater seal act as a one-way valve?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Air/fluid exits but cannot re-enter.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What does swinging of a chest drain with respiration indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Correctly sited — swinging is good; no swing = re-examine/reposition.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What does bubbling of a chest drain indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: An active air leak. No swing = blocked or drain displaced.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why must you never lift the chest drain bottle above the patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Retrograde flow back into the pleura.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why must you never clamp a bubbling chest drain?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: It can cause a tension pneumothorax.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What discharge advice is given regarding smoking after a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Smoking cessation (↓bleb formation + recurrence risk).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the flying advice after a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: No flying for ~1–2 weeks after CXR resolution.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is the scuba diving advice after a spontaneous pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Permanently no scuba diving (pressure changes risk re-expansion and tension) — unless definitive surgery, typically bilateral pleurectomy, has been performed. That surgical route is the only way back for someone whose livelihood depends on diving.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What should prompt a patient to return after pneumothorax discharge?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Worsening breathlessness / chest pain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: When is a follow-up CXR reviewed after a conservatively managed primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: At 2–4 weeks.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Summarise the primary vs secondary pneumothorax exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Primary = tall thin young man, bleb, no lung disease; secondary = underlying lung disease (COPD commonest) — worse outcome, drain earlier.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Summarise the size measurement and conservative-management exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Size = lung edge to chest wall at the hilum: <2cm = small, ≥2cm = large. Primary <2cm + no SOB → conservative (discharge). BTS 2023: conservative applies to a minimally symptomatic PSP regardless of size, absent high-risk features.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why must you not confuse hyperresonance and stony dullness on the SBA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Hyperresonant percussion = pneumothorax; stony dull = effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Summarise the tension pneumothorax exam pearl (diagnosis and signs).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Tension = clinical diagnosis, do NOT wait for CXR. Signs: trachea away, hypotension, distended neck veins, hyperresonance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Summarise the tension pneumothorax immediate treatment exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Needle decompression (14G) at the 4th–5th ICS, anterior axillary line → then chest drain (definitive). Finger thoracostomy is preferred if the patient is ventilated or in arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Under BTS 2023, what drives pneumothorax management (not size)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Symptoms + high-risk characteristics + patient priorities. High-risk features (favour a chest drain): haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, bilateral PTX, underlying lung disease, age ≥50 with significant smoking history, haemopneumothorax.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What is ambulatory management of a pneumothorax?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Outpatient management using a one-way valve device (e.g. pleural vent) — a BTS 2023 option for a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax, avoiding admission.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: After a FIRST primary spontaneous pneumothorax, what is the commonly quoted recurrence risk, and when is it highest?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Commonly quoted at ~25–30% within the first year (published series range widely, 23–50% — quote it as a ballpark, not a hard constant). Risk is highest during that first year and is higher in smokers, which is why smoking cessation is a genuine recurrence-reduction intervention rather than generic lifestyle advice.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Per BTS 2023, after how many pneumothoraces should elective definitive surgery be considered — and who should be considered earlier?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Consider elective surgery after a SECOND IPSILATERAL pneumothorax OR a FIRST CONTRALATERAL pneumothorax (i.e. a second event overall). Consider it earlier where recurrence prevention especially matters: at-risk occupations — professional divers, airline pilots, military personnel — or where the first presentation was a tension pneumothorax.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: What does definitive surgery for recurrent pneumothorax actually consist of, and why does it matter for a professional diver?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: VATS bullectomy (resect the offending bleb/bulla) PLUS a pleural procedure to obliterate the pleural space: chemical pleurodesis (talc), mechanical/abrasive pleurodesis, or pleurectomy (surgical stripping of the parietal pleura — the most durable option). This matters because the standard discharge advice of 'permanently no scuba diving' applies to the unoperated patient; successful definitive surgery is the route back for someone whose livelihood depends on diving or flying, so an at-risk occupation is a reason for EARLY thoracic surgical referral rather than simply issuing the blanket ban.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: Why does the BTS 2023 pneumothorax algorithm not apply to iatrogenic pneumothorax, and how is iatrogenic pneumothorax usually managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: BTS 2023 deliberately scopes traumatic and iatrogenic pneumothorax OUT of its spontaneous-pneumothorax recommendations, so the symptom/high-risk-feature table does not apply to them. Iatrogenic pneumothorax (post CT-guided lung biopsy, central line or pacemaker insertion, ventilator barotrauma) usually resolves rapidly and often needs no intervention — observation ± supplemental oxygen, with repeat imaging to confirm resolution. Drain only if the patient is symptomatic, the pneumothorax is large, or the patient is ventilated.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: A patient with a known pneumothorax is about to be intubated and ventilated. What must happen first, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: A chest drain generally goes in FIRST. Positive-pressure ventilation (invasive ventilation or NIV) forces air into the pleural space and can convert a simple pneumothorax into a TENSION pneumothorax. Any pneumothorax in a patient going onto positive pressure is therefore a different risk category from the same pneumothorax in a spontaneously breathing patient — this is a classic SBA stem and a real foundation-year scenario.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.front: When can a chest drain be removed after a pneumothorax, and how should the removal be performed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax.back: Remove when the lung is FULLY RE-EXPANDED on CXR AND the air leak has stopped (the drain is no longer bubbling). Remove the tube during EXPIRATION or a VALSALVA manoeuvre so air cannot be drawn back into the pleural space as the tube leaves. Repeat the CXR after removal, before discharge, to confirm there is no recurrence. (Full ongoing drain aftercare — daily checks, suction settings, complications — is covered under LUNG FUNCTION → Oxygenation & Respiratory Support → Chest Drain Management.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Define pulmonary hypertension (PH), including the diagnostic threshold.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: ↑pulmonary arterial pressure (mean PAP >20 mmHg) → right heart pressure overload → cor pulmonale → systemic venous congestion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What mean PAP defines pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Mean PAP >20 mmHg.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How is pulmonary hypertension classified?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Into 5 WHO groups by cause — the spine of the topic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the unifying mechanistic thread for every feature of PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Every feature (ECG, CXR, signs) = the right heart struggling against high pulmonary resistance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is WHO Group 1 PH, and what are its examples?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: PAH (pulmonary arterial hypertension — primary vascular). Examples: idiopathic; connective tissue disease (scleroderma, SLE); congenital heart disease (Eisenmenger); HIV; drugs (fenfluramine).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is WHO Group 2 PH, and what are its examples?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Left heart disease — the commonest cause overall. Examples: LV failure, mitral/aortic valve disease, systemic hypertension.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is WHO Group 3 PH, and what are its examples?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Chronic lung disease / hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction. Examples: COPD (commonest in this group), ILD, OSA, high altitude.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is WHO Group 4 PH, and what is its mechanism?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: CTEPH (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension) — recurrent / inadequately treated PE → organised clot → obstructed vessels.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is WHO Group 5 PH, and what are its examples?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Misc — multifactorial / unclear mechanisms. Examples: sarcoidosis, haematological disorders (sickle cell), metabolic, compression of pulmonary vessels.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which WHO group is the commonest cause of PH overall?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Group 2 (left heart disease).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which WHO group receives PAH-specific vasodilator drug therapy — and is there any other licensed use?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Group 1 (PAH). The one other licensed use is riociguat in inoperable or persistent/recurrent Group 4 CTEPH. Groups 2 and 3 do not receive PAH-specific drugs — in Group 2 they are harmful.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which connective tissue diseases are causes of Group 1 PAH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Scleroderma and SLE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which drug is a recognised cause of Group 1 PAH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Fenfluramine.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the commonest cause of Group 3 PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: COPD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Outline the pathophysiological chain of PH.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: ↑pulmonary vascular resistance (any cause) → RV pressure overload → RV hypertrophy → RV failure (cor pulmonale) → back-pressure → systemic venous congestion (↑JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What does RV failure in pulmonary hypertension produce, and what is it called?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Cor pulmonale, leading to back-pressure → systemic venous congestion (↑JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What are the early symptoms of pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Exertional dyspnoea (main presenting symptom), fatigue, exertional syncope (fixed low cardiac output — cannot augment with exercise), chest pain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the main presenting symptom of pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Exertional dyspnoea.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Why does exertional syncope occur in PH, and why is it a high-yield clue?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: It reflects a fixed low cardiac output — the RV cannot increase output on demand (obstructed outflow). It is a high-yield clinical clue to PH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What are the advanced / cor pulmonale features of pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly (± pulsatile liver), ascites, pleural effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What are the clinical signs of pulmonary hypertension on examination?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Loud P2 (pulmonary valve closure), RV heave (parasternal), tricuspid regurgitation murmur (pansystolic, LSE, louder on inspiration).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What causes the loud P2 in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Pulmonary valve closure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What are the characteristics of the tricuspid regurgitation murmur in PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Pansystolic, at the left sternal edge (LSE), louder on inspiration.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What does the ECG show in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: RVH (dominant R in V1–3, deep S in V5–6), right axis deviation, RBBB, P pulmonale (peaked P in II — RA enlargement).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is P pulmonale on ECG, and what does it indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: A peaked P wave in lead II — indicates RA enlargement.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What does the CXR show in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Dilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally ('pruning'); RV/RA enlargement; peripheral oligaemia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is 'pruning' on a CXR in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Dilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the role of NT-proBNP in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: ↑ — a right heart strain marker; correlates with severity and prognosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the key screening test for pulmonary hypertension, and what does it do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Echo — estimates pulmonary artery pressure (via TR jet velocity); assesses RV size/function; excludes left heart disease (Group 2); guides referral.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How does echo estimate pulmonary artery pressure in PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Via the tricuspid regurgitation (TR) jet velocity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Right heart catheterisation — direct measurement of PAP and pulmonary vascular resistance; confirms diagnosis; vasoreactivity testing (to guide CCB therapy in Group 1).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What does vasoreactivity testing on right heart catheterisation guide?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: CCB therapy in Group 1.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What do PFTs identify in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Group 3 (obstructive/restrictive lung disease).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which imaging test screens for Group 4 PH (CTEPH), and what does CTPA add?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: V/Q scan is the screening test — more sensitive than CTPA for chronic organised thrombus, and a NORMAL V/Q effectively excludes CTEPH. CTPA (or conventional pulmonary angiography) then defines the lesions and helps decide operability, but a negative CTPA does NOT exclude CTEPH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What do autoantibodies (ANA, anti-Scl-70, anti-dsDNA) identify in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Connective tissue disease (Group 1 — scleroderma, SLE).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the guiding principle of pulmonary hypertension management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Treat the underlying cause first (by WHO group). PAH-specific vasodilator drugs are for Group 1 only — not for other groups.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How is Group 2 PH (left heart disease) treated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Treat the left heart (diuretics, ACEi, valve surgery).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How is Group 3 PH treated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Optimise the underlying COPD/ILD. Add LTOT only if the patient meets the standard chronic hypoxaemia criteria — it reduces hypoxic vasoconstriction, but it is prescribed for the hypoxaemia rather than for the PH itself. There is no PAH-specific drug therapy for Group 3.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How is Group 4 PH (CTEPH) treated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Lifelong anticoagulation + pulmonary endarterectomy (potentially curative). If inoperable: riociguat and/or balloon pulmonary angioplasty.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What supportive treatments are used across all PH groups?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: O₂ (especially Group 3); diuretics (peripheral oedema/ascites); anticoagulation (lifelong in Group 4 CTEPH; no longer routine in idiopathic Group 1 PAH); avoid pregnancy; supervised exercise.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the aim of PAH-specific therapy in Group 1?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: To reduce pulmonary vascular resistance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which prostanoids are used in Group 1 PAH, and how are they given?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Epoprostenol (IV), iloprost (inhaled).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) are used in Group 1 PAH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Bosentan, macitentan.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which PDE-5 inhibitors are used in Group 1 PAH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Sildenafil, tadalafil.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: When are calcium channel blockers (CCBs) used in Group 1 PAH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Only if vasoreactive on right heart catheter testing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the end-stage management option for refractory PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Lung or heart-lung transplant — for refractory Group 1 PAH or Group 4 CTEPH not suitable for endarterectomy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Summarise the 5 WHO groups of PH (exam pearl).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: 1 = PAH (CTD/idiopathic), 2 = left heart (commonest), 3 = lung/hypoxia (COPD), 4 = CTEPH (chronic PE), 5 = misc.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the classic PH exam vignette regarding examination and syncope?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Loud P2 + exertional syncope = classic PH exam vignette; syncope = fixed low output.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Why must PAH-specific drugs not be used in Group 2 PH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: They can worsen LV failure — PAH-specific drugs (sildenafil, ERAs, prostanoids) are for Group 1 only.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Which connective tissue disease has the highest PAH risk, and how should it be monitored?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) — the highest PAH risk among CTDs; screen annually with echo.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: In Group 3 PH, what does LTOT do — and in whom is it actually indicated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: LTOT reduces hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. It is indicated only in patients who meet the standard chronic hypoxaemia criteria — it is prescribed for the hypoxaemia, not for the PH itself. Alongside it, optimise the underlying COPD/ILD; there is no PAH-specific drug therapy for Group 3.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is riociguat, and where is it used in pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: A soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator that reduces pulmonary vascular resistance. Used in Group 1 PAH and in inoperable/persistent Group 4 CTEPH. (Do not combine with PDE-5 inhibitors — hypotension.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: A patient has suspected pulmonary hypertension on echocardiography. Where must they be referred, and what happens only there?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Prompt referral to a nationally designated specialist PH centre. Right heart catheterisation and the initiation of PAH-specific drugs happen ONLY at those centres — never in a general respiratory or cardiology clinic. Care is then shared: the centre owns diagnosis, drug decisions and risk assessment; the local team manages diuretics, oxygen, comorbidity and acute illness.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: Describe WHO functional class I–IV in pulmonary hypertension.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: I = no limitation of ordinary physical activity. II = slight limitation; comfortable at rest but ordinary activity causes symptoms. III = MARKED limitation; less than ordinary activity causes symptoms. IV = symptoms at rest, with signs of right heart failure; any activity worsens them. Effectively the NYHA class of the pulmonary circulation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What contraceptive advice must a woman of childbearing age with PAH be given, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Pregnancy is contraindicated in PAH — maternal mortality is very high, and higher still in Eisenmenger syndrome — because the fall in systemic vascular resistance and rise in circulating volume cannot be met by a fixed, obstructed pulmonary circulation. Contraception is therefore discussed at diagnosis with every woman of childbearing age, and planned with the specialist centre, because several PAH drugs are teratogenic and some reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraception. An unplanned pregnancy warrants urgent specialist PH centre referral.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: What is the prognosis of idiopathic PAH, and where does palliative care fit?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: PAH is progressive and incurable — treatment slows it but does not reverse the vasculopathy, and survival is measured in years rather than decades, though it is markedly better in those who respond to treatment and keep responding. Palliative care runs IN PARALLEL with active disease-targeted treatment — breathlessness, syncope, fatigue, advance care planning — delivered via the specialist centre MDT. It is not 'giving up' and is currently under-used.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: How does right heart catheterisation distinguish pre-capillary from post-capillary pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: Pre-capillary PH: the wedge pressure is NORMAL, so the obstruction lies in the pulmonary vasculature itself (WHO Groups 1, 3 and 4). Post-capillary PH: the wedge pressure is RAISED, so the pressure is being transmitted back from the left heart (Group 2). Being pre-capillary does not by itself make vasodilators appropriate: PAH-specific drugs are for Group 1 (plus riociguat in inoperable Group 4), are not used in Group 3, and are harmful in Group 2 — the 'Group 1 yes, Group 2 no' rule.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.front: In suspected CTEPH, which imaging test screens and which defines operability — and who decides?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hyper.back: V/Q scan is the screening test of choice: more sensitive than CTPA for chronic organised thrombus, and a NORMAL V/Q effectively excludes CTEPH. CTPA or conventional pulmonary angiography is then used to define the lesions and decide operability (proximal accessible disease vs distal). Operability is decided by a CTEPH multidisciplinary team at an expert centre — never locally. The diagnosis is only made after ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is lifelong whether or not endarterectomy is performed.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Repeated pharyngeal airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas (≥10 sec cessation) → recurrent micro-arousals + intermittent hypoxia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: How long must airflow cease to count as an apnoea in OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: ≥10 seconds.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Who is the classic OSA patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: An overweight, middle-aged man (also children with enlarged tonsils).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What are the two consequence streams of OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Sleep fragmentation → daytime symptoms; and intermittent hypoxia → cardiovascular risk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Outline the pathophysiological cycle of OSA.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Sleep → pharyngeal dilator muscles become hypotonic → airway sucked closed on inspiration → apnoea → struggle to breathe → brief arousal (patient unaware; hundreds per night) → airway reopens → cycle repeats throughout the night.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Why does the airway collapse during sleep in OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: The pharyngeal dilator muscles become hypotonic, so the airway is sucked closed on inspiration.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Describe Stream 1 of OSA consequences (sleep fragmentation).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Hundreds of micro-arousals → never reaches deep restorative sleep → excessive daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, mood change, morning headache.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Describe Stream 2 of OSA consequences (intermittent hypoxia).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Repeated desaturations → sympathetic activation → hypertension (especially resistant), ↑MI/stroke risk, arrhythmias (AF), cor pulmonale.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What type of hypertension is especially associated with OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Resistant hypertension.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the biggest modifiable risk factor for OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Obesity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: List the risk factors for OSA.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Obesity (biggest modifiable RF), male sex, middle age, large neck circumference, enlarged tonsils/adenoids (children), retrognathia/craniofacial abnormality, alcohol/sedatives (↑muscle relaxation), smoking, hypothyroidism, acromegaly.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Why do alcohol and sedatives increase OSA risk?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: They increase muscle relaxation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Which endocrine conditions are risk factors for OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Hypothyroidism and acromegaly.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What are the nocturnal clinical features of OSA (often partner-reported)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, nocturnal choking/gasping, restless sleep, nocturia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What are the daytime clinical features of OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Excessive daytime sleepiness (falling asleep driving, in meetings), unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, poor concentration, personality change, low libido.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What are the consequences of severe/untreated OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Resistant hypertension, cor pulmonale / right heart failure, AF, ↑MI/stroke risk, type 2 diabetes worsening, road traffic accidents.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and how is it scored?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: A screening tool — the patient rates likelihood of dozing in 8 everyday situations (0–3 each; max 24). >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness, warranting investigation. It is SUBJECTIVE and quantifies sleepiness only: it does not diagnose OSA, correlates poorly with the AHI, and a normal score does not exclude OSA. It cannot separate OSA from simple snoring — a sleep study does that.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What Epworth Sleepiness Scale score indicates excessive daytime sleepiness?
What sleep study is used first in the UK to diagnose OSA, and what does it measure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Home respiratory polygraphy is the first-line UK study — airflow, oximetry, respiratory effort, sometimes body position — giving the Apnoea–Hypopnoea Index (AHI) in events per hour. Overnight oximetry alone is the simpler alternative where polygraphy is unavailable. Full polysomnography (adding sleep staging, EEG and ECG) is the reference standard but is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected other sleep disorders.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the Apnoea–Hypopnoea Index (AHI), and what counts as an event?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: The average number of apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep. An apnoea is a cessation of airflow lasting at least 10 seconds; a hypopnoea is a REDUCTION rather than cessation of airflow, also lasting at least 10 seconds, accompanied by oxygen desaturation and/or an arousal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the role of home oximetry in OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Overnight pulse oximetry — frequent saw-tooth desaturations are suggestive. It is the simpler, cheaper alternative where home respiratory polygraphy is not available. Note the UK order: polygraphy first-line, oximetry as the alternative, full polysomnography reserved for uncertainty.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What oximetry pattern is suggestive of OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Frequent desaturations (a saw-tooth pattern).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What AHI range is normal?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: <5 events/hour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What AHI range defines mild OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: 5–14 events/hour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What AHI range defines moderate OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: 15–29 events/hour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What AHI defines severe OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: ≥30 events/hour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What conservative measures are recommended for all OSA patients?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Weight loss (most important modifiable factor; can resolve mild OSA), avoid alcohol and sedatives (↑muscle relaxation), smoking cessation, lateral sleep position, treat hypothyroidism/acromegaly if present.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the most important modifiable factor in OSA management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Weight loss — it can resolve mild OSA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the mainstay treatment for moderate/severe OSA, and how does it work?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) — a tight nasal/full-face mask delivers continuous positive pressure to pneumatically splint the upper airway open. Used every night.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What outcomes does CPAP improve in OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Reliably improves sleepiness, cognition and quality of life, and modestly lowers blood pressure (most in resistant hypertension). Randomised trials have NOT shown a reduction in major cardiovascular events — treat that benefit as plausible but unproven.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is a mandibular advancement device, and who is it for?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: An oral appliance that protrudes the lower jaw → opens the oropharyngeal space. For mild OSA, simple snorers, or CPAP-intolerant patients.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What surgical option is often curative for OSA in children, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Tonsillectomy — for children with enlarged tonsils, often curative.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is UPPP (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty), and how effective is it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: It resects the uvula/soft palate; variable results in adults.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What are the DVLA notification rules for OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Tiered, not blanket. OSA without sleepiness likely to impair driving: may drive, no notification. MILD OSAS with excessive sleepiness: must not drive until satisfactorily controlled, and notify the DVLA only if it is not controlled within 3 months. MODERATE or SEVERE OSAS with excessive sleepiness: must not drive and MUST notify the DVLA; resume only once the sleep service confirms symptom control and documented CPAP compliance. Group 2 (bus/lorry) is held to the same standard more strictly, with at least annual review. Above every tier: nobody with sleepiness likely to impair driving may drive, whatever the AHI. It is the PATIENT who notifies — your duty is to advise clearly and document it.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Which patients with OSA must notify the DVLA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Anyone with moderate or severe OSAS and excessive sleepiness — Group 1 as well as Group 2 — must stop driving and notify. Mild OSAS with sleepiness notifies only if not controlled within 3 months. OSA without impairing sleepiness does not notify at all. Group 2 is held to the same standard more strictly and reviewed at least annually. It is a common error to think only Group 2 notifies.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Summarise the OSA definition and severity thresholds (exam pearl).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Apnoea = ≥10 sec cessation. Severity by AHI: mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥30.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What is the classic OSA vignette?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Obese middle-aged man + loud snoring + partner witnesses apnoeas + daytime sleepiness.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Distinguish the roles of the Epworth scale and polysomnography in OSA (exam pearl).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Epworth >10 = abnormal, but it is a subjective measure of sleepiness and cannot diagnose OSA or separate it from simple snoring. A sleep study makes the diagnosis — in the UK, home respiratory polygraphy first-line, with full polysomnography as the reference standard reserved for uncertainty.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Summarise the OSA treatment exam pearl (mainstay and alternatives).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: CPAP = mainstay for moderate-to-severe OSAHS — and NICE also offers it in MILD OSAHS where symptoms affect quality of life and lifestyle measures have failed, so it is not moderate/severe only. Mandibular advancement device for mild disease or CPAP intolerance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Why must weight loss and avoidance of alcohol/sedatives be emphasised in OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Weight loss is the most important modifiable factor; alcohol and sedatives worsen pharyngeal collapse.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: What cardiovascular consequences should make you think of OSA?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Resistant hypertension (think OSA in any patient with poorly controlled BP), AF, ↑MI/stroke, cor pulmonale.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: How does OSA cross-reference with pulmonary hypertension?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: OSA is a Group 3 cause of pulmonary hypertension (hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction → cor pulmonale).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Per NICE, when is CPAP offered in OSA (not just moderate/severe)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: CPAP is offered for symptomatic OSAHS that affects quality of life across all severities — including mild OSA where lifestyle measures (weight loss, alcohol avoidance) have not worked. It remains the mainstay for moderate/severe disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: A patient with moderate OSA has been started on CPAP. What is the adherence benchmark, and how should CPAP be followed up?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Adherence is the central practical problem — a machine in the cupboard treats nothing. Benefit is dose-dependent, and the conventional benchmark is ≥4 hours per night on most nights; more hours give more improvement in sleepiness and blood pressure. Follow-up: review the machine download / telemonitoring data in the first few weeks (hours used, nights used, mask leak, residual AHI), because that is when nearly all dropout happens and when problems are still fixable. Once CPAP is optimised and the patient is established, NICE supports annual review. Frame early failure as a solvable technical problem, not 'non-compliance'.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Name the four common reasons patients abandon CPAP, and the fix for each.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: 1) Mask fit or leak (air in the eyes, noisy leak, pressure marks) → re-fit and re-size, try a different interface (nasal pillows / nasal mask / full-face), adjust straps rather than over-tightening. 2) Nasal dryness or congestion (dry mouth and nose, blocked nose, nosebleeds) → heated humidification, the NICE answer for CPAP-related upper-airway side effects; plus nasal saline, treat rhinitis, and a chin strap or full-face mask if mouth leak is drying the airway. 3) Claustrophobia → desensitisation: hold the mask on while awake, then wear it with the machine running in the daytime, then part of the night, building up. 4) Pressure intolerance ('too much air', cannot breathe out, aerophagia) → re-titration: ramp, expiratory pressure relief, or an auto-titrating device.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: A patient with OSA is still excessively sleepy despite being on CPAP. How do you work through it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: In order: (1) Is it actually being used? Check the adherence download — hours per night and nights used; most 'CPAP failure' is under-use. (2) Is it working? Check the residual AHI and the leak figure — a high residual AHI is a titration or interface problem, not a failed treatment. (3) Is something else causing the sleepiness? Exclude depression, shift work or simply insufficient time in bed, drugs (sedatives, opioids, antihistamines, alcohol) and narcolepsy. (4) Only then, with adherent and optimised CPAP and no other explanation, consider a specialist-initiated wakefulness-promoting agent (solriamfetol is NICE-approved for residual excessive sleepiness in OSA; modafinil is an alternative) as an adjunct — added to CPAP, never instead of it.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Set out the DVLA rules for a Group 1 (car/motorcycle) driver with OSA — it is tiered, not blanket.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: OSA WITHOUT sleepiness likely to impair driving: may continue to drive, and there is no need to notify the DVLA. MILD OSAS with excessive sleepiness: must not drive until the sleepiness is satisfactorily controlled, and must notify the DVLA only if it is not controlled within 3 months. MODERATE or SEVERE OSAS with excessive sleepiness: must not drive AND must notify the DVLA; driving may resume only once the sleep clinic confirms both symptom control and documented CPAP compliance. Overriding rule: nobody with sleepiness likely to impair driving may drive, whatever the AHI. Group 1 licences are reviewed at least every 3 years.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: How do the DVLA rules differ for a Group 2 (bus/lorry) driver with OSA, and what is the doctor's own legal duty?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: Group 2 applies the same standard more strictly: licensing depends on confirmed symptom control plus documented CPAP compliance verified by the sleep service, and the licence is reviewed at least annually (Group 1: at least every 3 years). The doctor's duty is to ADVISE — it is the patient who must notify the DVLA. Tell them clearly, and document that you did. You inform the DVLA yourself only if the patient continues to drive against that advice, having first tried to persuade them and told them you intend to do so.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Weight loss is the most important modifiable factor in OSA — how is it actually delivered?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: A 5–10% reduction in body weight can meaningfully lower the AHI and can resolve mild OSA outright. Deliver it by referring to a structured or specialist weight-management service, not by bare 'lose some weight' advice in clinic. Weight-loss pharmacotherapy is available via specialist weight-management services where criteria are met — note these drugs are licensed for weight management (with OSA among the qualifying comorbidities), not as treatments for OSA itself. Bariatric surgery: consider at BMI ≥40, or BMI 35–39.9 with a significant health condition that would improve with weight loss — OSA counts (NICE). Lower thresholds apply for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African and African-Caribbean family background.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.front: Why does OSA matter before an anaesthetic, and what changes in the perioperative plan?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sle.back: OSA is a perioperative risk factor: the same pharyngeal collapse that causes the disease is worsened by anaesthetic agents, sedatives and opioids. Screen surgical patients — STOP-BANG is the standard pre-op tool. Anticipate a difficult airway (difficult mask ventilation and intubation). Minimise long-acting opioids and sedatives, favouring regional and multimodal non-opioid analgesia. Continue the patient's own CPAP peri- and post-operatively, so ask them to bring their machine in, and arrange extended recovery/post-operative monitoring for hypoxia. Day surgery is not automatically contraindicated — OSA is a reason to plan carefully, not an automatic bar.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: A severe type 1 (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction → mast cell degranulation → histamine release → airway / breathing / circulation compromise. Rapid onset is the hallmark.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the hallmark of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Rapid onset.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the underlying mechanism of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Mast cell degranulation → histamine release.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the common food triggers of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Nuts, shellfish, egg, milk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the common triggers of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Foods (nuts, shellfish, egg, milk), insect venom (bee/wasp stings), drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs, contrast media), latex, and idiopathic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Which drugs are common triggers of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Penicillins, NSAIDs, contrast media.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the core framing of anaphylaxis management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: It is an emergency. The entire management reduces to: Recognition → IM adrenaline. Everything else is adjunctive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What clinically defines anaphylaxis (vs an allergic reaction)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Anaphylaxis = acute onset + life-threatening A/B/C compromise, usually with skin changes. Skin changes alone (urticaria, angioedema) without A/B/C = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Do skin changes alone make a diagnosis of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: No — skin changes alone (urticaria, angioedema) without A/B/C compromise = an allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the airway features of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Swelling, hoarseness, stridor — upper airway oedema threatening occlusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the breathing features of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: SOB, wheeze (bronchospasm), hypoxia, increasing respiratory fatigue.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the circulation features of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Hypotension, tachycardia, collapse, light-headedness, pallor.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What are the skin features of anaphylaxis, and what is their diagnostic caveat?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Urticaria, itching, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, eyes). Usually present, but not required alone.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the first and most important action in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IM adrenaline — give before antihistamines and steroids.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What concentration, route, and site is used for adrenaline in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IM adrenaline 1:1000 — into the anterolateral thigh (middle third).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the adult dose of IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: 500 mcg (0.5 mL). Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How often can IM adrenaline be repeated in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: After 5 minutes if no improvement.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Why is adrenaline given IM not IV in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IM, not IV — IV is specialist-only (arrhythmia risk).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How is Airway + Breathing (A/B) managed in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Secure airway (call anaesthetics early if stridor). High-flow O₂ via non-rebreathe. Salbutamol nebuliser if wheeze.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: When should anaesthetics be called in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Early, if stridor is present.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How is Circulation (C) managed in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IV access; IV fluid bolus (500–1000 mL crystalloid adult; 10 mL/kg child). Monitor ECG and BP.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What IV fluid bolus is given in anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: 500–1000 mL crystalloid in an adult; 10 mL/kg in a child.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How should the patient be positioned in anaphylaxis (D — Position)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Lie flat + raise legs (improves venous return and cerebral perfusion); if pregnant, left lateral tilt. Sit up only if breathing is the dominant problem. Do NOT sit or stand the patient up suddenly — it can precipitate cardiac arrest (empty ventricle).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: When should an anaphylaxis patient be sat up rather than lain flat?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Only if breathing is the dominant problem.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What adjuncts are used in anaphylaxis, and when (RCUK 2021)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Only AFTER A/B/C is stabilised — never instead of adrenaline. A non-sedating oral antihistamine (cetirizine) for residual skin symptoms. Corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended (removed from the 2021 algorithm).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the role of corticosteroids (hydrocortisone) in acute anaphylaxis (RCUK 2021)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: No longer routinely recommended for emergency treatment — removed from the 2021 algorithm (no evidence they prevent biphasic reactions; can delay discharge). Previously 200 mg IV hydrocortisone was given.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Why are steroids no longer routine, and antihistamines de-emphasised, in acute anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Adrenaline is the only life-saving treatment and the priority. Steroids were removed from the 2021 algorithm (no proven benefit for biphasic reactions); antihistamines only help skin symptoms and are given after stabilisation, not as acute treatment.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the IM adrenaline (1:1000) dose for a child <6 months?
What is the IM adrenaline (1:1000) dose for a child 6 months – 6 years?
What is the IM adrenaline (1:1000) dose for a child 6 – 12 years?
What is the IM adrenaline (1:1000) dose for >12 years / adult?
How is refractory anaphylaxis defined?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Respiratory/cardiovascular compromise persisting despite 2 IM adrenaline doses.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How is refractory anaphylaxis managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Continue IV fluid resuscitation (adults 500–1000 mL; children 10 mL/kg boluses); senior/expert help immediately; IV adrenaline infusion — specialist/ITU only (arrhythmia risk requires monitoring); consider intubation if airway deteriorating.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Who can give an IV adrenaline infusion in refractory anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Specialist/ITU only (arrhythmia risk requires monitoring).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is serum mast cell tryptase, and when is it taken?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: A marker confirming mast cell degranulation. Ideally 3 timed samples: as soon as possible after treatment starts; 1–2 h (no later than 4 h) after symptom onset; and >24 h / convalescence as baseline.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the ideal serial sampling schedule for mast cell tryptase?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Sample 1: ASAP after treatment starts. Sample 2: 1–2 h (no later than 4 h) after symptom onset. Sample 3: >24 h / convalescence (baseline).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is a biphasic reaction, and how does it shape the observation period (RCUK 2021)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Recurrence of anaphylaxis hours later without re-exposure. Observation is risk-stratified and timed FROM RESOLUTION OF SYMPTOMS, not from arrival: 2 h (good response to a single dose given within 30 min of onset, full resolution, has an auto-injector and supervision after discharge), 6 h (2 doses needed or prior biphasic), 12 h (severe — >2 doses, severe asthma, possible ongoing absorption, or late presentation). Children under 16 treated for suspected anaphylaxis are admitted under a paediatric team.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is given for persisting skin symptoms in the immediate post-acute phase?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: A non-sedating antihistamine.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What auto-injector provision is part of discharge planning after anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Two adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed (EpiPen/Jext) + technique demonstrated.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What discharge planning steps follow an anaphylaxis event?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Two adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed (EpiPen/Jext) + technique demonstrated; allergy clinic referral (all new diagnoses); written action plan + trigger avoidance advice; medical alert bracelet (Medic-Alert) discussion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Who should be referred to an allergy clinic after anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: All new diagnoses.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the recognition exam pearl for anaphylaxis.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Anaphylaxis = acute onset + A/B/C compromise — skin changes alone ≠ anaphylaxis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the adrenaline exam pearl (importance, site, repeat).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IM adrenaline = first and most important — anterolateral thigh, repeat at 5 min.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the IM vs IV adrenaline exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: IM, not IV (IV adrenaline is specialist-only — arrhythmia risk).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the adult dose exam pearl for adrenaline.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Adult dose: 500 mcg (0.5 mL 1:1000); know doses by age.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the refractory anaphylaxis exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Refractory = persists after 2 doses → IV fluids + senior help + adrenaline infusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the mast cell tryptase exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Serial mast cell tryptase (ASAP, 1–2 h, >24 h baseline) supports the diagnosis — but a normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis, particularly food-triggered reactions.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the biphasic reaction exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Biphasic reaction — observe before discharge.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Summarise the discharge exam pearl for anaphylaxis.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: 2 auto-injectors + allergy referral on discharge.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What hypersensitivity type is anaphylaxis, and how does it cross-reference?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Type 1 hypersensitivity (IgE/mast cell) — cross-ref hypersensitivity reactions.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Which anaphylaxis mimics do NOT respond to adrenaline — and what should you do if you are unsure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Two: (1) Inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO, formerly vocal cord dysfunction) — paradoxical cord adduction, not oedema; (2) ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema — bradykinin-mediated, not mast-cell mediated, and still life-threatening. BUT the RCUK safety rule overrides the uncertainty: where the diagnosis is in doubt, IM adrenaline is unlikely to cause harm — give it. The harm of withholding adrenaline in true anaphylaxis vastly outweighs the harm of giving it to a mimic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: How do life-threatening asthma, vasovagal faint and a panic attack differ from anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Life-threatening asthma: wheeze/hypoxia/silent chest, usually no urticaria and no exposure — but can be clinically indistinguishable, especially in children, and the two coexist; adrenaline still helps (a recognised rescue in life-threatening asthma unresponsive to standard treatment), so this is a safe mistake. Vasovagal faint: BRADYcardia (not tachycardia), pallor, sweating, rapid recovery when laid supine, no urticaria, no bronchospasm. Panic attack: subjective throat tightness and breathlessness but NO objective A/B/C compromise and no skin changes — saturations and BP normal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the single biggest risk factor for a FATAL food anaphylaxis, and which risk factors for death are modifiable?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Co-existing asthma — especially if poorly controlled — is the single biggest risk factor for fatal food anaphylaxis (death is usually from bronchospasm, not upper airway occlusion). The two MODIFIABLE risk factors are: delayed adrenaline, and upright posture at the time of collapse. Risk of death peaks in adolescents and young adults (~10-24 years). This is also why the 12-hour observation criterion singles out severe asthma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Which cofactors turn a mild allergic reaction into anaphylaxis, and what is food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Cofactors: exercise, alcohol, NSAIDs, intercurrent infection, and underlying mast-cell disease (mastocytosis — suspect if the BASELINE tryptase is persistently raised). Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis is the classic example: the patient eats wheat safely every day but reacts after a run. The food alone is tolerated; the food PLUS the cofactor is not. Unless you ask specifically about exercise, alcohol and NSAIDs in the hours around the reaction, the trigger looks idiopathic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What must a patient be told about using their adrenaline auto-injector at discharge?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: (1) Carry BOTH devices at all times and check they are in date. (2) Use it early — outer thigh, through clothing if necessary. (3) After using one, call 999 and say the word 'anaphylaxis' — even if feeling better; the word changes the ambulance response. (4) Lie flat with the legs raised; sit up ONLY if breathing is the problem, and lie back down as soon as possible; NEVER stand up. (5) Use the second device 5 minutes after the first if not improving. (6) Always attend hospital after any use, because of the biphasic risk.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: Why must a patient who has just used an adrenaline auto-injector never stand up?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: The empty-ventricle mechanism. The patient is vasodilated and effectively fluid-depleted; standing removes the venous return that is holding cardiac output up, the right ventricle empties, and cardiac arrest can follow. Deaths have occurred at the exact moment of standing. The hospital algorithm already says never to sit or stand the patient up suddenly — the same rule must be carried into discharge advice, because the street is where it is most likely to be broken. Tell them plainly: lie down, legs up, do not stand up, not even to walk to the ambulance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What does the allergy clinic actually do after an episode of anaphylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: It confirms the trigger — skin prick testing, allergen-specific IgE, and where genuine doubt remains a supervised challenge (the gold standard) — and then builds the avoidance advice and written emergency plan around that answer. It also assesses whether the patient is a candidate for venom immunotherapy, and checks the convalescent (baseline) tryptase for underlying mast-cell disease. Referral is therefore not administrative. See the Allergy & Immunodeficiency note (Immunology / Serology) for how the tests are performed and interpreted.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.front: What is venom immunotherapy, who is it for, and how effective is it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis.back: Escalating then maintenance subcutaneous venom injections given over several years under specialist supervision, for patients who have had a systemic (anaphylactic) reaction to a wasp or bee sting. It is highly effective — roughly 95% protection for wasp venom and about 80% for bee venom. It is the disease-modifying treatment for venom anaphylaxis: it converts a patient who would otherwise carry adrenaline for life into one who is largely protected. NICE recommends that people who have had a systemic reaction to insect venom are referred for specialist assessment for venom immunotherapy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What does NICE recommend for smokers who want to quit?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: NICE: offer a choice of effective quit aids alongside behavioural support — NRT, a nicotine-containing e-cigarette (vape), varenicline, cytisine, or bupropion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: How is the smoking cessation topic framed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: The classic three pharmacological agents (a comparison) + two current additions (a nicotine vape and cytisine) + one special case: pregnancy (different rules apply). It is the universal cross-topic intervention — appears in COPD, IHD, lung cancer, PAD, OSA, and stroke prevention.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is the mechanism of NRT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Nicotine replacement — reduces withdrawal symptoms.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is the mechanism of varenicline (Champix)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Nicotinic receptor partial agonist — reduces craving (agonist) + blocks nicotine reward (antagonist).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is the mechanism of bupropion (Zyban)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Noradrenaline/dopamine reuptake inhibitor + nicotinic antagonist — reduces craving and withdrawal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: When is NRT started relative to the quit date?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: At the quit date.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: When is varenicline started, and for how long is it continued?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: 1 week before the quit date; continue for 12 weeks.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: When is bupropion started relative to the quit date?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: 1–2 weeks before the quit date.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the key side effects of NRT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Nausea, headache, flu-like symptoms, local irritation (patch/gum).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the key side effects of varenicline?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Nausea (commonest), insomnia, vivid/abnormal dreams, mood change.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is the commonest side effect of varenicline?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Nausea.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the key side effects of bupropion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Seizures (most important), insomnia, dry mouth, headache.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is the most important side effect of bupropion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Seizures.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the cautions/contraindications for NRT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Caution in acute MI and unstable angina; remove the patch before sleep if vivid dreams.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the cautions/contraindications for varenicline?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Caution: depression / history of self-harm; contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the contraindications for bupropion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Contraindicated in epilepsy (lowers seizure threshold), pregnancy and breastfeeding, eating disorders, and bipolar.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: Why is bupropion contraindicated in epilepsy?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: It lowers the seizure threshold.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the three distinguishing hooks for the smoking cessation agents?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Varenicline = partial agonist + vivid dreams + mood caution; bupropion = seizure risk + CI in epilepsy; NRT = combine patch + fast-acting for high dependence.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What is long-acting (baseline) NRT, and what is the dosing caveat?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Transdermal patch (16h or 24h) — gives a steady background level. The 24h patch: remove before sleep if causing insomnia or vivid dreams.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.front: What are the short-acting (craving relief) forms of NRT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessati.back: Gum, lozenge, nasal spray, inhalator, sublingual tablet — faster absorption to manage acute cravings.
