conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Klebsiella → alcoholic + red-currant jelly sputum; Legionella → air-con + hyponatraemia; Mycoplasma → cold agglutinins / erythema multiforme; Coxiella → farmer; psittaci → parrot; PCP → HIV / clear chest / exertional desaturation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: how are atypical pneumonias treated and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Macrolide or doxycycline (not penicillin — Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall; Legionella/Chlamydophila/Coxiella are intracellular and/or lack classic peptidoglycan).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: summarise CURB-65 management bands.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: 0–1 home; 2 admit; ≥3 severe/ITU.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: what are the antibiotic timing and CXR follow-up rules?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Don't delay antibiotics — within 4 hours. A follow-up CXR is not routine (NICE) — consider one at 6 weeks only with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease (e.g. smokers, over 50).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: summarise the empyema criteria and action.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Frank pus or organisms = empyema → drain. Otherwise drain if pH <7.2 (glucose <2.2, LDH >1000) — a complicated parapneumonic effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: how is PCP treated and prophylaxed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Co-trimoxazole + steroids if hypoxic; prophylaxis if CD4 <200.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: what are the consolidation signs?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Bronchial breathing + dullness + focal crackles.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Exam pearl: which lobe does aspiration pneumonia affect and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Right middle/lower lobe (vertical R main bronchus).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: NICE: which adults with community-acquired pneumonia should be considered for a corticosteroid, and for how long?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Adults in hospital with high-severity CAP — consider a corticosteroid in addition to antibiotics, for 4–7 days or until discharge if sooner. One of the named important changes to practice in the current NICE pneumonia guidance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Which corticosteroid does NICE suggest starting with in high-severity CAP, and what is the alternative?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Consider starting with IV hydrocortisone; use an alternative such as dexamethasone if hydrocortisone is unsuitable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: A patient with CAP is no better at 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics. What are the five forks of the differential?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: 1. Complication — empyema, lung abscess, necrotising pneumonia. 2. Wrong bug — atypical, resistant organism, TB. 3. Wrong host — undiagnosed immunosuppression, PCP. 4. Obstruction — endobronchial tumour or foreign body. 5. Wrong diagnosis — PE, pulmonary oedema, organising pneumonia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: What triggers the 48–72 hour pneumonia review, and what do you do first if a complication is suspected?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Trigger: fever persisting, CRP not falling, or a worsening oxygen requirement at 48–72 h of appropriate antibiotics. If a complication is suspected: repeat CXR, thoracic ultrasound and a pleural tap of any collection (pH, glucose, LDH, MC&S); CT chest if abscess or necrosis is suspected. Do not simply broaden the antibiotic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: What does NICE say about a follow-up chest X-ray after pneumonia?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Do not routinely offer a follow-up CXR after discharge. Consider one at 6 weeks only for people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease (e.g. smokers, people over 50), as a shared decision. The old universal 6-week film is no longer the rule.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: Give the BTS recovery milestones after pneumonia — what patients actually ask about.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: ~1 week: fever resolved. ~4 weeks: chest pain and sputum substantially reduced. ~6 weeks: cough and breathlessness substantially reduced. ~3 months: most symptoms resolved but fatigue may persist. ~6 months: back to normal.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.front: What belongs in the discharge bundle after an admission with pneumonia?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia.back: Check pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination status and arrange what is outstanding; offer smoking cessation; and if the pneumonia is recurrent or involves the same lobe twice, look for an underlying cause (bronchial obstruction, bronchiectasis, aspiration/unsafe swallow, immunodeficiency). Warn about persistent fatigue and advise a graded return to activity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the respiratory support escalation ladder?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula → non-invasive ventilation → mechanical ventilation → ECMO.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the two most-examined anchors in respiratory support?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Oxygen saturation targets (which patient gets what %) and the CPAP vs BiPAP distinction (Type 1 vs Type 2 respiratory failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What delivery options sit at the supplemental O₂ rung of the ladder?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Nasal cannula / mask / NRB / Venturi.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What flow does high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) deliver, and what else does it provide?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Up to 60 L/min + gentle PEEP.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Which form of non-invasive support is used for Type 1 vs Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Type 1 → CPAP; Type 2 → BiPAP. Strictly only BiPAP ventilates — in UK usage "NIV" means bilevel. CPAP is one constant distending pressure: it recruits alveoli and improves oxygenation but does not augment tidal volume or clear CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What does invasive mechanical ventilation require?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: ETT (endotracheal tube) + sedation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Where and for whom is ECMO used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Specialist centres; reversible failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the SpO₂ target for most acutely ill patients?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: 94–98%. Titrate O₂ to achieve and maintain this range.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the SpO₂ target and delivery for a patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Target SpO₂ 88–92% via a 24–28% Venturi mask, pending blood gases. The RISK sets the target — COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, severe kyphoscoliosis, bronchiectasis, CF — not a gas that has already proved hypercapnia; if the gas is normal, change to 94–98%. Controlled oxygen avoids worsening hypercapnia, mainly by not reversing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (V/Q mismatch); reduced hypoxic drive and the Haldane effect are lesser contributors. Drive nebulisers with air, not O₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Why is controlled oxygen used in CO₂ retainers?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: It avoids worsening hypercapnia. The main mechanism is V/Q mismatch — high-concentration oxygen reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so blood returns to poorly ventilated units that cannot clear CO₂. Reduced ventilatory drive ('hypoxic drive') and the Haldane effect are smaller contributors. Target SpO₂ 88–92%.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What should nebulisers be driven with in CO₂ retainers, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Air, not O₂ — to avoid worsening hypercapnia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: How is oxygen given to the critically ill (shock, arrest, anaphylaxis)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Start 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask — hypoxia kills acutely. Titrate down once stabilised. Never withhold O₂ in a crashing patient.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Should you ever withhold oxygen in a crashing patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: No — never withhold O₂ in a crashing patient; hypoxia kills acutely.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the single most examined O₂ prescribing rule?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: High-flow O₂ in the critically ill; controlled O₂ in CO₂ retainers (COPD).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What FiO₂ and flow does a nasal cannula deliver, and what are its key notes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: FiO₂ roughly 24–50%, flow 1–6 L/min (most often 2–4 L/min). Comfortable; patient can talk/eat; variable FiO₂ (affected by breathing pattern). Above about 6 L/min they are drying and uncomfortable without adding useful FiO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What FiO₂ and flow does a simple face mask (Hudson) deliver, and what are its key notes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: FiO₂ 40–60%, flow 5–10 L/min. Mild-moderate hypoxia; variable FiO₂; must run ≥5L (avoid CO₂ re-breathing).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Why must a simple face mask run at ≥5 L/min?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: To avoid CO₂ re-breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What FiO₂ and flow does a non-rebreather mask (reservoir) deliver, and what are its key notes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: FiO₂ ~60–80% in practice, flow 15 L/min. Severe/critically ill; variable FiO₂ — it entrains air around the mask, and the delivered FiO₂ falls as inspiratory flow rises. The highest FiO₂ available from a simple mask (high-flow nasal oxygen can deliver more, and more reliably).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Which device gives the highest O₂ delivery without intubation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: The non-rebreather mask (reservoir).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What FiO₂ and flow does a Venturi mask deliver, and where is it used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: FiO₂ 24–60%, flow per valve colour. Fixed/precise FiO₂ → use in COPD / CO₂ retainers. Colour-coded valves: blue 24%, white 28%, yellow 35%, red 40%, green 60%.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the Venturi mask colour-coded valve percentages?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Blue 24%, white 28%, yellow 35%, red 40%, green 60%.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Why is the Venturi mask described as fixed performance?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Because the valve entrains a fixed ratio of air to oxygen, so the delivered FiO₂ is known — unlike cannulae, simple masks and reservoir masks, whose FiO₂ varies with the breathing pattern. The caveat: it is only fixed performance if total flow exceeds the patient’s inspiratory flow, so turn the flow up above the figure printed on the valve in a very tachypnoeic patient.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Which oxygen device guarantees a known inspired O₂ concentration?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: The Venturi mask, among the standard oxygen masks — cannulae, simple masks and reservoir masks are all variable performance. High-flow nasal oxygen and a mechanical ventilator also deliver a set FiO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What does PEEP do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration, ↓atelectasis, improves oxygenation, ↓work of breathing, recruits collapsed lung units.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Which respiratory support modes add PEEP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: HFNC (small amount), CPAP/BiPAP (controlled), mechanical ventilator (precise titration).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: How does high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) work?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Delivers up to 60 L/min of warmed, humidified oxygen via wide-bore nasal prongs. Generates low-level PEEP, washes out nasopharyngeal dead space, reduces work of breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the role of HFNC?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: A bridge between standard O₂ and NIV — for patients failing standard O₂ who aren't yet in Type 2 failure. Well-tolerated, allows talking and eating. Mainly for Type 1 respiratory failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: For which type of respiratory failure is HFNC mainly used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Type 1 respiratory failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What pressure does CPAP deliver, and what does BiPAP deliver?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP = a constant single pressure throughout the breathing cycle. BiPAP = two pressures — higher iPAP (inspiration) + lower ePAP (expiration).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the action of CPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Splints airways and alveoli open; improves oxygenation; reduces work of breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the action of BiPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Actively assists ventilation — iPAP supports inspiration → ↓CO₂, ↑tidal volume.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Which failure type does CPAP treat, and which does BiPAP treat?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP = Type 1 RF (↓O₂, normal CO₂); BiPAP = Type 2 RF (↓O₂ + ↑CO₂). Note acidosis is not part of the definition of type 2 failure — it is what marks the acute, uncompensated form that needs NIV. Chronic compensated retainers have a normal pH and do not need acute NIV.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the indications for CPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Acute pulmonary oedema / cardiogenic, OSA, CCF.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the indications for BiPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: AECOPD with respiratory acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy (pH <7.35, PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa), neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the exam rule for CPAP vs BiPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP = oxygenation problem (Type 1); BiPAP = ventilation/CO₂ problem (Type 2).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: How is a COPD exacerbation with acidosis managed regarding BiPAP and intubation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: BiPAP once the gas shows respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa) persisting despite optimal medical therapy. A pH <7.25 does NOT mean intubate — it predicts a higher chance of NIV failure, so give NIV in HDU/ICU with immediate access to intubation and a documented escalation plan.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the indications for invasive mechanical ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: NIV failed/contraindicated; GCS ≤8 (can't protect airway); refractory hypoxia; haemodynamic instability; cardiac arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What GCS level indicates a patient can't protect their airway (an indication for intubation)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: GCS ≤8.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What access is used for invasive mechanical ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Endotracheal tube (ETT) for short-term; tracheostomy for prolonged ventilation. Requires sedation ± paralysis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the key settings for invasive mechanical ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume (~6 mL/kg ideal body weight — lung protective), PEEP, I:E ratio. Aim: shortest duration possible.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: How does ECMO work?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Blood removed → oxygenated + CO₂ removed → returned.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the key characteristics and limits of ECMO?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Specialist ECMO centres only; reversible respiratory failure only; a bridge to recovery / transplant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: When is ECMO indicated?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: When all other measures have failed and the underlying cause is potentially reversible (e.g. severe ARDS, viral pneumonitis). Not a long-term solution.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the O₂ targets exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: 94–98% for most patients; 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD and similar) via a 24–28% Venturi, pending gases; 15L NRB for the critically ill.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the Venturi exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Venturi = fixed/precise FiO₂ (the fixed-performance standard mask) → use in COPD. Cannula/mask/NRB = variable performance. Turn the flow up above the valve’s marked rate if the patient is very tachypnoeic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the CPAP vs BiPAP exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP = Type 1 RF (oxygenation — pulmonary oedema, OSA); BiPAP = Type 2 RF (ventilation — COPD + hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the BiPAP-in-COPD exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: BiPAP in COPD: use when pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa despite optimal medical therapy. pH <7.25 → still NIV, but delivered at HDU/ICU level with a documented escalation plan. pH ≥7.35 → medical treatment first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the PEEP exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: PEEP = prevents alveolar collapse, recruits lung, improves oxygenation. Added by HFNC, CPAP/BiPAP, and mechanical ventilator.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What should nebulisers be driven with in a COPD exacerbation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Air, not O₂ (avoids worsening hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the escalation ladder exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Escalation ladder: O₂ → HFNC → NIV → mechanical ventilation → ECMO. Never skip steps without clinical indication.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the ECMO exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: ECMO = reversible failure only, specialist centres. Not a long-term solution — a bridge to recovery or transplant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Should oxygen be given to a breathless but non-hypoxic patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: No — oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness. Do not give it if SpO₂ is already ≥94%. Routine O₂ in acute MI or stroke without hypoxia is not recommended and can be harmful (avoid hyperoxia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Oxygen is a drug — how must it be prescribed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: On the drug chart against a written target saturation range (not a fixed flow rate), with the delivery device recorded and signed for at each drug round. Nursing staff titrate the device up or down to keep SpO2 in range. In an emergency, give high-concentration oxygen immediately and prescribe it retrospectively — never delay oxygen to find a drug chart. Oxygen is also a fire hazard: it vigorously supports combustion, so no smoking, no naked flames and no paraffin-based emollients near the face — counselled explicitly for anyone on home oxygen.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Why is an SpO2 above the prescribed target range a problem, not a success?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Because oxygen is being given that the patient does not need. Excess oxygen is harmful (hyperoxia), and in a patient at risk of hypercapnic failure it can drive a rising PaCO2 and respiratory acidosis. Above range means step the device down and wean, exactly as below range means step it up.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What is the MAIN mechanism by which high-concentration oxygen raises PaCO2 in COPD?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: V/Q mismatch. Poorly ventilated lung units are normally protected by hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which diverts blood away from them. High-concentration oxygen relaxes that vasoconstriction, so blood returns to units that cannot clear CO2 and the PaCO2 rises. BTS ranks this above the reduction in ventilatory drive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Rank the mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: 1) V/Q mismatch from loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction — the most important. 2) Reduced ventilatory drive (the classic 'hypoxic drive') — real but a smaller contributor. 3) The Haldane effect — oxygenated haemoglobin carries less CO2, releasing it into plasma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: A hypoxic COPD patient is at risk of CO2 retention. Should oxygen be withheld?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: No. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient for fear of CO2 retention. Treat the hypoxaemia using a controlled device (24-28% Venturi) to a target of 88-92%, then manage a rising CO2 with NIV if the pH falls. Hypoxia kills faster than hypercapnia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: In COPD, what should nebulisers be driven with — and what if only oxygen is available?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Air, not oxygen. If only oxygen is available to drive the nebuliser, limit it to 6 minutes.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Why can pulse oximetry read normal or high in carbon monoxide poisoning?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhaemoglobin, so the oximeter counts it as saturated. The SpO2 looks normal or high while the patient is profoundly hypoxic. Diagnosis needs a blood gas with co-oximetry to measure carboxyhaemoglobin directly.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: List the situations in which a pulse oximetry reading cannot be trusted.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal/high), poor peripheral perfusion (shock, cold peripheries, vasoconstriction), methaemoglobinaemia (reading drifts toward ~85%), darker skin pigmentation (overestimates true saturation, so occult hypoxaemia is missed), and nail varnish, dirt or motion artefact. If the clinical picture and the oximeter disagree, believe the patient and get an ABG.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What does SpO2 tell you about ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Nothing. SpO2 measures oxygenation only. A patient can sit at 92% with a rising PaCO2 and a falling pH while the monitor looks reassuring. Only a blood gas shows the CO2.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the contraindications to non-invasive ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Untreated pneumothorax (positive pressure can tension it — drain first); vomiting or high aspiration risk; facial trauma or burns, and recent upper airway or upper GI surgery; inability to protect the airway (reduced consciousness, copious secretions, fixed upper airway obstruction); and haemodynamic instability or cardiac arrest. These patients need intubation, not a mask.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are typical starting pressures for CPAP and for BiPAP?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP: a single pressure of about 5-10 cmH2O with FiO2 titrated to the target range. BiPAP: start ePAP 4-5 cmH2O and iPAP 10-15 cmH2O.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: On BiPAP the CO2 is not falling. Which setting should you change?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Increase the iPAP. It is the gradient between iPAP and ePAP that augments tidal volume and clears CO2 — raising the FiO2 improves the oxygen number without doing anything for the CO2.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: When should the ABG be repeated after starting NIV, and what shows it is working?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Repeat at about 1 hour, and after any significant change in settings. Working: pH rising toward normal, PaCO2 falling, respiratory rate settling, patient more comfortable. Failing: pH static or falling, CO2 unchanged or climbing, increasing drowsiness, exhaustion or mask intolerance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: A patient on NIV is becoming sleepy. What does this mean?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: They are deteriorating, not settling. Rising CO2 causes drowsiness, so a falling conscious level on NIV is a sign of failure and needs an urgent gas and escalation review — not reassurance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What complications does NIV itself cause?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Pressure sores over the nose bridge (the commonest reason patients refuse to continue), dry eyes and dry mouth, gastric distension, and aspiration.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What are the main complications of invasive mechanical ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (risk rises with every day tubed); barotrauma/volutrauma causing pneumothorax and lung injury — which is why tidal volumes are kept at about 6 mL/kg ideal body weight; hypotension from raised intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return and preload; and sedation-related delirium, ICU-acquired weakness and immobility risks.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: A patient becomes hypotensive immediately after intubation and ventilation. What is the likely mechanism?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Positive pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and therefore preload and cardiac output. It is a predictable consequence of the ventilator rather than a new diagnosis, though sedation drugs contribute.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: How is a patient weaned off invasive ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Weaning starts the day ventilation begins. Use a daily sedation hold, then a spontaneous breathing trial on minimal support to test whether the patient can do the work themselves. Extubate when the underlying cause is improving, oxygenation is adequate on low settings, the patient is awake enough to protect the airway, and can cough. Tracheostomy if ventilation is prolonged or weaning repeatedly fails.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What should you watch for immediately after extubation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Post-extubation stridor from laryngeal oedema, and the need for reintubation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is respiratory failure, and how is it defined?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: The lungs fail to oxygenate and/or remove CO₂, defined on ABG.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the central fork in respiratory failure, and what does it drive?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 (oxygenation failure) vs Type 2 (ventilation failure) — drives the cause, the management, and which form of non-invasive support to use.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the ABG definition of Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ↓PaO₂ (<8 kPa), normal or low CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the ABG definition of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ↓PaO₂ + ↑PaCO₂ (>6 kPa).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the core problem in Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Oxygenation failure (V/Q mismatch — blood not oxygenated).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the core problem in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Ventilation failure (can't blow off CO₂).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the causes of Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, asthma (early), ILD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the causes of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: COPD (commonest), severe asthma (late/tiring), neuromuscular disease (GBS, MND), opiates, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, chest wall deformity. Note OSA alone does not cause type 2 failure — it is the daytime hypoventilation of OHS that does.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the commonest cause of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: COPD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Which form of non-invasive support is used in Type 1 respiratory failure, and what does it do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: CPAP — it splints alveoli open and improves oxygenation. Note it does not ventilate, so strictly it is not NIV: it is non-invasive support.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Which form of non-invasive support is used in Type 2 respiratory failure, and what does it do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: BiPAP — the true NIV: it actively ventilates and so clears CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the O₂ target in Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 94–98% (standard).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Who gets an 88–92% oxygen target, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure — COPD, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall or neuromuscular disease — to avoid worsening hypercapnia. The risk sets the target; the ABG then confirms or releases it. Everyone else: 94–98%.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the tie-in rule linking respiratory failure type to non-invasive support?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 → CPAP (oxygenation problem); Type 2 → BiPAP (ventilation problem).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the danger sign of a tiring Type 1 respiratory failure patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 RF has ↓PaO₂ with low/normal CO₂ (patient hyperventilating to compensate); as the patient tires → respiratory muscles fail → can no longer hyperventilate → CO₂ starts to rise → normal or rising CO₂ = danger signal → progresses to Type 2 RF → exhaustion → arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is a normal or rising CO₂ a danger signal in a Type 1 RF patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It signals the patient is tiring — respiratory muscles can no longer hyperventilate, heralding progression to Type 2 RF, exhaustion, and arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is a normal PCO₂ life-threatening in acute asthma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: The patient should be blowing off CO₂; normalisation = exhaustion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the clinical features of hypoxia (both types of RF)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, cyanosis, confusion/agitation, tachycardia, use of accessory muscles.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the Type 2-specific (hypercapnia) clinical features?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: CO₂ retention flap (asterixis — outstretched hands), bounding pulse, warm peripheries (vasodilation), headache, drowsiness → coma ('CO₂ narcosis').

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the CO₂ retention flap, and what does it indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Asterixis (a flap on outstretched hands) — a sign of hypercapnia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why do bounding pulse and warm peripheries occur in Type 2 RF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Vasodilation from ↑CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is Type 1 respiratory failure managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: High-flow O₂ (target 94–98%); CPAP if not responding; treat the cause (e.g. antibiotics for pneumonia, diurese pulmonary oedema); consider HFNC.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is Type 2 respiratory failure managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Controlled O₂ (88–92%); treat the cause (bronchodilators for COPD, naloxone for opiates); BiPAP (NIV) if respiratory acidosis persists despite optimal medical therapy — pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6 kPa, the 7.25–7.35 band being the one usually managed on a respiratory ward. pH <7.25 does not rule NIV out: it predicts NIV failure, so deliver NIV in HDU/ICU with a documented escalation plan.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the indications for BiPAP (NIV) in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Respiratory acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy: pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6 kPa. pH 7.25–7.35 is the band usually managed on a respiratory ward; below 7.25 NIV can still be used, but in HDU/ICU with a documented escalation plan.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What does a pH below 7.25 mean for NIV in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Not that NIV is contraindicated — it predicts a higher chance of NIV failure. NIV is still appropriate, but delivered in HDU/ICU with a documented escalation plan. Intubate if NIV fails, is contraindicated, or the patient deteriorates — unless NIV has been agreed as the ceiling of care.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Severe Type 1 respiratory failure caused by increased alveolar-capillary permeability → protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → atelectasis, ↓compliance, refractory hypoxia. The heart is fine — the capillaries are leaky.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the key distinction of ARDS pulmonary oedema from cardiac causes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It is non-cardiogenic — the heart is fine, the capillaries are leaky.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the commonest cause of ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Sepsis / pneumonia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: List the inflammatory insults that cause ARDS.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Sepsis/pneumonia (commonest), aspiration of gastric contents, massive blood transfusion (TRALI), major trauma/burns, acute pancreatitis, COVID-19, cardiopulmonary bypass.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the unifying theme of ARDS aetiology?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: A massive inflammatory insult (pulmonary or systemic) → diffuse alveolar damage → capillary leak → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the clinical features of ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute severe dyspnoea, tachypnoea, refractory hypoxia (doesn't correct with O₂), bilateral fine crackles, low SpO₂ despite high FiO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the hallmark of ARDS, and why does it distinguish it from other Type 1 RF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Refractory hypoxia — hypoxia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen alone (distinguishes ARDS from most other causes of Type 1 RF).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 1 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute onset — within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 2 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Bilateral infiltrates — CXR or CT showing bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, lobar collapse, or nodules. Resembles pulmonary oedema + air bronchograms.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 3 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Non-cardiogenic — respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Echo or wedge pressure if doubt.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 4 for ARDS, including the severity grades?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <300 mmHg (<40 kPa): mild 200–300 mmHg, moderate 100–200 mmHg, severe <100 mmHg. Lower ratio = worse disease. The ratio is measured with PEEP or CPAP ≥5 cmH₂O.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio defines severe ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: <100 mmHg.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Is there a specific cure for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: No — management is supportive (no specific cure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is the cause treated in ARDS management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Antibiotics for sepsis/pneumonia, amylase monitoring for pancreatitis, stop the offending transfusion (TRALI). Treating the cause is the step that addresses the underlying disease — but it is not the only intervention that changes outcome: lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning in moderate-to-severe ARDS, and dexamethasone in some ARDS (including COVID-19) all carry a mortality benefit.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is lung-protective ventilation in ARDS, and why is it used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Low tidal volume (~6 mL/kg predicted body weight (calculated from height and sex, not actual weight)) — avoids volutrauma. Adequate PEEP — prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening. Permissive hypercapnia is acceptable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What tidal volume is used in lung-protective ventilation for ARDS, and against which weight?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Low tidal volume, ~6 mL/kg predicted body weight — PBW is calculated from height and sex, not actual weight, because lung size tracks height rather than adiposity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the role of PEEP in ARDS ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is permissive hypercapnia in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Allowing a higher CO₂ is acceptable as part of lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the role of prone positioning in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 12–16 hours/day — promotes uniform lung inflation, ↓dorsal atelectasis, improves V/Q matching. Mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: In which ARDS severity does prone positioning give a mortality benefit?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Moderate-severe ARDS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What supportive / ITU measures are used in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Conservative fluid balance (avoid further oedema); vasopressors; renal support; ECMO if refractory. High mortality (30–60%).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the mortality of ARDS?
Summarise the Type 1 vs Type 2 RF exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 = hypoxia alone (oxygenation failure, normal/low CO₂) → CPAP. Type 2 = hypoxia + ↑CO₂ (ventilation failure) → BiPAP.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the tiring-Type-1 danger sign exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Tiring Type 1 → rising CO₂ = danger sign (exhaustion). Normal CO₂ in acute asthma is life-threatening.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the oxygen target exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 88–92% for anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall or neuromuscular disease); 94–98% for everyone else. Never give high O₂ freely to CO₂ retainers.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the ARDS exam pearl (mechanism and severity).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS = non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — leaky capillaries, heart is fine. It is a severe Type 1 RF.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the Berlin criteria exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute (<1 wk) + bilateral infiltrates + non-cardiogenic + PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the ARDS management exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS Rx: low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) + PEEP + prone positioning; treat cause; ITU. No specific cure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How did the 2023 global definition of ARDS broaden the Berlin criteria?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It included patients on high-flow nasal oxygen (≥30 L/min), allowed SpO₂/FiO₂ (≤315) as an alternative to PaO₂/FiO₂, and permitted lung ultrasound where ABGs/CT are unavailable — recognising ARDS earlier and in non-intubated/resource-limited settings. Berlin remains the classic exam definition.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Do corticosteroids have a role in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Yes — dexamethasone has shown a mortality benefit in some ARDS (notably COVID-19 ARDS), alongside treating the underlying cause and lung-protective supportive care. ARDS still has no single specific cure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is the hypoxia of ARDS 'refractory' — what is the physiological reason oxygen does not fix it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Because it is a right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt. Flooded alveoli are perfused but not ventilated, so shunted blood never meets alveolar gas and raising the FiO2 cannot oxygenate it — you only enrich blood passing the alveoli that still work. This is the difference from ordinary V/Q mismatch, which does respond to oxygen.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: If oxygen cannot correct a shunt, what does that imply about ARDS management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: You have to re-open the alveoli rather than add more oxygen. That is exactly what PEEP and prone positioning do — they recruit lung. It also explains why chasing a normal saturation with ever-higher FiO2 is futile and risks oxygen toxicity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What plateau pressure limit accompanies low tidal volume in lung-protective ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Plateau pressure 30 cmH2O or less. If it exceeds 30, reduce the tidal volume further. Plateau pressure is measured at an inspiratory pause and reflects alveolar pressure, unlike peak pressure which also includes airway resistance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the 'baby lung' concept in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS lungs are small rather than uniformly stiff — much of the lung is consolidated or collapsed, so the aerated volume remaining is child-sized. A normal tidal volume delivered into that small volume over-distends it, which is why ~6 mL/kg is used.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What mortality benefit did ARDSNet show for low tidal volume ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 6 mL/kg versus 12 mL/kg predicted body weight reduced mortality from about 40% to about 31% — one of the few interventions in ARDS that changes outcome.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is permissive hypercapnia accepted in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Because the tidal volume and plateau pressure limits take priority. Ventilating hard enough to normalise the CO2 and pH would injure the lung, so a high CO2 and low pH are tolerated in order to protect it.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How do the history and examination help distinguish ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS follows a preceding insult (sepsis, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, transfusion) with a normal or low JVP, often warm peripheries and no gallop. Cardiogenic oedema follows cardiac history, ischaemic pain, arrhythmia or fluid overload, with a raised JVP, S3 gallop, peripheral oedema and cool peripheries.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How do CXR, BNP and echo distinguish ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS: peripheral patchy bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size, effusions uncommon; BNP typically low; echo shows good LV function and normal filling pressures. Cardiogenic: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, perihilar bat's wing shadowing and effusions; BNP raised; echo shows impaired LV function or raised filling pressures. Cardiogenic oedema also improves with diuresis, ARDS does not.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Berlin criterion 3 says the failure must not be 'fully explained' by cardiac failure. Why does that wording matter?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Because ARDS and cardiac failure can coexist — a septic patient with poor ventricles can have both. The criterion does not require a normal heart, only that cardiac failure does not fully account for the picture. Echo is the practical arbiter; the pulmonary artery wedge pressure is now largely historical.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How should neuromuscular causes of Type 2 respiratory failure be monitored?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: With serial FVC, not blood gases. In GBS, myasthenia and MND the patient ventilates adequately until the muscles abruptly fail, so hypoxia and hypercapnia are late signs and a normal ABG is falsely reassuring. Escalate on a falling FVC trend.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What happens to lung function in ARDS survivors?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It largely recovers — improving over 6-12 months and often near-normal by a year. A reduced transfer factor (TLCO) is the commonest persisting abnormality, and some are left with fibrotic change on CT, more likely after prolonged high-pressure ventilation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: If the lungs recover, what causes the lasting disability in ARDS survivors?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Neuromuscular and psychological problems rather than respiratory ones: ICU-acquired weakness (critical illness myopathy and neuropathy), profound fatigue and exercise limitation lasting years, and post-intensive care syndrome — cognitive impairment, anxiety, depression and PTSD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is post-intensive care syndrome (PICS)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: New or worsened cognitive impairment (memory, attention, executive function) together with anxiety, depression and PTSD following critical illness. PTSD is strongly linked to delirium and to delusional ICU memories. It also affects families and carers (PICS-F). Follow-up, rehabilitation and explanation matter, as survivors are often discharged with no idea why they feel this way.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is VTE composed of, and how are DVT and PE related?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: VTE = DVT + PE — the same disease, two ends. Clot forms in the deep veins (usually legs) → embolises to the pulmonary arteries.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the significance of PE in maternal and post-operative mortality?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: VTE/PE is the leading cause of DIRECT maternal death (cardiac disease is the leading cause overall, per MBRRACE-UK), and is a major cause of post-operative mortality — hence universal VTE risk assessment and thromboprophylaxis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the two diagnostic spines and the management fork for PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Diagnostic spines: Wells score → D-dimer/CTPA. Management fork: stable → anticoagulate / unstable → thrombolyse.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Outline the pathophysiology of PE from thrombus to arrest.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Thrombus obstructs the pulmonary artery → V/Q mismatch (ventilated but not perfused) → ↑pulmonary vascular resistance → acute right heart strain → massive PE: RV failure → obstructive shock → arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the V/Q mismatch in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: The lung is ventilated but not perfused.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the three components of Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of stasis in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Immobility, long-haul flights, surgery, heart failure, paralysis, pregnancy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of endothelial injury in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Trauma, surgery, smoking, vasculitis, central lines.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of hypercoagulability in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Cancer (especially mucin-secreting), pregnancy, OCP/HRT, Factor V Leiden, thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, SLE, polycythaemia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the non-thrombotic causes of emboli?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Fat (long-bone fracture), air (central line, scuba), amniotic fluid (obstetric emergency), tumour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the VTE prophylaxis approach on admission?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: EVERY admission gets a VTE risk assessment. Those assessed as at risk, and without contraindications, are then offered LMWH (enoxaparin) as pharmacological prophylaxis ± mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression), alongside early mobilisation. Prophylaxis is not automatic — the risk assessment decides.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the contraindications to LMWH prophylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, acute stroke (haemorrhagic).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the contraindications to compression/TED stockings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PAD (peripheral arterial disease), severe leg oedema, neuropathy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a small/medium PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, low-grade fever, pleural rub.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Central chest pain, shock/collapse, cyanosis, ↑JVP, RV heave, loud P2 or gallop rhythm — signs of acute right heart strain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the signs of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, tenderness, erythema. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What calf circumference difference is considered significant in DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: >3cm difference.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the classic PE vignette?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Post-op / long-haul flight patient + sudden SOB + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia ± leg swelling.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the key components of the Wells 2-level PE score?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Clinical DVT signs (+3), PE most likely diagnosis (+3), heart rate >100 (+1.5), immobilisation ≥3 days OR surgery in the last 4 weeks (+1.5), prior DVT/PE (+1.5), haemoptysis (+1), active malignancy (+1). >4 = PE likely; ≤4 = PE unlikely.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a Wells score >4 (PE likely) managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Immediate CTPA. Start interim anticoagulation if any delay. CTPA +ve → treat; CTPA −ve → consider leg USS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a Wells score ≤4 (PE unlikely) managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: D-dimer first. D-dimer −ve → stop, consider alternative diagnosis. D-dimer +ve → CTPA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a haemodynamically unstable patient too sick for CTPA managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Bedside echo (RV dilatation = strong presumptive evidence) → thrombolyse empirically. Do not delay for imaging.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: CTPA — confirms PE, delineates extent, most sensitive/specific.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: When is a V/Q scan used in PE, and how is it reported?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Where iodinated contrast is contraindicated — significant renal impairment or contrast allergy. It is also an option in pregnancy, where V/Q and CTPA are BOTH acceptable and the choice is guided by the CXR and the radiation trade-off (maternal breast dose vs fetal dose) — CTPA is not contraindicated in pregnancy. Reports as high / intermediate / low probability.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is D-dimer used in PE, and what are its limitations?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: High sensitivity, poor specificity. Use to rule OUT in low-probability only. Raised in cancer, pregnancy, post-op, infection, age. Never used to rule in.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the commonest ECG finding in PE, and what is the classic but rare one?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Usually sinus tachycardia (commonest). RV strain: T inversion V1–4, RBBB, RAD. Classic but rare: S1Q3T3.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What does the ABG show in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Hypoxaemia + hypocapnia → respiratory alkalosis (blowing off CO₂ due to hyperventilation).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What does the CXR usually show in PE, and what are the rare findings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Usually normal. Rarely: wedge infarct, Westermark's sign (oligaemia distal to clot), raised hemidiaphragm, effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Westermark's sign?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Oligaemia distal to the clot on CXR.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the role of echo in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Bedside for unstable patients — RV dilatation/strain; rules out other causes (tamponade, LV failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: A patient with suspected PE has a negative or equivocal CTPA but a proximal DVT on leg ultrasound. What does that mean for management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Treat as VTE. A confirmed proximal DVT justifies anticoagulation in its own right — you do not need to demonstrate the PE as well, because the treatment is the same.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What blood tests are used in PE and what do they reflect?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, coagulation, troponin (RV stress reflecting strain), BNP (severity). There is NO routine thrombophilia screen — testing is limited to narrow indications and only where stopping anticoagulation is planned.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the first-line management of a haemodynamically stable PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: DOAC first-line: apixaban or rivaroxaban — start immediately (no heparin lead-in needed); dabigatran or edoxaban — need 5 days LMWH lead-in first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Which DOACs need a 5-day LMWH lead-in, and which can start immediately?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Apixaban or rivaroxaban start immediately (no lead-in); dabigatran or edoxaban need a 5-day LMWH lead-in first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Which exceptions to DOAC use in stable PE require LMWH bridge to warfarin?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Renal failure / antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive) → LMWH bridge → warfarin (INR 2–3).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why must warfarin be bridged with heparin until the INR is therapeutic?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Warfarin is initially prothrombotic (↓Proteins C & S first), so must bridge with heparin until the INR is therapeutic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the key intervention for a haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Thrombolysis (alteplase) — the key intervention. Supportive: O₂, cautious IV fluids (RV is preload-sensitive), ICU, vasopressors.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why must IV fluids be cautious in a massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Because the RV is preload-sensitive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the options if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails in massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Surgical or catheter embolectomy; percutaneous catheter-directed therapy in specialist centres. (IVC filter is reserved for patients who cannot be anticoagulated or recurrent PE despite anticoagulation — it does not treat the existing clot.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for a provoked PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: 3 months (clear precipitant, e.g. surgery, fracture).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for an unprovoked PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: At least 3 months, then reassess at 3 months — the NICE default for unprovoked VTE is to CONTINUE long-term unless bleeding risk is high (HAS-BLED ≥4 and unmodifiable).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for PE with active cancer or antiphospholipid syndrome — and does hereditary thrombophilia change it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Long-term, while the risk persists. Hereditary thrombophilia alone does NOT mandate indefinite anticoagulation — a provoked VTE in a factor V Leiden carrier is still treated for 3 months.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness along the vein. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant. May have Homan's sign (unreliable — calf pain on dorsiflexion).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Homan's sign, and how reliable is it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Calf pain on dorsiflexion — unreliable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a DVT diagnosed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: 2-level DVT Wells score → if likely: proximal leg USS (compression USS). If unlikely: D-dimer → USS if positive. Proximal DVT confirmed = treat as VTE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a DVT managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Same as PE — DOAC first-line (apixaban/rivaroxaban); duration by provoked/unprovoked. Do NOT offer compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome or recurrence (NICE) — they may still be used for symptomatic leg pain or swelling.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the complications of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE (embolisation — commonest serious complication); post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the commonest serious complication of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE (embolisation).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is post-thrombotic syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why should DOACs not be used in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Higher failure rate — use LMWH → warfarin (INR 2–3) instead.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the PERC rule?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE Rule-Out Criteria — a US emergency-medicine rule, NOT part of the UK/NICE pathway. In a patient already judged low-risk by clinical gestalt, meeting all 8 criteria is taken to exclude PE without a D-dimer. Criteria: age <50, HR <100, SpO₂ ≥95%, no unilateral leg swelling, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no prior PE/DVT, no surgery/trauma within 4 weeks. In the UK a PE-unlikely Wells score goes straight to a D-dimer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the PESI score?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — predicts 30-day mortality: class I/II = low risk (consider home treatment); class III–V = higher risk (admit).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the difference between submassive and massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Massive PE: haemodynamic instability (SBP <90 mmHg or drop >40 mmHg) — emergency thrombolysis. Submassive: haemodynamically stable but RV dysfunction. Low-risk: no RV strain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Hampton's hump?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Peripheral wedge-shaped opacity on CXR representing pulmonary infarction — points towards the hilum. Specific for PE but uncommon (~5%).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is pulmonary infarction?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Tissue death from PE — occurs peripherally (the dual bronchial-artery supply usually protects central lung). Presents with pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis and fever. CXR may show a wedge-shaped peripheral opacity (Hampton's hump), often with a small pleural effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Late complication of PE — unresolved thrombus organises and obstructs pulmonary vasculature → progressive pulmonary hypertension, RV failure, dyspnoea. Treated by pulmonary endarterectomy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is McConnell's sign?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Echo finding in acute PE: RV free wall hypokinesis with sparing of the RV apex — relatively specific for acute pulmonary embolism (vs chronic RV failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: When can PE be treated at home (outpatient)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PESI class I/II (low risk) + no haemodynamic instability + adequate home support + DOAC suitable — NICE supports early discharge or outpatient treatment for low-risk PE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is massive PE mortality without treatment?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: ~30–35% mortality without treatment. With appropriate anticoagulation: reduced to ~5%. Massive PE with shock: mortality >50% without immediate intervention.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: After an acute PE, what is the follow-up timeline?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Review at ~7 days post-discharge (BTS quality standard) — check adherence, tolerance, bleeding and that the diagnosis still fits → formal reassessment at 3 months (continue or stop anticoagulation?) → annual review for anyone on long-term anticoagulation (NICE), re-checking risk/benefit, renal and hepatic function and adherence.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: At the 3-month review of an unprovoked VTE, which score does NICE recommend for bleeding risk, and what does the threshold trigger?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: HAS-BLED — used to assess the risk of major bleeding when deciding whether to continue anticoagulation beyond 3 months for unprovoked VTE. Discuss stopping if HAS-BLED ≥4 and the risk cannot be modified. Modify what you can first (uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs/antiplatelets, harmful alcohol, labile INR). Do not base the decision on a predictive tool alone — it informs the conversation, it doesn't make the call.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: After an unprovoked VTE, what does NICE say about looking for cancer?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Do NOT offer further investigations for cancer (no routine CT abdomen/pelvis, tumour markers or blind imaging) unless there are relevant clinical symptoms or signs. What you DO offer: a review of the history, a physical examination, and baseline bloods — FBC, renal and hepatic function, PT and APTT. Then investigate anything abnormal those turn up.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Who should and should not be tested for thrombophilia after VTE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Antiphospholipid antibodies: consider in unprovoked VTE if stopping anticoagulation is planned (a positive, especially triple-positive, result means long-term warfarin rather than a DOAC). Hereditary thrombophilia: consider only if ALL of — unprovoked VTE AND a first-degree relative with VTE AND stopping is planned. Do NOT test anyone continuing anticoagulation (the result can't change the plan), and do NOT test after a provoked VTE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Which patients with a confirmed PE can be treated as outpatients, and what excludes that?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Low-risk PE — sPESI 0, PESI class I–II, or all Hestia criteria negative → consider outpatient treatment with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban, first dose before discharge). BTS exclusions (admit if any): HR >110, SBP <100 mmHg, need for inotropes or critical care, need for thrombolysis or embolectomy, SpO₂ <90% on air. Discharge needs written safety-netting advice, an anticoagulant alert card and a booked ~7-day review.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the main complications after a PE, and how common is CTEPH?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Recurrent VTE (highest in the first year off treatment, far higher after unprovoked events); bleeding on anticoagulation (GI and intracranial matter most); persistent breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance — roughly a third to a half are still symptomatic at 3 months ('post-PE syndrome'); and CTEPH in about 2% — organised unresolved thrombus obstructing the pulmonary arteries, suspected when breathlessness persists beyond 3 months, screened with echo then V/Q scan. CTEPH is WHO Group 4 pulmonary hypertension.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What epithelium lines most of the conducting (upper) airway, and what is its full descriptive name?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (PCCE).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are the two main functions of respiratory epithelium?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Conditioning inspired air (warming, humidifying, filtering) and mucociliary clearance of trapped debris and microbes.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: List regions lined by respiratory (PCCE) epithelium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Most of the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx below the vocal cords, trachea and bronchi.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Why is respiratory epithelium described as 'pseudostratified'?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Every cell contacts the basement membrane, but the nuclei lie at different levels, giving a false appearance of multiple layers.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which airway epithelial neurons regenerate, and what antibody protects the mucosa?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar neurons continuously replaced from basal stem cells — a rare regenerating neuron. Secretory (dimeric) IgA, transported across the epithelium via the poly-Ig receptor, is the principal mucosal antibody in airway mucus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Name the five cell types of respiratory epithelium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Ciliated columnar (most numerous), goblet, basal (stem), brush, and small-granule (neuroendocrine/Kulchitsky) cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which cell of respiratory epithelium is the most numerous and what does it do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: The ciliated columnar cell; its cilia drive the mucociliary escalator toward the pharynx.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What does the goblet cell secrete and how does it stain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Mucins forming the gel layer of the mucus blanket; it is PAS-positive and Alcian-blue positive.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the role of the basal cell, and why does it make the epithelium look stratified?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: It is the stem/reserve cell that regenerates the other cell types; being short and sitting on the basement membrane, its low nucleus adds to the layered appearance.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is a brush cell?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A columnar cell bearing blunt microvilli that acts as a chemosensory receptor, with an afferent nerve ending at its base.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the small-granule (neuroendocrine/Kulchitsky) cell and its clinical importance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A DNES cell with dense-core granules (serotonin, bombesin); it is the cell of origin of bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Describe the two layers of the airway mucus blanket.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A watery sol (periciliary) layer in which the cilia beat, and an overlying sticky gel layer that traps particles and microbes.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Describe the ciliary beat cycle.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A fast forward power stroke whose tip engages the gel layer to push mucus toward the pharynx, followed by a slow recovery stroke within the sol layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the ultrastructure of a motile cilium?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A '9 + 2' axoneme — nine peripheral microtubule doublets plus a central pair — with dynein arms that use ATP to slide the doublets, anchored by a basal body.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which epithelium lines the nasal vestibule?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous keratinised epithelium, with vibrissae (hairs) and sebaceous glands.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which epithelium covers the true vocal cords and why?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous (non-keratinised) epithelium, to withstand the abrasion of vibration.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Where is olfactory epithelium located and what special cells does it contain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: In the roof of the nasal cavity; it contains olfactory receptor neurons, sustentacular (supporting) cells and basal cells, with Bowman's glands beneath.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: How does the epithelium change across the epiglottis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous on the lingual/upper surface transitions to respiratory epithelium on the lower (laryngeal) surface.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: How does the nose warm inspired air?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Rich venous plexuses/swell bodies in the nasal conchae radiate heat to the air (and cause the alternating nasal cycle).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Contrast the epithelium of the true vocal cords, false cords and adenoid.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: True vocal cords: stratified squamous (to withstand vibration). False (vestibular) cords: respiratory pseudostratified ciliated columnar. The adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil) is also covered by respiratory PCCE, unlike the squamous-covered palatine and lingual tonsils.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is Waldeyer's ring?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: The ring of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (pharyngeal, palatine, tubal and lingual tonsils) guarding the entrance to the aerodigestive tract.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which stains highlight goblet-cell and gland mucin?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: PAS (magenta) and Alcian blue (blue).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is squamous metaplasia of the respiratory tract and its main cause?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Replacement of ciliated/goblet respiratory epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium, classically caused by cigarette smoking; it loses mucociliary clearance and can progress to dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is primary ciliary dyskinesia and the features of Kartagener syndrome?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: An autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect causing dysmotile cilia; the Kartagener triad is situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis (with male infertility as a further PCD feature). Screen with low nasal nitric oxide.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are the histological features of allergic rhinitis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Type I hypersensitivity change with mucosal oedema, eosinophil infiltrate and goblet-cell/gland hypersecretion.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are nasal polyps and what conditions are they associated with?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Oedematous, inflamed protrusions of respiratory mucosa; associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, aspirin sensitivity and cystic fibrosis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Where is Little's area and why is it clinically important?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: On the anterior nasal septum (Kiesselbach's plexus); it is the commonest site of epistaxis (nosebleeds).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Contrast the mucus defect in cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: In CF, defective CFTR chloride/water secretion dehydrates the periciliary layer, so normal cilia beat in thick sticky mucus. In PCD, the mucus is normal but the cilia are structurally abnormal (dynein-arm defect) and cannot beat. Both stall the mucociliary escalator, causing sinusitis and bronchiectasis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: List the airway generations from trachea to the start of gas exchange.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Trachea -> main (primary) bronchi -> lobar -> segmental bronchi -> bronchioles -> terminal bronchioles -> respiratory bronchioles (where gas exchange begins).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are the four structural trends as you move distally down the airway tree?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Epithelium becomes shorter (columnar -> cuboidal), cartilage and glands disappear, goblet cells disappear, and smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the single best histological feature distinguishing a bronchus from a bronchiole?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchi have cartilage plates and submucosal glands; bronchioles have neither.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Describe the epithelium and key wall features of a bronchus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; a continuous spiral smooth-muscle band; submucosal seromucous glands; irregular hyaline cartilage plates; and a fibroelastic adventitia.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: How does the cartilage change from trachea to intrapulmonary bronchus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The C-shaped tracheal rings break up into irregular plates/islands that encircle the intrapulmonary bronchus, and a complete smooth-muscle layer appears.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Define a bronchiole and give its size and key negatives.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: An airway <=1 mm in diameter with no cartilage, no glands and (in the terminal bronchiole) no goblet cells; it has a relatively prominent smooth-muscle layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What epithelium lines bronchioles?
