histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Simple ciliated columnar proximally, becoming simple cuboidal (often still ciliated) distally, with club cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What holds bronchioles open, given they lack cartilage?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Radial traction from the elastic recoil of the surrounding alveolar walls, plus smooth-muscle tone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Why are bronchioles the critical site of obstruction in asthma and COPD?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: They have no cartilage to splint them open, so smooth-muscle contraction and loss of elastic traction readily narrow or collapse them.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the terminal bronchiole and what does it supply?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The last purely conducting airway; each terminal bronchiole supplies one pulmonary acinus. (A secondary pulmonary lobule — the HRCT unit bounded by connective-tissue septa — is fed by several, ~3–5, terminal bronchioles.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are club (Clara) cells and where are they found?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Dome-shaped, non-ciliated secretory cells of the bronchiolar epithelium that increase distally.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: List the functions of club cells.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Secrete surfactant-like material and club-cell secretory protein (CC16) to reduce surface tension and protect the lining; detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via cytochrome P450; and act as progenitor/stem cells for the bronchiolar epithelium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are neuroepithelial bodies?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Innervated clusters of pulmonary neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells at bronchiolar bifurcations that act as hypoxia chemoreceptors, releasing serotonin and bombesin; they are the cell of origin of bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What defines a respiratory bronchiole?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: A bronchiole whose cuboidal wall is interrupted by scattered alveoli — the first airway where gas exchange occurs.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the pulmonary acinus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Everything distal to a single terminal bronchiole — the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli — i.e. the functional gas-exchange unit.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Where is the boundary between the conducting and respiratory zones?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The terminal bronchiole ends the conducting zone; the respiratory bronchiole begins the respiratory (gas-exchange) zone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the Reid index and when is it increased?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The ratio of submucosal gland thickness to total bronchial wall thickness; it is increased (>0.4) in chronic bronchitis due to gland hypertrophy.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are the histological features of asthma in the airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchiolar smooth-muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy, bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, subepithelial basement-membrane fibrosis, goblet-cell metaplasia and eosinophilic inflammation; sputum shows Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals. The airflow obstruction is reversible.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is chronic bronchitis histologically?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Submucosal gland hypertrophy (increased Reid index) and goblet-cell hyperplasia with mucus hypersecretion, producing a chronic productive cough.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is bronchiectasis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Permanent, abnormal dilatation of bronchi from chronic infection/obstruction with destruction of the muscle and cartilage of the wall.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: From which cells do bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma arise?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchial neuroendocrine (small-granule/Kulchitsky) cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Why does the lumen of a bronchiole often look folded (scalloped) on a slide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Contraction of its prominent smooth-muscle layer throws the mucosa into folds.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Distinguish the pulmonary acinus, secondary lobule and primary lobule.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Acinus = everything distal to one terminal bronchiole (the gas-exchange unit). Secondary pulmonary lobule = the polyhedral, septum-bounded unit seen on HRCT, supplied by ~3–5 terminal bronchioles (several acini). Primary lobule = tissue distal to one respiratory bronchiole.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is Reisseissen's muscle?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The smooth muscle of the bronchioles, relatively prominent because there is no cartilage; it regulates airway calibre.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Which airway component maintains bronchial patency?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The hyaline cartilage plates in the bronchial wall.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What lung disease results from loss of radial traction on small airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Emphysema/COPD — destruction of alveolar attachments removes the tethering that holds bronchioles open, causing expiratory collapse and airflow limitation.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What causes bronchiolitis in infants, and what is the lesion?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV); inflammation of the bronchioles with epithelial damage, oedema and mucus that obstruct the small airways.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Trace where the smooth muscle is located relative to the cartilage in a bronchus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The smooth muscle forms a band internal to (deep to) the cartilage plates, between the mucosa/submucosa and the cartilage.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are alveoli and roughly how many/what surface area do they provide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The thin-walled air sacs where gas exchange occurs — about 300 million, giving a total surface area of ~70 m2.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Off which structures do alveoli open?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: State Fick's law of diffusion in the context of the alveolus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Diffusion rate is proportional to (surface area x pressure difference) divided by barrier thickness — so the alveolus maximises area and minimises thickness.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the interalveolar septum?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The shared wall between adjacent alveoli, containing the capillary network, pneumocytes, fused basement membranes, elastic/collagen interstitium and macrophages.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: On H&E, how do you usually identify type I pneumocytes?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Mainly by their flat nuclei bulging into the airspace — their gas-exchange cytoplasm is too thin to resolve by light microscopy.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How do type II pneumocytes appear on a slide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: As rounded, cuboidal cells at the corners of alveolar septa, with foamy/vacuolated cytoplasm.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: List the three layers of the blood-air barrier that gas crosses.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: (1) Type I pneumocyte cytoplasm plus its surfactant film, (2) the fused basal laminae of the pneumocyte and endothelium, and (3) the capillary endothelial cytoplasm — then plasma and the red-cell membrane to haemoglobin (total ~0.2–0.5 μm).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How thick is the blood-air barrier?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: About 0.2-0.5 micrometres on the thin (exchange) side.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the difference between the thin and thick sides of the septum?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The thin side has fused pneumocyte and endothelial basement membranes for efficient gas exchange; the thick side contains interstitium (elastic, collagen, fibroblasts, fluid) for support and fluid handling.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Compare type I and type II pneumocytes in surface area and cell number.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Type I cover ~95% of surface but are ~40% of cell number; type II cover ~5% of surface but are ~60% of cell number (more numerous).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which pneumocyte is the gas-exchange cell and can it divide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The type I pneumocyte; it is a simple squamous cell that cannot divide (it is replaced by proliferating type II cells).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which pneumocyte acts as the stem cell of the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The type II pneumocyte, which can regenerate both type I and type II cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is surfactant made of and by which cell?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A phospholipid-protein film — chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) with phosphatidylglycerol and cholesterol, plus surfactant proteins A-D — made by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the main function of surfactant?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: It lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at end-expiration and reducing the work of breathing.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does surfactant relate to Laplace's law?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) predicts small alveoli would empty into larger ones; surfactant lowers surface tension more in small alveoli, stabilising them so they stay open.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: When does surfactant production begin and become adequate in the fetus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: It appears around 24 weeks and is usually adequate by about 35 weeks of gestation.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are the roles of surfactant proteins A/D versus B/C?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A and D are innate-immune opsonins (collectins); B and C help spread and stabilise the phospholipid film.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is an alveolar macrophage (dust cell) and where does it come from?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A tissue-resident phagocyte — chiefly fetal-derived and locally self-renewing (blood monocytes are recruited only during inflammation) — that patrols the airspace and interstitium, ingesting dust, microbes and spent surfactant; it clears via the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are heart-failure cells?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages seen in chronic pulmonary venous congestion (e.g. left heart failure); they stain with Perls' Prussian blue.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are the pores of Kohn and their significance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Small openings between adjacent alveoli that allow collateral airflow — but also let macrophages, fluid and infection spread from alveolus to alveolus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How is fetal lung maturity assessed before delivery?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: By the amniotic-fluid lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio — >2 indicates mature surfactant (<2 predicts RDS) — and by the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol; antenatal corticosteroids accelerate maturity while maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia) delays it.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which immunomarker identifies type II pneumocytes and lung adenocarcinoma?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) marks type II pneumocytes and primary lung adenocarcinoma; it is also positive in thyroid tissue/carcinoma, and is used to distinguish a lung primary from a metastasis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and its histology?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Surfactant deficiency due to prematurity (worse with maternal diabetes) causing widespread atelectasis and hyaline membranes; prevented by giving the mother antenatal corticosteroids before preterm delivery, and treated with exogenous surfactant plus respiratory support (CPAP/ventilation).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is a hyaline membrane and in which conditions is it seen?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A glassy eosinophilic layer of dead cells and plasma proteins lining alveoli, seen in diffuse alveolar damage — ARDS and neonatal RDS.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does ARDS damage the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Diffuse alveolar damage kills type I pneumocytes and leaks protein-rich exudate that forms hyaline membranes; the refractory hypoxaemia is due chiefly to intrapulmonary shunt and V/Q mismatch (flooded, non-ventilated alveoli), which is why it responds to PEEP rather than to supplemental oxygen alone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does emphysema impair gas exchange?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Destruction of alveolar septa reduces the total surface area and elastic recoil available for exchange.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Why do pulmonary oedema and pulmonary fibrosis both cause hypoxaemia?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Both thicken the blood-air barrier — oedema adds interstitial/alveolar fluid, fibrosis adds collagen — increasing the diffusion distance (Fick's law).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What structural elements give the alveolar septum its elastic recoil?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Elastic (and collagen) fibres in the interstitium of the septum, produced by fibroblasts.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which two epithelial cells line the alveolus, and what seals them into a continuous sheet?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I and type II pneumocytes, sealed together by tight (occluding) junctions that keep fluid out of the airspace.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Summarise the division of labour between type I and type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I is the thin squamous gas-exchange surface; type II makes surfactant, clears fluid, provides defence and acts as the alveolar stem cell for repair.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: On light microscopy, why do you usually see only the nucleus of a type I pneumocyte?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Its gas-exchange cytoplasm is only ~0.1-0.2 micrometres thick — below the resolution of the light microscope — so only the flattened nucleus is visible.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Give the surface-area and cell-number percentages for type I pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I cells cover ~95% of the alveolar surface but make up only ~40% of the cell number.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Give the surface-area and cell-number percentages for type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II cells cover ~5% of the surface but make up ~60% of the cell number (they are the more numerous cell).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why can't type I pneumocytes regenerate the alveolar lining themselves?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: They are terminally differentiated and cannot divide; they are replaced by type II cells that proliferate and transdifferentiate into type I.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which junction type joins pneumocytes and what does it achieve?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Occluding tight junctions, which form a barrier keeping fluid and solutes out of the alveolar airspace (keeping the alveolus dry).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name markers of the type I pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Aquaporin-5 (AQP5), podoplanin (T1alpha) and caveolin-1.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Describe the ultrastructure of a type II pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: A cuboidal cell with short apical microvilli, abundant RER and Golgi, and characteristic membrane-bound osmiophilic lamellar bodies storing surfactant.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the diagnostic organelle of the type II pneumocyte?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: The lamellar body — a whorled, osmiophilic, membrane-bound store of surfactant.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: List the four functions of type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: (1) Synthesise/secrete/recycle surfactant, (2) act as the alveolar stem/progenitor cell (self-renew and become type I), (3) help clear alveolar fluid via ENaC and Na/K-ATPase, and (4) innate defence (secrete SP-A/SP-D). (Xenobiotic P450 detoxification is mainly the club cell's role.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How do type II pneumocytes keep the alveolus dry?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: They actively pump Na+ (via apical ENaC and basolateral Na/K-ATPase), drawing fluid out of the airspace across the epithelium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name markers of the type II pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Surfactant proteins SP-B and SP-C are lineage markers; the diagnostic immunohistochemistry markers used clinically are TTF-1 and Napsin A (Napsin A is an aspartic protease).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Outline the surfactant life-cycle.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Lipids and surfactant proteins are made in RER, processed in Golgi, packaged into lamellar bodies, secreted by exocytosis, unfold into tubular myelin (SP-B and Ca2+ dependent) to feed the surface film, then are recycled by type II cells or cleared by macrophages.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the main lipid of surfactant and roughly what fraction is lipid vs protein?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is the main lipid; surfactant is ~90% lipid and ~10% protein.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Contrast the roles of surfactant proteins A/D versus B/C.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic collectins that mediate innate immunity (opsonisation) and, for SP-A, regulate secretion and tubular myelin; SP-B and SP-C are hydrophobic proteins that spread and stabilise the lipid film.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is tubular myelin and which surfactant protein is essential for it?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: A lattice-like intermediate form of secreted surfactant that feeds the surface film; it requires SP-A and SP-B (plus calcium) to form.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why is SP-B deficiency clinically important?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Congenital SP-B deficiency prevents tubular myelin/functional surfactant formation and is lethal in neonates (fatal respiratory failure).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How is the alveolar lining repaired after type I cell death?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II pneumocytes proliferate and then transdifferentiate into new type I cells, restoring the thin gas-exchange surface.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What histological change signals acute alveolar injury?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II (pneumocyte) hyperplasia — a plump cuboidal lining replacing the normal flat type I lining.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why can reactive type II hyperplasia be a diagnostic pitfall?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: The enlarged, atypical-looking reparative type II cells can mimic malignancy on cytology after ARDS or infection.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How does aberrant alveolar repair contribute to fibrosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Repeated or dysregulated type II-driven repair recruits fibroblasts and deposits collagen instead of cleanly re-epithelialising, producing fibrosis (e.g. IPF).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the histology and cause of neonatal RDS in pneumocyte terms?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Immature type II cells produce insufficient surfactant, causing atelectasis and hyaline membranes; congenital SP-B deficiency is a fatal form.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What happens to pneumocytes in ARDS / diffuse alveolar damage?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I pneumocytes undergo necrosis and hyaline membranes form (exudative phase); reactive type II hyperplasia appears in the organising phase.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which markers identify lung adenocarcinoma, and which pneumocyte lineage does it reflect?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: TTF-1 and Napsin A; these reflect a type II pneumocyte (or club-cell) lineage. TTF-1 is negative in squamous cell carcinoma (which is p40/p63 positive) but positive in small-cell carcinoma and thyroid, so Napsin A helps confirm adenocarcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Accumulation of PAS-positive surfactant material in the alveoli due to defective macrophage clearance, usually from anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How does high-concentration oxygen damage the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: It generates free radicals that injure the fragile type I pneumocytes, producing diffuse alveolar damage (a cause of ARDS).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name the genetic causes of fatal neonatal surfactant deficiency.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Congenital SP-B (SFTPB) deficiency and ABCA3 transporter deficiency — both autosomal recessive and lethal in neonates; ABCA3 loads phospholipid into the lamellar bodies. (SP-C/SFTPC mutations instead cause autosomal-dominant familial pulmonary fibrosis in later life.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the partnership underlying mucociliary clearance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells secrete the sticky mucus that traps particles and microbes, and cilia move that mucus toward the pharynx — together forming the mucociliary escalator, the airway's primary innate defence.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does a goblet cell appear on H&E and how does it stain specially?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A pale, clear, cup-shaped ('goblet') cell with an apical theca of mucin and a nucleus squashed to the base; it is PAS-magenta and Alcian-blue positive.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the ultrastructure of a goblet cell.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A unicellular exocrine gland with a narrow base containing the nucleus and abundant RER/Golgi, widening into an apical theca packed with mucinogen granules.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Which mucins do goblet cells and submucosal glands secrete?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells secrete mainly MUC5AC; submucosal glands add MUC5B — both gel-forming mucins.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: By what mechanism do goblet cells release mucin?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Merocrine exocytosis (regulated release of granule contents without loss of cytoplasm or membrane).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What happens to mucins on hydration?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: They are huge glycoproteins that swell 100-1000 times in water to form the sticky gel layer of the mucus blanket.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does goblet-cell number change along the airway?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells are numerous in the trachea and bronchi and disappear by the bronchioles, where club (Clara) cells take over the secretory role.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Besides mucins, what antimicrobial substances are in the airway mucus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins and secretory IgA.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the '9+2' axoneme of a motile cilium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Nine peripheral microtubule doublets (an A tubule plus an incomplete B tubule) arranged around a central pair of single microtubules.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What are dynein arms and what do they do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: ATPase motor proteins projecting from the A tubule of each doublet; they generate the force for ciliary beating by walking along the adjacent doublet.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What do radial spokes and nexin links do in the axoneme?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Radial spokes connect the doublets to the central sheath; nexin (dynein-regulatory) links tie adjacent doublets together so that dynein-driven sliding is converted into bending.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the basal body and how does its structure differ from the axoneme?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: The basal body anchors the cilium and is a centriole-derived structure of nine microtubule triplets (9x3) with no central pair, whereas the axoneme is nine doublets plus a central pair (9x2 + 2).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How many cilia are on a ciliated cell and how long are they?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Roughly 200-300 cilia per cell, each about 5-10 micrometres long.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is a primary cilium and why does it matter clinically?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A single, non-motile 9+0 cilium (no central pair, no dynein arms) present on most cells as a sensory antenna; renal tubular primary cilia sense flow via polycystin-1/2, and their defects cause autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD). Primary cilia also transduce Hedgehog signalling — cilium disorders are collectively 'ciliopathies'.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the two phases of the ciliary beat.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A fast, stiff power stroke in which the tip engages the gel layer to push mucus forward, followed by a slow, curled recovery stroke within the watery sol layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is a metachronal wave and how fast does it move mucus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Neighbouring cilia beating slightly out of phase produce a coordinated wave that propels mucus at about 1 cm/min toward the pharynx (beat frequency ~12-15 Hz).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why is periciliary (sol) layer depth critical for clearance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Cilia must beat within a watery sol layer of the right depth; if the mucus is dehydrated (as in CF) the layer collapses and clearance stalls even though the cilia are structurally normal.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Contrast the cores and motility of cilia, microvilli and stereocilia.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Cilia have a microtubule (9+2) core and are motile (dynein-powered); microvilli and stereocilia have actin cores and are non-motile (stereocilia are giant microvilli, not true cilia).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is primary ciliary dyskinesia?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: An autosomal recessive disorder of ciliary structure — most often an outer/inner dynein-arm defect (DNAH5), but also radial-spoke, central-pair or nexin-DRC defects — causing dyskinetic (or immotile) cilia and failed mucociliary clearance; screened by low nasal nitric oxide and confirmed with high-speed video microscopy, EM and genetics.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: List the features of Kartagener syndrome.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia comprising situs inversus, bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis, often with infertility and recurrent otitis media.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why does primary ciliary dyskinesia cause situs inversus in ~50% of patients?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Embryonic nodal cilia are unusual — 9+0 (no central pair) but still MOTILE, rotating to generate leftward nodal flow that sets left-right asymmetry; when they are immotile, laterality is randomised, so about half of PCD patients develop situs inversus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does cystic fibrosis impair mucociliary clearance if the cilia are normal?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A CFTR defect produces dehydrated, abnormally thick and sticky mucus; the cilia are structurally normal but cannot move the viscous mucus, so the escalator jams and infection/bronchiectasis follow.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: State the key contrast between PCD and CF.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Both cause bronchiectasis and sinusitis, but PCD is a ciliary (motor) defect whereas CF is a mucus (hydration/CFTR) defect with structurally normal cilia.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is goblet-cell hyperplasia and what causes it?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: An increase in goblet-cell number (or their appearance in normally goblet-free sites, i.e. metaplasia) from chronic irritation such as smoking, asthma or chronic bronchitis, causing mucus hypersecretion.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does smoking affect the mucociliary apparatus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Smoke paralyses and strips cilia and drives squamous metaplasia while increasing goblet cells/mucus, so clearance falls and secretions accumulate (smoker's cough).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why does primary ciliary dyskinesia often cause male infertility?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: The sperm flagellum shares the same 9+2 axoneme and dynein motors, so the same defect renders sperm immotile.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How is cystic fibrosis diagnosed, and why are affected men usually infertile?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: By a raised sweat chloride (>60 mmol/L) — CFTR normally reabsorbs Cl- in sweat ducts, so its loss gives salty sweat; the commonest mutation is ΔF508 (autosomal recessive). Male infertility is due to congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) — obstructive, with normal spermatogenesis, unlike the immotile-sperm infertility of PCD.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the ciliary rootlet?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A striated cytoskeletal structure extending from the basal body into the cytoplasm that anchors the cilium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does 'lung parenchyma' mean?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The functional gas-exchange tissue of the lung — respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli — held in an elastic connective-tissue framework.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Distinguish the conducting from the respiratory portion of the lung.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Conducting portion (no gas exchange): trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles. Respiratory portion (gas exchange = parenchyma): respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is a bronchovascular bundle?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: An airway travelling together with an accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery of similar calibre; finding one locates the other.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Where do pulmonary veins run, relative to the airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Separately from the airways, out in the interlobular septa (not within the bronchovascular bundle).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define the pulmonary acinus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Everything distal to a single terminal bronchiole (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli) — the functional gas-exchange unit.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define the pulmonary lobule.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The secondary pulmonary lobule — the smallest lung unit bounded by connective-tissue interlobular septa, supplied by several (~3-5) terminal bronchioles and containing multiple acini; it is the unit of HRCT interpretation. (The tissue distal to ONE terminal bronchiole is the acinus.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define a bronchopulmonary segment and its clinical relevance.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: A region supplied by a segmental bronchus with its own segmental artery; it is a surgically resectable unit (segmentectomy).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What epithelium forms the pleura?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Simple squamous mesothelium over a thin layer of elastic connective tissue.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Distinguish visceral and parietal pleura, including innervation.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Visceral pleura covers the lung (autonomic innervation, insensate to pain; bronchial/pulmonary blood supply); parietal pleura lines the chest wall (somatic innervation via intercostal/phrenic nerves, pain-sensitive; systemic blood supply).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which pleura is responsible for pleuritic pain, and why?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The parietal pleura, because it has somatic (intercostal/phrenic) innervation; the visceral pleura is insensate.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is in the pleural cavity normally?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: A thin film of serous fluid that lubricates movement of the two pleural layers against each other.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Describe the two components of the lung's dual blood supply.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood for gas exchange (low pressure, high flow, follows the airways); the bronchial circulation carries systemic oxygenated blood that nourishes the airways, vessels and pleura.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Why do pulmonary emboli rarely cause lung infarction?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Because the lung has a dual blood supply (pulmonary and bronchial); if pulmonary flow is blocked, the bronchial circulation usually keeps the tissue alive unless it too is compromised (e.g. in heart failure).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Contrast the central and peripheral bronchogenic carcinomas.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Central (hilar, smoking-related): squamous cell carcinoma (keratin pearls) and small-cell carcinoma (neuroendocrine, paraneoplastic). Peripheral: adenocarcinoma (commonest, TTF-1/Napsin A positive, glands/mucin, also in non-smokers) and large-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does the lung's elastic-fibre framework do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: It provides elastic recoil for expiration and holds the bronchioles open by radial traction; it extends from the pleura through the septa around airways and vessels.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does the pulmonary interstitium contain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The connective tissue of the septa — collagen and elastin plus fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells and occasional lymphocytes; it has a thin (exchange) side and a thick (support) side.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the lung.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Two plexuses — a superficial (pleural) and a deep (bronchovascular) network — draining to the hilar lymph nodes; notably, there are no lymphatics in the alveolar walls themselves.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is BALT?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue — mucosal lymphoid aggregates guarding the airways.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Name the two opposite ways the connective-tissue framework can fail.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Loss of elastin causes emphysema (floppy, over-inflated, obstructive); expansion of the interstitium with collagen causes fibrosis (stiff, restricted).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which stain demonstrates the lung's elastic framework and is useful in emphysema and pleural invasion?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Elastic stains such as Verhoeff-van Gieson or orcein.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which stain highlights interstitial fibrosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Masson trichrome (collagen stains blue/green).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which immunomarkers identify mesothelial cells (e.g. mesothelioma)?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Calretinin and WT-1.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is emphysema at the tissue level and its two main patterns?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Destruction of elastin and alveolar walls causing permanent airspace enlargement and loss of recoil; centriacinar (smoking-related, upper zones) and panacinar (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower zones).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is the histological hallmark of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Interstitial collagen deposition with honeycombing and fibroblast foci (usual interstitial pneumonia, UIP pattern), giving stiff lungs and a restrictive defect.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Contrast lobar pneumonia and bronchopneumonia.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Lobar pneumonia consolidates a whole lobe with alveolar exudate; bronchopneumonia is patchy consolidation centred on airways, distributed by lobule.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is a pneumothorax and its effect on the lung?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Air in the pleural cavity abolishing the negative intrapleural pressure, so the elastic lung recoils and collapses.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is anthracosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Harmless accumulation of inhaled carbon in alveolar macrophages and septa; heavy dust exposure can progress to pneumoconiosis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Why is asbestos exposure relevant to the pleura?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Asbestos causes pleural plaques, fibrosis and malignant mesothelioma of the pleural mesothelium.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is the single most useful question when assessing a cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: How long has it lasted? Duration is the master key: acute <3 weeks, subacute 3–8 weeks, chronic >8 weeks — each has a different differential.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is the commonest cause of an acute cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) — self-limiting. The key job in acute cough is to spot pneumonia (fever, focal signs, breathlessness) among the many benign viral coughs.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What are the red-flag features of a cough that mandate an urgent chest X-ray and 2-week-wait referral?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Cough >3 weeks, especially with haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, a hoarse voice, or in a smoker / ex-smoker — suspected lung cancer (and consider TB).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What are the 'big three' causes of a chronic cough with a normal chest X-ray?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip), asthma (including cough-variant), and GORD. They frequently coexist, so treatment is often a stepwise empirical trial. Always also stop any ACE inhibitor.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip)?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Chronic cough from secretions dripping down the posterior pharynx in rhinitis / sinusitis — with throat-clearing, a blocked / runny nose and a cobblestone pharynx. Treated with an antihistamine or nasal corticosteroid.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What are the features of cough-variant asthma?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: An isolated, often nocturnal dry cough with wheeze, atopy and triggers (cold air, exercise, allergens), but sometimes cough is the only symptom. Confirm with spirometry + reversibility, FeNO and a peak-flow diary.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: How does GORD cause a chronic cough and how is it recognised?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Acid reflux (± micro-aspiration and a vagal reflex) triggers cough that is worse lying flat and after meals, often with acid brash / heartburn. A proton-pump-inhibitor trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: Which drug classically causes a dry cough, and by what mechanism?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) — from accumulation of bradykinin and substance P. The dry cough can start weeks to months after starting the drug and settles within weeks of stopping; switch to an ARB.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What sputum pattern suggests bronchiectasis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Copious daily purulent (mucopurulent) sputum with recurrent chest infections, often with clubbing and coarse crackles. Confirm with high-resolution CT (dilated, thick-walled airways).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What does pink, frothy sputum suggest?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Pulmonary oedema (usually left heart failure) — with a nocturnal cough, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What does rusty-coloured sputum classically suggest?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Pneumococcal (lobar) pneumonia — Streptococcus pneumoniae.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What are the important causes of haemoptysis in a patient with cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Lung cancer, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, bronchiectasis and pneumonia — haemoptysis with a chronic cough, weight loss or a smoking history is cancer or TB until excluded.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What features suggest tuberculosis as the cause of a chronic cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Night sweats, weight loss, fever, haemoptysis and risk factors (contacts, immunosuppression / HIV, birth in an endemic area). Investigate with chest X-ray and sputum for acid-fast bacilli / culture.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is the classic presentation of interstitial lung disease / pulmonary fibrosis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A dry cough with progressive exertional breathlessness, finger clubbing and fine bibasal (Velcro) crackles. Confirm with high-resolution CT and lung function (restrictive, low transfer factor).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is pertussis (whooping cough)?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A Bordetella pertussis infection causing paroxysms of coughing with an inspiratory 'whoop' and post-tussive vomiting, often lasting weeks (the '100-day cough'). It is a notifiable disease.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: A sudden coughing fit with choking, especially in a child, points to what?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: An inhaled foreign body — with a unilateral wheeze / reduced air entry; it may lodge in the right main bronchus. Diagnosed and removed at bronchoscopy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is the pivotal first investigation in the work-up of a chronic cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A chest X-ray — a normal film points to the big three (treated empirically), while an abnormal film (mass, consolidation, effusion, fibrosis) directs targeted investigation.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What features distinguish the cough of COPD?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A smoker / ex-smoker with a chronic productive cough and sputum plus progressive breathlessness; spirometry shows irreversible airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and what exposure clue should you seek?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: An immune (allergic) reaction to an inhaled organic antigen causing cough and breathlessness — ask about birds (bird-fancier's lung), mouldy hay (farmer's lung) and occupational exposures.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: How do you manage a chronic cough with a normal chest X-ray?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Treat the big three stepwise (upper airway cough syndrome → asthma → GORD), stop any ACE inhibitor, and address smoking. Reserve referral / bronchoscopy for refractory or red-flag cases.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: Which examination findings point to specific causes of cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Focal crackles → pneumonia; fine bibasal crackles + clubbing → ILD; coarse crackles → bronchiectasis; wheeze → asthma / COPD; stony dullness → pleural effusion.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What features suggest COVID-19 as a cause of an acute or subacute cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A new continuous dry cough with fever, fatigue, myalgia and loss of taste / smell (anosmia), ± breathlessness. It is a common acute / subacute cough — confirm with a lateral-flow or PCR test and watch for silent hypoxia (low sats with little distress).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: Besides the ACE inhibitor, what simple reversible factor should always be addressed in a chronic cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Smoking (and vaping / environmental irritants) — smoking cessation both reduces the cough and lowers the risk of the serious causes it can mask.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What does a bovine (non-explosive) cough suggest?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with vocal-cord paralysis — the cough lacks its normal explosive glottic closure. It raises concern for a mediastinal / lung mass compressing the nerve.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is a post-infective (post-viral) cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A subacute cough (3–8 weeks) lingering after a viral URTI, from transient airway hyperresponsiveness and mucus hypersecretion. It is self-limiting — reassure, but exclude pertussis if there are paroxysms.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What causes a barking cough with stridor in a young child?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), usually parainfluenza — a seal-like barking cough, inspiratory stridor and hoarse voice, worse at night. Treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What causes cough, wheeze and feeding difficulty in a young child (under two)?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Bronchiolitis, usually RSV, typically in a child under two (peak 3–6 months) — coryza then a cough with wheeze / fine crackles and poor feeding. Management is supportive (oxygen, feeding support).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is acute bronchitis and how is it managed?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A usually viral, self-limiting inflammation of the large airways causing an acute productive cough with a clear chest / normal CXR. Antibiotics are usually not needed — treat symptomatically.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What suggests cystic fibrosis as a cause of a chronic productive cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A young patient with recurrent infections (Pseudomonas, Staph), copious sputum, steatorrhoea / pancreatic insufficiency, poor growth and infertility. Diagnosed with the sweat test and genetics.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What suggests recurrent aspiration as a cause of cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Coughing during or after swallowing, a neurological deficit (stroke, bulbar palsy, reduced consciousness) and recurrent right-lower-lobe pneumonia. Assess swallow (SALT, videofluoroscopy).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What suggests sarcoidosis in a patient with a dry cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A dry cough and breathlessness in a young adult with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray, erythema nodosum and, sometimes, a raised serum ACE and calcium.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: Which local complications of lung cancer can present alongside a cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Haemoptysis, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy), SVC obstruction (facial / neck swelling), a Pancoast tumour (Horner's, arm pain) and a pleural effusion.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: How is pertussis managed and prevented?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: An early macrolide reduces transmission (limited effect on the cough once paroxysms are established); it is notifiable. Prevention is by vaccination in pregnancy and childhood; infants risk apnoea.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A chronic cough with sputum eosinophilia but normal spirometry and no airway hyperresponsiveness (unlike asthma). It has a raised FeNO and responds well to inhaled corticosteroids.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What history suggests occupational asthma as a cause of cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Cough / wheeze that is worse at work and improves on days off and holidays. Ask about the job and exposures (isocyanates, flour, animals), and confirm with serial peak-flow readings at and away from work.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What does the timing of a cough add to the diagnosis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Morning productive cough → COPD / bronchiectasis (clearing overnight secretions); nocturnal → asthma, GORD or heart failure; only when awake, never in sleep → habit (psychogenic) cough.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What is a habit (psychogenic / tic) cough?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A dry, often honking cough in children / adolescents that is absent during sleep and when distracted, with normal examination and investigations. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What complications can a severe or chronic cough itself cause?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Cough syncope, rib fractures, urinary (stress) incontinence, exhaustion, vomiting, headache and disturbed sleep.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: How do you distinguish haemoptysis from haematemesis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: Haemoptysis is bright red, frothy, alkaline, mixed with sputum and coughed up; haematemesis is dark / coffee-ground, acidic, may contain food, is vomited and is often accompanied by melaena.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.front: What clues suggest an atypical pneumonia such as Legionella?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Cough.back: A dry cough with marked systemic upset, a source (travel, hotel / air-conditioning), hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs and relative bradycardia. Treat with a macrolide or tetracycline.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is haemoptysis and why is it a red-flag symptom?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Coughing up blood from the lungs or airways. It is lung cancer, tuberculosis and pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise, so it warrants prompt assessment and imaging.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: How do you distinguish haemoptysis from haematemesis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Haemoptysis is bright red, frothy, alkaline, mixed with sputum and coughed up; haematemesis is dark / coffee-ground, acidic, may contain food, is vomited and is often accompanied by melaena.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is pseudohaemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Blood that appears to be coughed up but actually arises from the nasopharynx, mouth or gums (or, rarely, Serratia colonisation) — there is no true lower-airway source. Examine the nose, mouth and throat.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: How is massive haemoptysis defined?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Roughly >200 mL of blood in 24 hours (definitions vary), or any bleeding that threatens the airway or causes haemodynamic compromise. It is a life-threatening emergency.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Why does massive haemoptysis kill, and what does that imply for management?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Patients die by asphyxiation (drowning in blood), not exsanguination — so the airway is the priority: protect the airway, give oxygen, and lie the patient with the bleeding side down to protect the good lung.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Outline the emergency management of massive haemoptysis.
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: ABC / resuscitation, protect the airway (consider intubation), bleeding side down, correct any coagulopathy (reverse anticoagulation, platelets / clotting factors), then CT angiography → bronchial artery embolisation (± thoracic surgery).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What are the 'big three' causes of haemoptysis to exclude in an adult?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Lung cancer (smoker >40, weight loss), tuberculosis (night sweats, risk factors) and pulmonary embolism (pleuritic pain, breathlessness, VTE risk).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What features suggest lung cancer as the cause of haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: A smoker or ex-smoker over 40 with a chronic cough, weight loss, a hoarse voice or clubbing. It needs an urgent CT chest, a 2-week-wait referral and bronchoscopy with biopsy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What features suggest tuberculosis as the cause of haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Night sweats, weight loss, fever and risk factors (contacts, immunosuppression / HIV, birth in an endemic area). Confirm with chest X-ray and sputum for acid-fast bacilli / culture.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What features suggest pulmonary embolism as the cause of haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness and hypoxia with VTE risk factors (immobility, surgery, malignancy). Confirm with a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which condition is the commonest cause of recurrent haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Bronchiectasis — recurrent haemoptysis with copious daily purulent sputum and recurrent chest infections; confirmed on high-resolution CT.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is an aspergilloma and how does it present?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: A fungal ball (mycetoma) of Aspergillus that colonises a pre-existing cavity (often old TB) — it can cause recurrent or massive haemoptysis. CXR shows a mass within a cavity with an air crescent.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is a pulmonary-renal syndrome, and which two diagnoses cause it?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: The combination of haemoptysis (diffuse alveolar haemorrhage) and glomerulonephritis (haematuria / AKI). The classic causes are ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA) and anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What are the features of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) causing haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Upper airway disease (sinusitis, saddle-nose, nasal crusting), lung nodules / haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis, with a positive cANCA (anti-PR3).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What are the features of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (haemoptysis) plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies and linear IgG on renal biopsy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: How can mitral stenosis cause haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Raised left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure can rupture dilated bronchial veins. Look for a malar flush and a mid-diastolic murmur; it is a cardiac (not primary lung) cause.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: How can heart failure / pulmonary oedema cause blood in the sputum?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Pulmonary oedema produces pink, frothy sputum from a raised pulmonary capillary pressure, usually with orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea rather than frank haemoptysis.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which drugs / disorders can unmask or worsen haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs, heparin), antiplatelets and bleeding disorders / thrombocytopenia — a coagulopathy can turn a minor airway lesion into significant bleeding. Check clotting and platelets.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is the first-line investigation for haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: A chest X-ray. If it is non-diagnostic (or the bleeding is significant / persistent), proceed to CT chest (CTPA if PE is suspected) and then bronchoscopy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is the role of bronchoscopy in haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: To localise the bleeding site, obtain biopsies / washings, and provide local control (e.g. tamponade, adrenaline, laser). It is especially useful for a central lesion or persistent bleeding.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is the definitive treatment for massive haemoptysis from a localised bronchial source?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Bronchial artery embolisation (interventional radiology) — most massive haemoptysis arises from the high-pressure bronchial arteries. Surgical resection is reserved for failure or a resectable lesion.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which blood tests should be sent in significant haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: FBC, clotting screen, group & save / crossmatch and U&E (renal function); add ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies if a pulmonary-renal syndrome is suspected.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is the commonest overall cause of haemoptysis, and why does it not reassure you?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Acute respiratory-tract infection / acute bronchitis (benign, blood-streaked sputum). It is common, but haemoptysis is only attributed to it once the serious causes (cancer, TB, PE) have been excluded.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is cryptogenic haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Haemoptysis with no cause found after full investigation (chest X-ray, CT and bronchoscopy) — occurring in a substantial minority of cases; most settles, but ongoing surveillance is prudent in smokers.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu), and how can it cause haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: An autosomal-dominant disorder with mucocutaneous telangiectasia, recurrent epistaxis and arteriovenous malformations — a pulmonary AVM can bleed, causing haemoptysis.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What is the role of tranexamic acid in haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: An adjunct (oral, IV or nebulised antifibrinolytic) that can reduce non-massive or bridging haemoptysis while the cause is treated. It is not the first priority in massive bleeding — airway control and bronchial artery embolisation come first — and it does not replace definitive treatment.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What iatrogenic causes of haemoptysis should you consider?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Recent bronchoscopy or lung biopsy, a Swan-Ganz (pulmonary artery) catheter, and anticoagulation — ask about recent procedures and medications.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What causes of haemoptysis are more likely in a returning traveller or immunosuppressed patient?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Tuberculosis (and reactivation), invasive aspergillosis, and parasitic lung disease (e.g. paragonimiasis) — take a travel, contact and immunosuppression history.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which examination findings help localise the cause of haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Clubbing (cancer, bronchiectasis, ILD), focal crackles / consolidation (pneumonia), coarse crackles (bronchiectasis), a malar flush and mid-diastolic murmur (mitral stenosis), and lymphadenopathy / cachexia (cancer).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: What bedside test is essential in any patient with haemoptysis, and why?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: A urine dipstick for blood — haemoptysis plus haematuria suggests a pulmonary-renal syndrome (vasculitis / Goodpasture's), which needs urgent immunology and renal input.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: How does massive haemoptysis differ in priority from the diagnostic work-up of minor haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: In massive haemoptysis, resuscitation and airway / bleeding control come first (side down, correct clotting, embolisation); the search for the underlying cause follows once the patient is stabilised. Minor haemoptysis is worked up electively (CXR → CT ± bronchoscopy).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which lung cancers are most prone to cause haemoptysis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: Central, endobronchial tumours — classically squamous cell carcinoma (and small cell) — and carcinoid tumours (typically central and vascular), because they erode into the airway. Peripheral adenocarcinomas bleed less often.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Which vasculitis antibody pattern fits GPA versus microscopic polyangiitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: GPA is typically cANCA / anti-PR3 positive; microscopic polyangiitis is typically pANCA / anti-MPO positive. Both can cause a pulmonary-renal syndrome with haemoptysis.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.front: Summarise the two decisions that must be made first in any haemoptysis.
signs__RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis.back: (1) Is it truly haemoptysis (not haematemesis or a nasopharyngeal bleed)? and (2) is it massive (an airway emergency)? Only then do you work through the differential to find the source.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is stridor and where does it arise?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A harsh, high-pitched sound from turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway (larynx / trachea). It is a red-flag sign of airway obstruction, not a diagnosis.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: How do you distinguish stridor from wheeze?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Stridor is usually inspiratory and comes from the upper airway (larynx / trachea); wheeze is expiratory and comes from the lower airways (asthma / COPD).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What does the phase of stridor tell you about the level of obstruction?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Inspiratory stridor → supraglottic; expiratory or biphasic stridor → glottic, subglottic or tracheal obstruction.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is the first priority in any patient with stridor?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: The airway, not the diagnosis — assess its severity and be ready to secure it. Call a senior anaesthetist and ENT early if it looks critical.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What signs indicate a critical airway / impending complete obstruction?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Exhaustion, drowsiness, cyanosis, a softening stridor with worsening distress (a tiring airway), drooling and tripod positioning, and inability to speak or swallow.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is the commonest cause of stridor in a child?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), usually caused by parainfluenza virus.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the features and management of croup?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A barking (seal-like) cough, coryza, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, worse at night, in a child who looks relatively well. Treat with a single dose of oral dexamethasone; add nebulised adrenaline if severe.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the features of epiglottitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: An acutely toxic, febrile child who is drooling, sitting forward (tripod), with a muffled 'hot-potato' voice and NO cough. It is a life-threatening airway emergency, classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is the golden rule in suspected epiglottitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Do NOT examine the throat (a tongue depressor can precipitate complete obstruction) and do not lie the child flat or distress them. Keep them calm with a parent, get senior anaesthetics / ENT, and secure the airway in theatre before giving IV antibiotics.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: How do croup and epiglottitis differ?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Croup: gradual, barking cough, coryzal, child looks well-ish. Epiglottitis: rapid, toxic, drooling, no cough, muffled voice — far more dangerous.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the features of an inhaled foreign body causing stridor?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A sudden choking episode in a previously well child, then stridor or a unilateral wheeze / reduced air entry. It often lodges in the right main bronchus and is removed at bronchoscopy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is laryngomalacia?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: The commonest congenital cause of stridor — a floppy supraglottis giving positional inspiratory stridor in an infant (worse when supine / feeding, better prone). It is benign and usually resolves by 18–24 months.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: How is anaphylaxis with stridor managed?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: IM adrenaline immediately (500 micrograms in an adult), high-flow oxygen and removal of the trigger, with IV fluids for hypotension. Let the patient sit up if breathing is the problem (lie flat with legs raised only if hypotensive). Corticosteroids are no longer part of the routine emergency algorithm; antihistamines only relieve residual skin symptoms after stabilisation. Check serial mast-cell tryptase.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is ACE-inhibitor angioedema, and how does it differ from allergic angioedema?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Bradykinin-mediated swelling of the lips, tongue and airway in a patient on an ACE inhibitor — it can start months to years after starting the drug, has no urticaria, and responds poorly to adrenaline / steroids. Stop the ACE inhibitor.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is bacterial tracheitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A toxic child with stridor and thick purulent secretions, usually Staphylococcus aureus, often following a viral illness. It needs airway support and IV antibiotics.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the main adult causes of stridor?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Anaphylaxis / angioedema, a laryngeal or tracheal tumour, post-intubation subglottic stenosis, bilateral vocal-cord palsy, an inhaled foreign body and deep-neck infections.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What features suggest a laryngeal tumour as a cause of stridor?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Progressive stridor with a persistently hoarse voice, in a smoker, with weight loss and sometimes dysphagia or a neck node. Assess with flexible nasendoscopy and biopsy.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: Why can thyroid or neck surgery cause stridor?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve(s): unilateral palsy causes hoarseness, but bilateral palsy causes stridor from cords that cannot abduct.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the signs of an inhalation (airway burn) injury, and what is the key action?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Facial burns, soot in the mouth / nose, singed nasal hairs, a hoarse voice and carbonaceous sputum. Intubate early, before progressive oedema closes the airway.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is the role of nebulised adrenaline in upper-airway obstruction?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: It causes mucosal vasoconstriction that temporarily reduces airway oedema (in croup or post-extubation stridor) — it buys time but is not definitive, and the effect can wear off (rebound).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: Why are corticosteroids given in croup?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: They reduce laryngeal oedema; a single dose of oral dexamethasone (or nebulised budesonide) shortens the illness and is given even in mild croup.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What does a flow-volume loop show in a fixed upper-airway obstruction?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Flattening of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs (a 'box-like' loop) — a variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens the inspiratory limb, an intrathoracic one the expiratory limb.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: How is stable / chronic stridor investigated?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Flexible nasendoscopy / laryngoscopy, CT of the neck and thorax, and a flow-volume loop — done in a controlled setting; avoid provoking manoeuvres in acute stridor.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What are the classic plain-radiograph signs of croup and epiglottitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Croup: the 'steeple sign' (subglottic narrowing) on an AP neck film. Epiglottitis: the 'thumbprint sign' (a swollen epiglottis) on a lateral neck film — but imaging must never delay securing the airway.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: Does stridor at rest or only on exertion matter?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Stridor at rest indicates more severe obstruction (typically >50% narrowing) and a higher risk of decompensation than stridor only on exertion or crying.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: Which vaccine dramatically reduced the incidence of epiglottitis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: The Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine — epiglottitis is now rare in vaccinated children (but still occurs in adults and the unvaccinated).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is a retropharyngeal abscess and how does it present?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A deep-neck-space infection in a child with fever, neck stiffness / hyperextension, drooling and a muffled voice. A lateral neck X-ray shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissue.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is quinsy (peritonsillar abscess)?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A collection beside the tonsil, usually in an adolescent / adult, with trismus, a muffled 'hot-potato' voice, uvular deviation and severe unilateral sore throat. It needs drainage and antibiotics.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What is Ludwig's angina?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular / floor-of-mouth spaces (usually dental in origin) that elevates the tongue and threatens the airway — an airway emergency.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What causes stridor with a thyroid mass?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: A large or retrosternal goitre compressing the trachea — often positional; consider malignancy, and image with CT (with a flow-volume loop).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: Summarise the two questions to answer first in any stridor.
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: (1) Is the airway critical (secure it if so)? and (2) child or adult, acute or progressive? — which narrows the differential once the airway is safe.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.front: What does biphasic stridor with a barking cough after prolonged ventilation suggest?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Stridor.back: Subglottic stenosis — scarring below the cords after prolonged or repeated intubation; it gives a fixed, often biphasic stridor and needs ENT assessment (dilatation / surgery).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What is pleuritic chest pain, and where does it localise?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Sharp chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration, coughing or movement. It localises to the pleura, pericardium or chest wall — not the crushing central pressure of ACS.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: Which serious causes must be excluded first in pleuritic chest pain?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: The killers: pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax (tension is an immediate emergency), then pneumonia and pericarditis — before settling on a musculoskeletal or viral cause.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: Does 'pleuritic' or 'reproducible on palpation' safely exclude a heart attack or aortic dissection?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: No. ACS and aortic dissection can present atypically (especially in diabetics, women and the elderly), so keep them in mind — only settle on a chest-wall cause once the killers are cleared.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What features suggest a pulmonary embolism as the cause of pleuritic pain?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Pleuritic pain + breathlessness ± haemoptysis, with tachycardia and hypoxia and VTE risk factors (surgery, immobility, malignancy, OCP / pregnancy). Signs are often few and the CXR normal.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: How is a suspected pulmonary embolism investigated?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: The two-level Wells score: 'PE likely' → CTPA; 'PE unlikely' → D-dimer (CTPA only if positive). A V/Q scan is an alternative if CTPA is contraindicated (e.g. renal failure, pregnancy).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What ECG changes may be seen in a pulmonary embolism?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Most commonly a sinus tachycardia. The classic (but uncommon) pattern is S1Q3T3, with signs of right heart strain (right axis deviation, RBBB, T-wave inversion in V1–V3).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What are the features of a pneumothorax causing pleuritic pain?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness with a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced breath sounds on the affected side. Typical in a tall, thin young person, in COPD, or after trauma.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What are the signs of a tension pneumothorax, and how is it managed?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Severe respiratory distress with a deviated trachea (away), distended neck veins and hypotension. It is a clinical diagnosis needing immediate needle decompression — do not wait for a chest X-ray.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: Where is emergency needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax performed?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Classically the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (large-bore cannula); many now use the 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. A chest drain then follows.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: How does the management of a secondary (e.g. COPD) pneumothorax differ from a primary one?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: A secondary pneumothorax (underlying lung disease) is more dangerous: patients are usually admitted and treated with a chest drain, whereas small primary pneumothoraces in a well patient may be observed or aspirated.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What features suggest pneumonia as the cause of pleuritic pain?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Fever, a productive cough, focal crackles / bronchial breathing / dullness, a pleural rub, and raised inflammatory markers, with consolidation on the chest X-ray. Score severity with CURB-65.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What are the characteristic features of pericarditis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Sharp pain, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward, often after a viral prodrome, with a pericardial friction rub. It can progress to a pericardial effusion / tamponade.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What are the ECG changes of pericarditis?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Widespread saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation with PR-segment depression. The changes are diffuse, not territorial; the only reciprocal change is PR elevation with ST depression in aVR (± V1) — unlike the territorial reciprocal ST depression of a STEMI.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: How is acute pericarditis treated?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (e.g. ibuprofen) plus colchicine, with rest; treat any underlying cause. Colchicine reduces recurrence.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What is Dressler's syndrome?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: An autoimmune pericarditis occurring weeks after a myocardial infarction (or cardiac surgery) — pleuritic pain, fever, a pericardial rub and a pericardial / pleural effusion.

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: How does a pleural effusion present, and how is the fluid classified?
signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.back: Pleuritic pain (early), breathlessness, stony dullness, reduced expansion and reduced breath sounds. Fluid is classified as transudate vs exudate using Light's criteria (protein and LDH ratios).

signs__RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain.front: What is costochondritis (and Tietze's syndrome)?
