conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Ventilation is a mechanical process: changing thoracic volume alters pressure (Boyle's law — ↑volume → ↓pressure), and air flows down the resulting pressure gradient. Air flows in when alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric, making E wrong.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which statement about intrapleural pressure is correct?
options: It is negative at rest (~−5 cmH₂O), acting as a vacuum holding the lung open
It becomes positive during quiet inspiration
It is always positive at rest
It equals atmospheric pressure at end-expiration
It is generated entirely by surfactant
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: It is negative at rest (~−5 cmH₂O), acting as a vacuum holding the lung open
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Intrapleural pressure is negative at rest (~−5 cmH₂O) — the 'vacuum' holding the lung open against the chest wall; it can turn positive during forced expiration or a tension pneumothorax. It arises from the opposing pulls of inward lung recoil and outward chest-wall spring, not surfactant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Transpulmonary pressure is best defined as:
options: Alveolar minus intrapleural pressure — the distending pressure keeping alveoli open
The pressure inside the alveoli during expiration
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Alveolar minus intrapleural pressure — the distending pressure keeping alveoli open
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Transpulmonary pressure = alveolar − intrapleural pressure. It is the distending pressure that keeps the alveoli open.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A young man is stabbed in the chest and develops a pneumothorax with lung collapse. Which mechanism explains why the affected lung collapses?
options: Surfactant is destroyed by the trauma
Airway resistance rises sharply, trapping air
Air entering the pleural space abolishes the negative intrapleural pressure, so the lung recoils shut
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Air entering the pleural space abolishes the negative intrapleural pressure, so the lung recoils shut
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The negative intrapleural pressure normally holds the lung expanded against the chest wall. Air in the pleural space abolishes this negative pressure, and the lung's elastic recoil pulls it shut.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Regarding the mechanics of a normal breath, which statement is correct?
options: Inspiration is passive and expiration is active at rest
Expiration at rest is passive, driven by elastic recoil
The external intercostals do about two-thirds of the work of inspiration
The diaphragm relaxes and descends during inspiration
Forced expiration relies on the external intercostals
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Expiration at rest is passive, driven by elastic recoil
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: At rest, inspiration is active (diaphragm contracts and descends — the main muscle, ~⅔ of the work — with external intercostals) and expiration is passive, driven by elastic recoil. Forced expiration is active, using internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A breathless patient in the emergency department is visibly using their sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles to breathe. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Increased work of breathing (accessory muscle recruitment)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Increased work of breathing (accessory muscle recruitment)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) are recruited in exertion or distress — their use is the clinical sign of increased work of breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Compliance is defined as the change in volume per unit change in pressure. In which condition would you expect INCREASED compliance?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Emphysema (COPD)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Emphysema increases compliance (too stretchy, poor recoil) because destroyed elastic tissue lets the lungs over-distend with air trapping. Fibrosis, oedema, ARDS and neonatal RDS all reduce compliance (stiff or fluid-filled lung).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A premature neonate develops respiratory distress with stiff lungs and alveolar collapse. Which underlying deficiency is responsible?
options: Deficiency of surfactant, normally produced by type II pneumocytes
Loss of elastic tissue in the alveoli
Increased airway resistance from mucus plugging
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Deficiency of surfactant, normally produced by type II pneumocytes
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes and reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing collapse and increasing compliance. Deficiency in prematurity causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (stiff lungs, alveolar collapse).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: According to Laplace's law as applied to alveoli, why would small alveoli tend to empty into larger ones in the absence of surfactant?
options: Small alveoli have lower surface tension
Radius has no effect on collapsing pressure
Pressure to keep a bubble open ∝ tension / radius, so small alveoli have higher collapsing pressure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Pressure to keep a bubble open ∝ tension / radius, so small alveoli have higher collapsing pressure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: By Laplace's law, the pressure needed to keep a bubble open is proportional to tension/radius. So a smaller radius means a higher collapsing pressure, and small alveoli would empty into large ones. Surfactant lowers surface tension more in small alveoli, stabilising them and equalising pressures.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which statement correctly links airway resistance to disease?
options: Airway resistance is independent of airway radius
Radius dominates resistance; bronchoconstriction, mucus, or narrowing raises resistance and work of breathing
Increased resistance mainly causes an inspiratory flow limitation
Resistance is highest in pulmonary fibrosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Radius dominates resistance; bronchoconstriction, mucus, or narrowing raises resistance and work of breathing
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: As with the vascular Poiseuille r⁴ relationship, radius dominates resistance. Bronchoconstriction, mucus or airway narrowing raises resistance and the work of breathing. In obstructive disease this causes expiratory (not inspiratory) flow limitation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The work of breathing is raised in both fibrosis and asthma, but for different reasons. Which pairing is correct?
options: Fibrosis — high resistive forces; asthma — high elastic forces
Both are due to high elastic forces only
Both are due to high resistive forces only
Fibrosis — high elastic forces (compliance); asthma — high resistive forces (airway resistance)
Neither raises the work of breathing
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Fibrosis — high elastic forces (compliance); asthma — high resistive forces (airway resistance)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Work of breathing overcomes (a) elastic forces (compliance — high in fibrosis) and (b) resistive forces (airway resistance — high in asthma/COPD). It is raised in both disease types but for different reasons.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: In mechanical terms, which best summarises the difference between obstructive and restrictive disease?
options: Obstructive = trouble getting air OUT (↑resistance); restrictive = trouble getting air IN (↓compliance)
Obstructive = trouble getting air IN; restrictive = trouble getting air OUT
Both cause trouble getting air IN
Obstructive is caused by reduced compliance
Restrictive is caused by increased airway resistance
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Obstructive = trouble getting air OUT (↑resistance); restrictive = trouble getting air IN (↓compliance)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Obstructive disease (↑airway resistance ± ↑compliance/air trapping) causes trouble getting air OUT — expiratory limitation. Restrictive disease (↓compliance, stiff lung) causes trouble getting air IN.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does applied PEEP or CPAP improve oxygenation mechanically?
options: By applying positive pressure that keeps alveoli open, counteracting collapse
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: By applying positive pressure that keeps alveoli open, counteracting collapse
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: PEEP/CPAP applies positive pressure that keeps alveoli open, counteracting collapse.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which of the following is a CAPACITY rather than a single volume?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Functional residual capacity
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Volumes are single; capacities are sums of volumes. FRC (= ERV + RV) is a capacity. TV, IRV, ERV and RV are single volumes.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is made up of which components?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ERV + RV
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: FRC = ERV + RV — the air left after a normal expiration (the resting end-expiratory point). TV + IRV = inspiratory capacity; IRV + TV + ERV = vital capacity; VC + RV = total lung capacity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why can spirometry NOT measure residual volume, FRC, or total lung capacity?
options: They are too small to detect
They change too rapidly to record
They all include residual volume — the air that stays behind and cannot be blown out
They are only present in disease
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: They all include residual volume — the air that stays behind and cannot be blown out
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: RV, FRC and TLC all include residual volume, and you cannot blow out the air that stays behind. They require body plethysmography or helium dilution.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which single spirometry value is most useful for separating obstructive from restrictive disease, and what is its normal value?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: FEV1/FVC ratio, normally >0.7 (>70%)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The FEV1/FVC ratio is the single most important value (normally >0.7 / >70%) and separates obstructive from restrictive disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient's spirometry shows FEV1/FVC of 0.58, with increased RV and TLC. Which pattern does this represent?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Obstructive disease with air trapping/hyperinflation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: FEV1/FVC <0.7 (LOW) is the hallmark of obstructive disease, and ↑RV with ↑TLC reflects air trapping/hyperinflation. Restrictive disease would show a preserved/high ratio (≥0.7) and reduced volumes.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which set of spirometry findings is characteristic of RESTRICTIVE disease?
options: FEV1 normal, FVC normal, ratio low
FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 with reduced FVC and reduced all volumes
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 with reduced FVC and reduced all volumes
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In restriction, FEV1 and FVC drop proportionally so the ratio is preserved (≥0.7, normal/high — the hallmark), FVC is reduced, and all volumes fall (small stiff lungs).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Explain the logic for WHY the FEV1/FVC ratio falls in obstruction but is preserved in restriction.
options: Obstruction: FVC drops more than FEV1; restriction: only FEV1 drops
Obstruction: high resistance slows expiration so FEV1 drops more than FVC → ratio falls; restriction: stiff small lungs drop FEV1 and FVC proportionally → ratio preserved
Both drop FEV1 more than FVC
The ratio depends only on residual volume
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Obstruction: high resistance slows expiration so FEV1 drops more than FVC → ratio falls; restriction: stiff small lungs drop FEV1 and FVC proportionally → ratio preserved
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In obstruction, high airway resistance slows expiration so FEV1 falls more than FVC → the ratio drops. In restriction, stiff small lungs reduce FEV1 and FVC proportionally → the ratio is preserved.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which list contains only OBSTRUCTIVE conditions?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: COPD, asthma and bronchiectasis are the obstructive examples. Pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, obesity, kyphoscoliosis and MND are restrictive (the last three chest-wall/neuromuscular).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A 55-year-old smoker has spirometry before and after salbutamol. FEV1 improves by only 4%. Which conclusion best fits?
options: COPD — largely irreversible, fixed airflow limitation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: COPD — largely irreversible, fixed airflow limitation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In COPD there is little improvement after bronchodilator (largely irreversible → fixed airflow limitation). Asthma shows significant reversibility (FEV1 improves ≥12% + 200 mL).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which spirometry response after salbutamol defines significant reversibility, as seen in asthma?
options: FVC unchanged with a fixed ratio
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: FEV1 improves by ≥12% and 200 mL
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Asthma shows reversible obstruction: FEV1 improves significantly (≥12% + 200 mL), reflecting variable/reversible airflow limitation. COPD shows little change (fixed).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: On a flow-volume loop, which shape indicates OBSTRUCTIVE disease?
options: A loop with no expiratory limb
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Scooped-out/concave expiratory limb
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Obstructive disease (COPD/asthma) produces a scooped-out/concave expiratory limb. A tall narrow loop is restrictive; a flattened loop suggests upper airway obstruction.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which flow-volume loop appearance suggests an UPPER airway obstruction?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Flattened loop
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A flattened loop is the appearance of upper airway obstruction. Scooped/concave = obstructive lung disease; tall narrow = restrictive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is most useful for which purpose?
options: Monitoring asthma (diurnal variability, treatment response) as a simple bedside/home measure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Monitoring asthma (diurnal variability, treatment response) as a simple bedside/home measure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: PEFR is the fastest expiratory flow — a simple bedside/home measure used to monitor asthma (diurnal variability and treatment response).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with alveolar haemorrhage has an unexpectedly RAISED transfer factor (TLCO). Why?
options: Extra haemoglobin in the alveoli binds more CO
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Extra haemoglobin in the alveoli binds more CO
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Transfer factor measures CO uptake. In alveolar haemorrhage, extra haemoglobin is present to bind CO, raising TLCO. In emphysema and fibrosis, loss of functioning alveolar-capillary surface lowers it.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does the transfer factor (TLCO) help distinguish causes of lung disease?
options: It is raised in both emphysema and fibrosis
It is always normal in obstructive disease
It is reduced in emphysema and fibrosis, but raised in pulmonary haemorrhage
It cannot be measured in fibrosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: It is reduced in emphysema and fibrosis, but raised in pulmonary haemorrhage
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: TLCO is reduced in emphysema and fibrosis (loss of functioning alveolar-capillary surface) but raised in pulmonary haemorrhage (extra haemoglobin binding CO), helping distinguish causes.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient is diagnosed with COPD. Which spirometry criterion is used, and how is severity graded?
options: FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 with reduced FVC; severity by TLCO
PEFR variability; severity by residual volume
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 (fixed); severity graded by FEV1 % predicted
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 (fixed); severity graded by FEV1 % predicted
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: COPD is diagnosed by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 (fixed obstruction), and severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with progressive breathlessness has spirometry showing FEV1/FVC of 0.82, reduced FVC, reduced TLC and a reduced TLCO. Which condition fits best?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Pulmonary fibrosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis gives a restrictive picture: ↓FVC with a normal/high ratio, ↓TLC and ↓TLCO. The preserved/high ratio excludes obstructive causes; the reduced TLCO reflects loss of alveolar-capillary surface.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with motor neurone disease has a restrictive spirometry pattern despite structurally normal lungs. Why?
options: The 'bellows' (respiratory muscles/chest wall) fail rather than the lung itself
There is air trapping and hyperinflation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The 'bellows' (respiratory muscles/chest wall) fail rather than the lung itself
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Neuromuscular/chest-wall disease gives a restrictive picture with normal lungs — the bellows fail, not the lung.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why is functional residual capacity (FRC) described as the physiologically important 'resting' volume?
options: It is where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall pull
It is the maximum air the lungs can hold
It can be measured directly by spirometry
It is the air moved in a forced breath
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: It is where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall pull
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: FRC is the 'resting' volume — the point where inward lung recoil balances the outward chest-wall pull (the resting end-expiratory point).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which statement best captures the organising principle of gas exchange at the alveolar-capillary membrane?
options: Gases are actively pumped across the membrane using ATP
O₂ and CO₂ are carried across by dedicated membrane transporters
Gases move by passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients, governed by Fick's law
Diffusion depends only on membrane surface area
Gases move against their partial-pressure gradients
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Gases move by passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients, governed by Fick's law
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Gas exchange is transfer of O₂ from alveoli to blood and CO₂ from blood to alveoli by passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients, governed by the membrane's properties (Fick's law).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which best describes the respiratory membrane across which gas exchange occurs?
options: Type II pneumocytes and capillary endothelium, ~5 µm thick
A membrane with small surface area (~7 m²)
A thick fibrous layer optimised for slow, controlled transfer
Alveolar epithelium alone, without basement membranes
Alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocytes) + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium, ~0.5 µm thick
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocytes) + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium, ~0.5 µm thick
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The respiratory membrane is alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocytes) + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium, only ~0.5 µm thick, with a huge surface area (~70 m²), very thin and richly perfused — optimised for rapid gas transfer.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: According to Fick's law of diffusion, the rate of diffusion is proportional to:
options: (surface area × partial-pressure gradient × solubility) / membrane thickness
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: (surface area × partial-pressure gradient × solubility) / membrane thickness
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Fick's law: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × partial-pressure gradient × solubility) / membrane thickness. Thickness is inversely related, so thinner is faster.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient has pulmonary fibrosis. Which Fick's-law factor is the primary cause of their impaired diffusion?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Increased membrane thickness
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Fibrosis (and pulmonary oedema) thickens the membrane, impairing diffusion. Emphysema and pneumonectomy work through reduced surface area instead. Both routes reduce the transfer factor (TLCO).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which pairing of a diffusion-impairing mechanism with its example is CORRECT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Reduced surface area — emphysema (alveolar destruction)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Emphysema causes alveolar destruction → reduced surface area. Fibrosis and pulmonary oedema increase membrane thickness; altitude and hypoventilation reduce the partial-pressure gradient.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: CO₂ is approximately 20× more soluble than O₂. What is the key clinical consequence in diffusion-limited disease such as fibrosis?
options: CO₂ retention occurs before any hypoxia
Both O₂ and CO₂ fail simultaneously
O₂ transfer fails before CO₂ transfer, so hypoxia occurs early with a normal or low CO₂
CO₂ can no longer be cleared at all
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: O₂ transfer fails before CO₂ transfer, so hypoxia occurs early with a normal or low CO₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Because CO₂ is far more soluble, it diffuses readily; in diffusion-limited disease O₂ transfer fails before CO₂ transfer, so hypoxia occurs early and CO₂ retention is late — early lung disease gives hypoxia with a normal or low CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why is CO₂ removal described as ventilation-dependent whereas O₂ uptake is more diffusion-dependent?
options: CO₂ cannot diffuse across the membrane at all
Ventilation has no effect on CO₂ levels
O₂ is more soluble than CO₂
CO₂ is carried only dissolved in plasma
CO₂ diffuses easily, so its clearance depends on how much you breathe, while O₂ uptake depends more on diffusion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CO₂ diffuses easily, so its clearance depends on how much you breathe, while O₂ uptake depends more on diffusion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: CO₂ diffuses easily, so its clearance depends on ventilation (how much air is moved), whereas O₂ uptake is more diffusion-dependent. This asymmetry underlies the two types of respiratory failure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which of these correctly gives the approximate O₂ partial pressures in the alveolus and in arriving venous blood?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Alveolus ~13.3 kPa (100 mmHg); venous ~5.3 kPa
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Alveolar O₂ is ~13.3 kPa (100 mmHg) and arriving venous O₂ is ~5.3 kPa, so O₂ diffuses alveolus → blood down its gradient (leaving arterial ~13 kPa equilibrated).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: For CO₂, which set of approximate partial pressures is correct (alveolus / venous arriving / arterial leaving)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ~5.3 kPa (40 mmHg) / ~6.1 kPa / ~5.3 kPa
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: CO₂: alveolus ~5.3 kPa (40 mmHg), venous arriving ~6.1 kPa, arterial leaving ~5.3 kPa (equilibrated). CO₂ diffuses blood → alveolus down its gradient.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why do diffusion problems often only become apparent under exercise until they are severe?
options: Equilibration is normally complete well before blood leaves the capillary, giving a large reserve
Haemoglobin only binds O₂ during exertion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Equilibration is normally complete well before blood leaves the capillary, giving a large reserve
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Equilibration is normally complete well before the blood leaves the capillary (lots of reserve), so diffusion problems only reveal themselves under stress (exercise) until they become severe.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What does the alveolar-arterial (A–a) gradient tell you?
options: The total oxygen content of arterial blood
Whether the problem is in the lung (gas exchange) or in ventilation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Whether the problem is in the lung (gas exchange) or in ventilation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The A–a gradient is the difference between alveolar O₂ and arterial O₂; it indicates whether the problem lies in the lung (gas exchange — raised gradient) or in ventilation (normal gradient).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient has hypoxaemia with a normal/low CO₂ and a raised A–a gradient. Which category and example fit best?
options: Type 1 respiratory failure caused by pure hypoventilation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Type 1 respiratory failure — pneumonia
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Type 1 failure is hypoxaemia with normal/low CO₂ due to gas exchange failure, with a raised A–a gradient (lung problem — O₂ can't cross). Causes include pneumonia, PE, oedema, fibrosis and early asthma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient has hypoxaemia AND hypercapnia with a normal A–a gradient. What does this indicate?
options: Type 1 respiratory failure from a diffusion defect
Type 2 respiratory failure from ventilatory failure (bellows fail, lung fine)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Type 2 respiratory failure from ventilatory failure (bellows fail, lung fine)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Type 2 failure is hypoxaemia + hypercapnia (high CO₂) from ventilatory failure, with a normal A–a gradient if pure hypoventilation — the bellows fail while the lung is fine. Causes include severe COPD, respiratory muscle weakness, opioid overdose and chest-wall disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: An IV-drug user is found with a reduced respiratory rate, hypoxaemia and a high CO₂. Arterial sampling shows a normal A–a gradient. What is the mechanism?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Hypoventilation (e.g. opioid overdose)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Hypoventilation (opioid overdose, neuromuscular disease) causes hypoxaemia with a normal A–a gradient and responds to O₂. The normal gradient with hypercapnia points to ventilatory failure rather than a lung gas-exchange problem.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which mechanism of hypoxaemia is the commonest, and how does it behave with supplemental O₂?
options: V/Q mismatch — responds to O₂; A–a gradient raised
Low inspired O₂ — A–a gradient raised
Diffusion impairment — does not respond to O₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: V/Q mismatch — responds to O₂; A–a gradient raised
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause; the A–a gradient is raised and it responds to O₂. Examples are pneumonia, PE and COPD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with ARDS remains hypoxic despite high-flow oxygen. Which mechanism does this poor response to O₂ most strongly suggest?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Shunt (blood bypasses ventilated alveoli)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A shunt is the mechanism that responds poorly to O₂ (the hallmark) because blood bypasses ventilated alveoli — a true shunt doesn't correct with supplemental O₂. Examples: consolidation, ARDS, cardiac shunt.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the key point that distinguishes a true shunt from V/Q mismatch?
options: A shunt only occurs at altitude
A shunt has a normal A–a gradient
V/Q mismatch never responds to O₂
A true shunt doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ because the blood never contacts ventilated alveoli
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: A true shunt doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ because the blood never contacts ventilated alveoli
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The shunt point: a true shunt doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ (blood never contacts ventilated alveoli), which distinguishes it from V/Q mismatch (which does respond to O₂).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which mechanism of hypoxaemia has a NORMAL A–a gradient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Hypoventilation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Hypoventilation and low inspired O₂ have a normal A–a gradient; V/Q mismatch, shunt and diffusion impairment all raise it.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A large pulmonary embolism causes hypoxaemia. Which gas-exchange mechanism explains this?
options: Ventilated but not perfused (dead space) → V/Q mismatch
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Ventilated but not perfused (dead space) → V/Q mismatch
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In PE, lung is ventilated but not perfused (dead space) → V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How is the transfer factor (TLCO) best described, and how does it change in emphysema and fibrosis?
options: The bedside measure of diffusion capacity; reduced in both emphysema and fibrosis
A measure of ventilation; raised in both
A measure of airway resistance; normal in both
A measure of haemoglobin; raised in emphysema only
The A–a gradient by another name
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The bedside measure of diffusion capacity; reduced in both emphysema and fibrosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: TLCO is the bedside measure of diffusion capacity. It falls in emphysema (↓surface area → ↓diffusion) and in fibrosis (↑thickness → diffusion defect).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve plots which variables, and what shape results?
options: PaO₂ on the y-axis vs SaO₂ on the x-axis → linear
SaO₂ (%) on the y-axis vs PaO₂ on the x-axis → sigmoid (S-shaped)
Hb concentration vs PaO₂ → flat line
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: SaO₂ (%) on the y-axis vs PaO₂ on the x-axis → sigmoid (S-shaped)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The curve plots O₂ saturation (SaO₂, %) on the y-axis against PaO₂ on the x-axis, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve. The shape lets Hb load fully in the lungs (flat top) and unload readily in tissues (steep middle).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the underlying reason for the sigmoid shape of the dissociation curve?
options: The 1.5% of O₂ dissolved in plasma
Active transport of O₂ into red cells
Cooperative binding — each O₂ that binds makes the next bind more easily
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Cooperative binding — each O₂ that binds makes the next bind more easily
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The sigmoid shape arises from cooperative binding — each O₂ molecule that binds haemoglobin makes the next one bind more easily.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: In what proportions is oxygen carried in the blood, and what is the main clinical implication?
options: ~50% bound to Hb, ~50% dissolved; dissolved O₂ dominates delivery
~98.5% bound to Hb, ~1.5% dissolved; delivery depends mainly on Hb concentration and saturation
~1.5% bound to Hb, ~98.5% dissolved; plasma is the main carrier
All O₂ is dissolved in plasma
All O₂ is bound to Hb with none dissolved
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ~98.5% bound to Hb, ~1.5% dissolved; delivery depends mainly on Hb concentration and saturation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: About 98.5% of O₂ is carried bound to haemoglobin (1 Hb carries 4 O₂) and ~1.5% dissolved in plasma. Delivery depends overwhelmingly on Hb concentration and saturation, not dissolved O₂ — which is why anaemia reduces delivery even with a normal PaO₂/SpO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with severe anaemia has a normal PaO₂ and SpO₂ of 98%. Why can tissue oxygen delivery still be inadequate?
options: The dissolved O₂ fraction is too high
O₂ content is reduced because there is less haemoglobin to carry it, despite normal saturation
PaO₂ must be low for delivery to fall
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: O₂ content is reduced because there is less haemoglobin to carry it, despite normal saturation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Oxygen content ≈ (Hb × SaO₂ × 1.34) + dissolved. In anaemia, SaO₂/PaO₂ can be normal but O₂ content is ↓ because there is less Hb — so delivery is reduced despite a normal SpO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the clinical 'flat top' payoff of the dissociation curve regarding SpO₂ monitoring?
options: SpO₂ can stay >90% until PaO₂ has already fallen substantially, so a falling SpO₂ is a late warning
SpO₂ falls immediately as PaO₂ starts to drop
Giving extra O₂ to a saturated patient greatly increases content
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: SpO₂ can stay >90% until PaO₂ has already fallen substantially, so a falling SpO₂ is a late warning
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Because the upper curve is flat, SpO₂ can stay >90% until PaO₂ has already fallen substantially — a falling SpO₂ is a late warning. Giving extra O₂ to an already-saturated patient adds little (you are on the plateau).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which set of factors causes a RIGHT shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ↑CO₂, acidosis (↑H⁺), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-DPG
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A right shift (lower affinity, unloads O₂ to tissues) is caused by ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺/↓pH (acidosis — Bohr effect), ↑temperature and ↑2,3-DPG. Exercise combines all of these → right shift.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which of the following causes a LEFT shift of the dissociation curve?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Left shift (higher affinity, holds O₂) is caused by ↓CO₂, alkalosis (↓H⁺/↑pH), ↓temperature, ↓2,3-DPG, and by fetal haemoglobin, carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A sprinting athlete's working muscle produces CO₂, acid and heat. What happens to the dissociation curve, and what is the benefit?
options: Left shift → Hb holds O₂ more tightly to protect the muscle
Right shift (Bohr effect) → Hb unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed
No change — the curve is fixed
Left shift → improved loading in tissues
Right shift → reduced O₂ delivery to muscle
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Right shift (Bohr effect) → Hb unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The Bohr effect: actively metabolising tissue produces CO₂, acid and heat → right shift → Hb unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed most (working muscle). 'Right = release.' The lungs do the reverse (blow off CO₂ → left shift → loading).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why is fetal haemoglobin (HbF) advantageous for the fetus?
options: It is right-shifted, releasing O₂ readily to fetal tissues
It carries no O₂, relying on dissolved plasma O₂
It binds CO₂ more tightly than adult Hb
It is left-shifted (higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA), letting the fetus pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta
It has the same affinity as adult HbA
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: It is left-shifted (higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA), letting the fetus pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: HbF is left-shifted (higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA), so the fetus can pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta — fetal Hb grabs the O₂ that maternal Hb releases.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient rescued from a house fire is drowsy but has an SpO₂ of 99% on the pulse oximeter. Why is carbon monoxide poisoning a 'double hit', and why is the SpO₂ misleading?
options: CO binds Hb ~250× more avidly than O₂ forming COHb and left-shifts the curve (less O₂ carried and less released); pulse oximetry can't distinguish COHb from O₂Hb so SpO₂ reads falsely normal
CO reduces Hb concentration and raises 2,3-DPG; SpO₂ reads low
CO right-shifts the curve, improving delivery; SpO₂ is accurate
CO only affects dissolved O₂; SpO₂ is unaffected
CO raises Hb affinity but increases O₂ release to tissues
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CO binds Hb ~250× more avidly than O₂ forming COHb and left-shifts the curve (less O₂ carried and less released); pulse oximetry can't distinguish COHb from O₂Hb so SpO₂ reads falsely normal
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: CO binds Hb with ~250× the affinity of O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and left-shifting the curve, so less O₂ is carried and the remaining O₂ is held more tightly and released less — a double hit. Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb, so SpO₂ reads falsely normal; co-oximetry is needed and treatment is 100% O₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why does stored (transfused) blood initially release oxygen to tissues less well?
options: ↓2,3-DPG → left shift → transfused blood initially releases O₂ less well
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ↓2,3-DPG → left shift → transfused blood initially releases O₂ less well
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Stored blood has ↓2,3-DPG → left shift → it initially releases O₂ less well to tissues.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does altitude/chronic hypoxia adapt oxygen delivery via the dissociation curve?
options: Left shift from alkalosis improves unloading
The curve does not shift at altitude
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ↑2,3-DPG → right shift → better tissue unloading
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In altitude/chronic hypoxia, ↑2,3-DPG causes a right shift → better tissue unloading, an adaptation that improves O₂ delivery.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: In what form is the majority of CO₂ transported in the blood, and what proportion does this represent?
options: Bound to the haem of haemoglobin, ~70%
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: As bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), ~70%
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Most CO₂ (~70%, the majority) is carried as bicarbonate, generated inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺). This conversion is the link to acid-base.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Carbamino compounds carry about 23% of CO₂. Why does this NOT compete with oxygen carriage?
options: Because CO₂ binds the haem group more weakly than O₂
Because it is converted to bicarbonate first
Because carbamino-CO₂ is carried in plasma, not red cells
Because CO₂ binds the globin part of haemoglobin, not the haem
Because O₂ and CO₂ never occupy the red cell simultaneously
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Because CO₂ binds the globin part of haemoglobin, not the haem
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Carbamino compounds form when CO₂ binds the globin part of haemoglobin (not the haem), so CO₂ carriage this way does not compete with O₂ (which binds the haem).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which is the central equation of CO₂ transport and acid-base balance?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The central equation is CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. It links CO₂ transport directly to blood [H⁺]/pH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the 'chloride shift' in red blood cells?
options: Cl⁻ leaves the cell as HCO₃⁻ enters, to maintain neutrality
H⁺ leaves the cell in exchange for Cl⁻
HCO₃⁻ exits the cell into plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ entering, maintaining electrical neutrality
Cl⁻ binds haemoglobin to buffer H⁺
CO₂ is exchanged for Cl⁻ across the membrane
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: HCO₃⁻ exits the cell into plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ entering, maintaining electrical neutrality
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: HCO₃⁻ generated in the red cell exits into plasma (the main transport form) in exchange for Cl⁻ entering — the chloride shift — which maintains electrical neutrality. The H⁺ produced is buffered by haemoglobin inside the cell.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the Haldane effect?
options: Oxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ better than deoxygenated Hb
Acidosis shifts the oxygen curve to the left
Rising CO₂ increases the O₂ affinity of Hb
CO₂ competes with O₂ for the haem group
Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ better than oxygenated Hb (better H⁺ buffer, binds more carbamino-CO₂)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ better than oxygenated Hb (better H⁺ buffer, binds more carbamino-CO₂)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The Haldane effect: deoxygenated Hb carries CO₂ better than oxygenated Hb (deoxy-Hb is a better buffer for H⁺ and binds more carbamino-CO₂). In tissues Hb releases O₂ → picks up CO₂; in lungs Hb binds O₂ → dumps CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How do the Bohr and Haldane effects complement each other?
options: Both promote O₂ loading in the tissues
Bohr: CO₂/acid promotes O₂ unloading in tissues; Haldane: O₂ promotes CO₂ unloading in lungs
Bohr acts only in the lungs; Haldane only in the kidney
Both reduce CO₂ carriage in the tissues
They oppose each other, cancelling out
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Bohr: CO₂/acid promotes O₂ unloading in tissues; Haldane: O₂ promotes CO₂ unloading in lungs
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Bohr = CO₂/acid promotes O₂ unloading (tissues); Haldane = O₂ promotes CO₂ unloading (lungs) — a reciprocal system optimising both gases at both ends.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient hypoventilates and retains CO₂. Using the central equation, what acid-base disturbance results?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Equation shifts right → ↑H⁺ → ↓pH → respiratory acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: ↑CO₂ (hypoventilation/retention) shifts the equation right → ↑H⁺ → ↓pH → respiratory acidosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: An anxious patient hyperventilates. What acid-base change occurs?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: ↓CO₂ → equation shifts left → ↓H⁺ → ↑pH → respiratory alkalosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: ↓CO₂ (hyperventilation) shifts the equation left → ↓H⁺ → ↑pH → respiratory alkalosis. Causes include anxiety, PE and altitude.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why are the lungs described as a rapid pH regulator?
options: They control HCO₃⁻ reabsorption over hours
They buffer H⁺ directly with haemoglobin in plasma
Changing ventilation changes CO₂ and therefore pH within minutes
They alter the chloride shift over days
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Changing ventilation changes CO₂ and therefore pH within minutes
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Changing ventilation changes CO₂ → changes pH within minutes, providing rapid respiratory compensation for metabolic disturbances. (The kidneys control HCO₃⁻ more slowly.)

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How do carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide alter acid-base balance, and where are they used?
options: ↑HCO₃⁻ reabsorption → metabolic alkalosis; used in COPD
Raise CSF pH → suppress the drive to breathe
Increase CO₂ excretion → respiratory alkalosis; used in DKA
Block the chloride shift → respiratory acidosis
Block the enzyme → ↓HCO₃⁻ reabsorption → mild metabolic acidosis; used in altitude sickness and glaucoma
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Block the enzyme → ↓HCO₃⁻ reabsorption → mild metabolic acidosis; used in altitude sickness and glaucoma
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase → ↓HCO₃⁻ reabsorption → mild metabolic acidosis, used in altitude sickness and glaucoma.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis shows deep, rapid, sighing breathing. What is this pattern and its purpose?
options: Cheyne-Stokes breathing from a delayed feedback loop
Kussmaul breathing — respiratory compensation blowing off CO₂ for a metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Kussmaul breathing — respiratory compensation blowing off CO₂ for a metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid, sighing) is the respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis such as DKA — the lungs blow off CO₂ to raise pH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which best describes the organising principle of the control of breathing?
options: Positive feedback with O₂ as the dominant signal
Feedback driven mainly by peripheral O₂ sensing
Purely voluntary control by the cerebral cortex
Negative feedback: chemoreceptors sense gases/pH, the brainstem sets rhythm, ventilation keeps CO₂/pH constant; CO₂ is the dominant signal
A fixed rhythm that does not adapt to demand
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Negative feedback: chemoreceptors sense gases/pH, the brainstem sets rhythm, ventilation keeps CO₂/pH constant; CO₂ is the dominant signal
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The system works by negative feedback — chemoreceptors sense blood gases/pH, the brainstem sets the rhythm, and ventilation adjusts to keep CO₂ (and pH) constant. The dominant signal is CO₂, not O₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which brainstem structure is the basic rhythm generator for breathing, and which fine-tunes it?
options: The medullary respiratory centre (dorsal + ventral groups) generates the rhythm; the pontine centres fine-tune it
Pontine centres generate the rhythm; the medulla fine-tunes it
The cerebral cortex generates the rhythm; the medulla fine-tunes it
The carotid bodies generate the rhythm
The phrenic nerve generates the rhythm
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The medullary respiratory centre (dorsal + ventral groups) generates the rhythm; the pontine centres fine-tune it
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The medullary respiratory centre (dorsal + ventral groups) is the basic rhythm generator; the pontine centres (pneumotaxic + apneustic) fine-tune it, smoothing the inspiration-expiration transition.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Through which nerve does the respiratory output reach the diaphragm?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Phrenic nerve (C3,4,5)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The output travels via the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5 — 'keeps the diaphragm alive') to the diaphragm, plus intercostal nerves to the intercostals.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The central chemoreceptors are the dominant minute-to-minute drivers of ventilation. What do they directly sense?
options: CSF pH, reflecting CO₂ (they respond to CO₂ indirectly via CSF [H⁺])
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CSF pH, reflecting CO₂ (they respond to CO₂ indirectly via CSF [H⁺])
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla sense CSF pH; they respond to CO₂ indirectly via CSF [H⁺] and are the main minute-to-minute driver of ventilation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Explain why CO₂, rather than H⁺, is the effective stimulus at the central chemoreceptors.
options: H⁺ crosses the blood-brain barrier faster than CO₂
CO₂ (not H⁺) crosses the blood-brain barrier easily and forms carbonic acid → H⁺ in the CSF, stimulating the central chemoreceptors
The central chemoreceptors cannot detect H⁺ at all
CO₂ binds the receptors directly without forming acid
H⁺ is buffered entirely in plasma
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CO₂ (not H⁺) crosses the blood-brain barrier easily and forms carbonic acid → H⁺ in the CSF, stimulating the central chemoreceptors
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: CO₂ (not H⁺) crosses the blood-brain barrier easily; in the CSF it forms carbonic acid → H⁺, and the ↑CSF [H⁺] stimulates the central chemoreceptors → ↑ventilation → blows off CO₂. So the central receptors sense CO₂ via CSF pH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The peripheral chemoreceptors mainly sense low PaO₂. At approximately what PaO₂ do they become a significant driver of ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Below ~8 kPa
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid + aortic bodies) respond mainly to low PaO₂ but only kick in significantly when PaO₂ falls below ~8 kPa. O₂ is the backup drive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which statement correctly summarises the normal hierarchy of respiratory drive?
options: CO₂ (via central chemoreceptors) is the dominant drive; O₂ (hypoxic drive, via peripheral chemoreceptors) is the backup
O₂ is the dominant drive; CO₂ is the backup
Both O₂ and CO₂ drive equally at all times
pH is the sole driver of ventilation
Stretch receptors are the dominant drive
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: CO₂ (via central chemoreceptors) is the dominant drive; O₂ (hypoxic drive, via peripheral chemoreceptors) is the backup
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Normally CO₂ (via central chemoreceptors) is the dominant drive — the system defends PaCO₂ tightly. O₂ (hypoxic drive, via peripheral chemoreceptors) is the backup, only significant when PaO₂ falls below ~8 kPa.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with severe COPD who chronically retains CO₂ is given high-flow oxygen and becomes drowsy with a rising CO₂. What is the classic explanation, and what SpO₂ target is recommended in retainers?
options: Oxygen toxicity to the alveoli; target 94–98%
Central chemoreceptors desensitised to chronic high CO₂ → reliance on hypoxic drive, which high-flow O₂ can remove → hypoventilation; target SpO₂ 88–92%
Loss of brainstem rhythm; no oxygen target needed
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Central chemoreceptors desensitised to chronic high CO₂ → reliance on hypoxic drive, which high-flow O₂ can remove → hypoventilation; target SpO₂ 88–92%
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: In chronic CO₂ retainers, central chemoreceptors become desensitised to chronically high CO₂ and the patient relies more on the hypoxic drive. High-flow O₂ can remove that drive → hypoventilation → worsening CO₂ retention, so the target SpO₂ is 88–92% (controlled oxygen, not none). The modern view adds V/Q and Haldane mechanisms, but the clinical rule stands.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The Hering-Breuer reflex is triggered by which input, and what is its effect?
options: Lung stretch receptors → over-inflation inhibits further inspiration (protective, mainly neonates/large breaths)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Lung stretch receptors → over-inflation inhibits further inspiration (protective, mainly neonates/large breaths)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The Hering-Breuer reflex arises from lung stretch receptors: lung over-inflation inhibits further inspiration — a protective reflex, mainly relevant in neonates and with large breaths.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with pulmonary oedema develops rapid shallow breathing. Which receptors are responsible?
options: J receptors (juxtacapillary), stimulated by pulmonary oedema/congestion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: J receptors (juxtacapillary), stimulated by pulmonary oedema/congestion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: J receptors (juxtacapillary) are stimulated by pulmonary oedema/congestion → rapid shallow breathing.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why does ventilation increase at the very start of exercise, before CO₂ has even risen?
options: Because PaO₂ has already fallen below 8 kPa
Because movement (proprioceptors) plus cortical input drive the increased ventilation of exercise
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Because movement (proprioceptors) plus cortical input drive the increased ventilation of exercise
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Proprioceptors (movement) plus cortical input drive the increased ventilation of exercise before CO₂ even rises.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: An elderly patient with heart failure has cyclical crescendo-decrescendo breathing with apnoeas. What is the pattern and a recognised cause?
options: Cheyne-Stokes breathing — heart failure, brainstem lesions or end of life (delayed feedback loop)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Cheyne-Stokes breathing — heart failure, brainstem lesions or end of life (delayed feedback loop)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is cyclical crescendo-decrescendo with apnoeas, caused by heart failure, brainstem lesions or the end of life — a delayed feedback loop.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with a medullary lesion develops chaotically irregular breathing (irregular in both rate and depth). Which pattern is this?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Ataxic (Biot's) — medullary lesion
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Ataxic (Biot's) breathing is chaotically irregular in rate and depth, from a medullary lesion. Contrast apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiratory gasps), which localises to the pons.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does opioid overdose cause Type 2 respiratory failure?
options: Opioids stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors → hyperventilation
Opioids raise CSF pH → increased drive
Opioids block carbonic anhydrase → metabolic acidosis
Opioids suppress the brainstem respiratory centre → ↓rate → CO₂ retention → Type 2 failure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Opioids suppress the brainstem respiratory centre → ↓rate → CO₂ retention → Type 2 failure
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Opioids suppress the brainstem respiratory centre → reduced rate → CO₂ retention → Type 2 respiratory failure (hypoxaemia + hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does central sleep apnoea differ mechanistically from obstructive sleep apnoea?
options: Central = airway collapse; obstructive = loss of drive
Central = loss of brainstem drive; obstructive = a mechanical problem
Both are caused by loss of drive
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Central = loss of brainstem drive; obstructive = a mechanical problem
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Central sleep apnoea is a loss of brainstem drive, whereas obstructive sleep apnoea is a mechanical problem.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A healthy volunteer tries to hold their breath indefinitely but is eventually forced to breathe. Why?
options: Falling O₂ alone forces the breath immediately
Rising CO₂ overrides voluntary cortical control
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Rising CO₂ overrides voluntary cortical control
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The cortex can override breathing voluntarily, but the brainstem reasserts control: rising CO₂ overrides voluntary control, so you cannot hold your breath to death.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: At altitude, hypoxia drives a change in breathing. What is the sequence and resulting acid-base state?
options: Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptor drive → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis
Hypoxia → central chemoreceptor drive → hypoventilation → respiratory acidosis
Hypoxia → J receptor stimulation → metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptor drive → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: At altitude, hypoxia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the ideal V/Q ratio for efficient gas exchange, and what do the two extremes represent?
options: V/Q ≈ 0; dead space and shunt are identical
V/Q ≈ ∞; the extremes are diffusion and hypoventilation
V/Q ≈ 1 (ventilation matched to perfusion); the extremes are dead space (V/Q → ∞) and shunt (V/Q → 0)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: V/Q ≈ 1 (ventilation matched to perfusion); the extremes are dead space (V/Q → ∞) and shunt (V/Q → 0)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The ideal is V/Q ≈ 1 (ventilation matched to perfusion). Dead space is ventilation without perfusion (V/Q → ∞) and shunt is perfusion without ventilation (V/Q → 0). Most lung disease causes hypoxaemia through V/Q mismatch.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What are the approximate resting values of ventilation and perfusion, and the overall V/Q ratio?
options: V ~4 L/min, Q ~5 L/min (cardiac output), V/Q ~0.8 overall
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: V ~4 L/min, Q ~5 L/min (cardiac output), V/Q ~0.8 overall
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Ventilation is ~4 L/min at rest; perfusion is ~5 L/min (= cardiac output); the overall V/Q ≈ 0.8 (close to 1). Matching matters more than the absolute values.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which description correctly matches DEAD SPACE?
options: Low V/Q; perfusion without ventilation; 'wasted perfusion'; classic cause pneumonia
High V/Q; ventilation without perfusion; 'wasted ventilation'; classic cause pulmonary embolism
V/Q ≈ 1; balanced exchange; classic cause ARDS
Low V/Q; ventilation without perfusion; classic cause atelectasis
High V/Q; perfusion without ventilation; classic cause consolidation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: High V/Q; ventilation without perfusion; 'wasted ventilation'; classic cause pulmonary embolism
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Dead space = high V/Q (→ ∞), ventilation without perfusion ('wasted ventilation'), classically caused by pulmonary embolism (clot blocks perfusion). It corrects with O₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which description correctly matches SHUNT?
options: High V/Q; ventilation without perfusion; corrects with O₂
Low V/Q; classic cause pulmonary embolism; corrects with O₂
Low V/Q (→ 0); perfusion without ventilation; 'wasted perfusion'; classically consolidation/collapse; does NOT correct with O₂
High V/Q; classic cause pneumonia; does not correct with O₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Low V/Q (→ 0); perfusion without ventilation; 'wasted perfusion'; classically consolidation/collapse; does NOT correct with O₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Shunt = low V/Q (→ 0), perfusion without ventilation ('wasted perfusion'), classically consolidation/collapse (pneumonia, ARDS, atelectasis). It does NOT correct with O₂ because blood never contacts ventilated alveoli.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with severe pneumonia remains hypoxic despite high-flow oxygen. What is the 'shunt point' that explains this?
options: A true shunt does not correct with supplemental O₂ because the shunted blood never meets ventilated alveoli, so added O₂ cannot reach it
The oxygen dose was too low
Shunt always causes hypercapnia that oxygen cannot fix
The A–a gradient is normal in a shunt
Oxygen worsens the shunt by causing vasoconstriction
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: A true shunt does not correct with supplemental O₂ because the shunted blood never meets ventilated alveoli, so added O₂ cannot reach it
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A true shunt is the one cause of hypoxaemia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen — the shunted blood never meets ventilated alveoli, so O₂ added to the alveoli cannot reach it. This distinguishes shunt from V/Q mismatch and diffusion defects, which do respond to O₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which components sum to give physiological dead space?
options: Anatomical (conducting airways, ~150 mL) + alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g. PE)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Anatomical (conducting airways, ~150 mL) + alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g. PE)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Physiological dead space = anatomical (conducting airways — trachea/bronchi, ~150 mL, never reach alveoli) + alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g. PE).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: In a normal upright lung, how do V/Q and its net effect differ between apex and base?
options: Apex low V/Q (shunt-like); base high V/Q (dead-space-like)
Base high V/Q because gravity reduces its perfusion
Apex and base both have V/Q ~1
Apex high V/Q because perfusion exceeds ventilation there
Apex high V/Q ~3 (over-ventilated, dead-space-like); base low V/Q ~0.6 (over-perfused, shunt-like)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Apex high V/Q ~3 (over-ventilated, dead-space-like); base low V/Q ~0.6 (over-perfused, shunt-like)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: At the apex, V/Q is high (~3) — relatively over-ventilated (dead-space-like); at the base, V/Q is low (~0.6) — relatively over-perfused (shunt-like). Both V and Q increase down the lung, but perfusion increases more because gravity pulls blood to the base.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why does tuberculosis favour the lung apex?
options: The apex has low V/Q and low O₂ tension
The apex has high V/Q and high O₂ tension, with relatively poor blood/immune cell delivery
The apex is the most perfused region
Gravity concentrates bacteria at the base
The base has higher O₂ tension favouring bacterial killing
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The apex has high V/Q and high O₂ tension, with relatively poor blood/immune cell delivery
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Regional V/Q variation explains disease distribution: TB favours the apex (high O₂, high V/Q, relatively poor blood/immune cell delivery).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How does the pulmonary circulation respond to alveolar hypoxia, and how does this differ from the systemic circulation?
options: It vasodilates, like the systemic circulation
It vasoconstricts, the same as the systemic circulation
It does not respond to hypoxia
It vasoconstricts (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), the opposite of the systemic circulation which vasodilates
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: It vasoconstricts (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), the opposite of the systemic circulation which vasodilates
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Unlike the systemic circulation (where hypoxia causes vasodilation), the pulmonary circulation responds to alveolar hypoxia with vasoconstriction — hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the purpose of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV)?
options: To divert blood away from poorly-ventilated (low-V/Q) alveoli toward well-ventilated ones, improving V/Q matching
To increase blood flow to poorly-ventilated alveoli
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: To divert blood away from poorly-ventilated (low-V/Q) alveoli toward well-ventilated ones, improving V/Q matching
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: HPV diverts blood away from poorly-ventilated (low-V/Q) alveoli toward well-ventilated ones → improves V/Q matching → optimises oxygenation. It is the lung's mechanism to minimise shunt.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with long-standing COPD develops right heart strain. Which V/Q-related sequence explains this cor pulmonale?
options: Chronic hypoxia → systemic vasodilation → high-output failure
Chronic hypoxia → left heart failure → pulmonary oedema
Chronic global hypoxia → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart strain
Acute shunt → immediate right heart failure
Dead space → reduced pulmonary pressure → right heart dilatation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Chronic global hypoxia → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart strain
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Chronic global hypoxia (e.g. COPD, altitude) → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart strain (cor pulmonale).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Using the oxygen-dissociation curve, why can the lung not fully compensate for V/Q mismatch?
options: High-V/Q areas can load unlimited extra O₂
Low-V/Q areas load extra O₂ to compensate
The curve is linear, so compensation is complete
High-V/Q areas are already on the flat plateau and cannot load extra O₂ to make up for low-V/Q areas, while low-V/Q areas drop steeply → net hypoxaemia
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: High-V/Q areas are already on the flat plateau and cannot load extra O₂ to make up for low-V/Q areas, while low-V/Q areas drop steeply → net hypoxaemia
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: High-V/Q areas are already on the flat plateau (cannot load extra O₂ to compensate for low-V/Q areas), but low-V/Q areas drop steeply on the curve → the net effect is hypoxaemia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why does V/Q mismatch tend to cause Type 1 rather than Type 2 respiratory failure?
options: Because O₂ is more soluble than CO₂
Because CO₂ is less affected (more soluble, and ventilation can compensate), so hypoxaemia occurs with a normal/low CO₂
Because CO₂ always accumulates in V/Q mismatch
Because the A–a gradient is normal
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Because CO₂ is less affected (more soluble, and ventilation can compensate), so hypoxaemia occurs with a normal/low CO₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: CO₂ is less affected (more soluble, and ventilation can compensate), so V/Q mismatch tends to cause Type 1 failure — hypoxaemia with normal/low CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with a large pulmonary embolism is hypoxic with a low CO₂. Which V/Q abnormality is responsible?
options: Diffusion impairment from a thickened membrane
Dead space (ventilated, not perfused) → V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia; CO₂ usually normal/low
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Dead space (ventilated, not perfused) → V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia; CO₂ usually normal/low
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A clot causes dead space; the resulting hypoxaemia is driven by V/Q redistribution to lower-V/Q units, with CO₂ usually normal/low.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: The body maintains a tight blood pH range. What is that range, and what are the three lines of defence in order of speed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: 7.35–7.45; buffers (instant), lungs (minutes), kidneys (hours-days)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Normal pH is 7.35–7.45. It is defended by buffers (instant), the lungs (minutes), and the kidneys (hours-days).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: According to the organising principle, blood pH is set by which ratio, and who controls each part?
options: HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control CO₂, the kidneys control HCO₃⁻
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control CO₂, the kidneys control HCO₃⁻
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: pH is set by the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory): lungs control CO₂, kidneys control HCO₃⁻. Every disorder is a problem with one, ± compensation by the other.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which line of defence is the only route to excrete fixed (non-volatile) acid?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The kidneys
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The kidneys respond slowly but powerfully adjust HCO₃⁻ and are the only route to excrete fixed acid (excrete H⁺ / reabsorb + generate HCO₃⁻). The lungs only adjust the CO₂/respiratory component.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Which correctly pairs a primary acid-base disorder with its primary change and pH direction?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Metabolic acidosis — ↓HCO₃⁻, pH ↓
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Metabolic acidosis = ↓HCO₃⁻ with pH ↓ (causes: DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea). Respiratory acidosis is ↑CO₂/pH↓; respiratory alkalosis is ↓CO₂/pH↑; metabolic alkalosis is ↑HCO₃⁻/pH↑.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient who has been vomiting for several days presents with a high pH and raised HCO₃⁻. What is the disorder?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Metabolic alkalosis (loss of gastric H⁺)
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis (↑HCO₃⁻, pH ↑) through loss of gastric H⁺. Other causes of metabolic alkalosis include diuretics and hyperaldosteronism.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: State the naming logic for acid-base disorders.
options: 'Respiratory' = the CO₂ (lung) problem; 'metabolic' = the HCO₃⁻ problem (everything else); 'acidosis/alkalosis' = the direction of pH
'Metabolic' refers only to the kidneys' handling of CO₂
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: 'Respiratory' = the CO₂ (lung) problem; 'metabolic' = the HCO₃⁻ problem (everything else); 'acidosis/alkalosis' = the direction of pH
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: 'Respiratory' = the problem is CO₂ (the lung); 'metabolic' = the problem is HCO₃⁻ (everything else); 'acidosis/alkalosis' = the direction of pH.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the key principle of compensation in acid-base disorders?
options: The compensating system overcorrects the pH past normal
Compensation always fully normalises the pH
The other system compensates to pull pH back toward normal but never fully overcorrects
Only the primary system can restore pH
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: The other system compensates to pull pH back toward normal but never fully overcorrects
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: If one system causes the problem, the other compensates to pull pH back toward normal — but never fully overcorrects (compensation does not overshoot).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: How is a metabolic acidosis compensated, and how quickly?
options: Renal retention of HCO₃⁻ over days
Renal excretion of HCO₃⁻ over days
Respiratory — hyperventilate to blow off CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing in DKA) — fast
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Respiratory — hyperventilate to blow off CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing in DKA) — fast
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Metabolic acidosis is compensated by the respiratory system — hyperventilating to blow off CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing in DKA), which is fast (minutes).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with chronic COPD has a respiratory acidosis. Why is their HCO₃⁻ raised, and what does this tell you?
options: The raised HCO₃⁻ is the primary problem, indicating metabolic alkalosis
Renal compensation has occurred over days (retaining HCO₃⁻); the raised HCO₃⁻ marks the disorder as chronic
The kidney compensates within minutes, so this must be acute
The lungs raised the HCO₃⁻ directly
A raised HCO₃⁻ means there is no compensation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Renal compensation has occurred over days (retaining HCO₃⁻); the raised HCO₃⁻ marks the disorder as chronic
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: The kidney takes days to compensate, so a chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD) has a raised HCO₃⁻ (renal compensation has happened), whereas an acute one does not — the HCO₃⁻ tells you the chronicity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: Why do metabolic disturbances get rapid compensation but respiratory disturbances take days?
options: Renal compensation is fast; respiratory is slow
Respiratory compensation is fast (minutes) and renal compensation is slow (days), so metabolic problems get quick respiratory compensation while respiratory problems await renal compensation
Buffers provide all compensation over days
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Respiratory compensation is fast (minutes) and renal compensation is slow (days), so metabolic problems get quick respiratory compensation while respiratory problems await renal compensation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Respiratory compensation is fast (minutes); renal compensation is slow (days). So metabolic problems get quick respiratory compensation, but respiratory problems take days for renal compensation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: On an ABG, CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are moving in OPPOSITE directions relative to pH. What does the 'matching' rule suggest?
options: A single disorder with appropriate compensation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: A mixed disorder
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: If CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ move in opposite directions relative to pH → think a mixed disorder. If they move together (one primary, one compensating) → single disorder with compensation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: What is the anion gap equation, and what does it subdivide?
options: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); separates the causes of metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); separates the causes of metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Anion gap = (Na⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) — it separates the causes of metabolic acidosis into raised-gap and normal-gap.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient has a metabolic acidosis with a RAISED anion gap. Which cause fits, and what is the mnemonic?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Ketones in DKA (added acid); 'MUDPILES'
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: A raised anion gap is caused by added acid — lactate, ketones (DKA), urate (renal failure), toxins (methanol, salicylate) — mnemonic 'MUDPILES'. Normal-gap (hyperchloraemic) causes are HCO₃⁻ loss (diarrhoea, RTA, Addison's).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A child with prolonged diarrhoea has a metabolic acidosis. What type of anion gap is expected and why?
options: Raised anion gap from added acid
Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) from HCO₃⁻ loss
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) from HCO₃⁻ loss
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Diarrhoea causes a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis through HCO₃⁻ loss.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A patient with salicylate poisoning has an ABG showing an early respiratory alkalosis followed by a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. How is this classified?
options: A single respiratory alkalosis with compensation
A mixed disorder — early respiratory alkalosis + later high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: A mixed disorder — early respiratory alkalosis + later high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Salicylate poisoning is a mixed disorder — early respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation) plus later high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.question: A tiring patient with acute severe asthma has a respiratory rate of 30 and shallow breaths of around 250 mL. Their minute ventilation is unchanged from an hour ago, but the PaCO₂ has risen from 3.2 kPa to 4.9 kPa. What best explains this?
options: The bronchospasm has resolved and CO₂ is normalising appropriately
Dead space consumes a larger fraction of each shallow breath, so alveolar ventilation has fallen despite an unchanged minute ventilation
Increased CO₂ production from respiratory muscle work is the sole explanation
A right shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve has increased CO₂ carriage
The rising PaCO₂ reflects improved V/Q matching
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.answer: Dead space consumes a larger fraction of each shallow breath, so alveolar ventilation has fallen despite an unchanged minute ventilation
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Foundations of.explanation: Alveolar ventilation is (tidal volume − dead space) × rate, and dead space is fixed at around 150 mL. At 250 mL per breath, 150 mL of every breath is wasted, so alveolar ventilation is only (250 − 150) × 30 = 3 L/min despite a minute ventilation of 7.5 L/min. PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation, so it rises.
